sum: Queries, keys and values from first principles: one attention step worked by hand for three tokens, why scores are divided by √d_k, the causal mask, multi-head attention, the n² cost, and what attention heads actually learn.
prereq: lm1
Text becomes a sequence of token IDs, and each ID is turned into a vector by looking up a row of the embedding table; attention operates on those vectors.
dl7

Recurrent encoder–decoders squeezed a whole sentence into one fixed vector; Bahdanau attention let the decoder take a weighted average over all encoder states instead, with weights from a softmax over scores.
ml5
Softmax turns a vector of scores into positive weights that sum to 1, exaggerating the gaps between scores; cross-entropy trains those probabilities against the right answer.
dl3
A gradient that passes through a saturated function (one whose slope is near zero) almost vanishes, which stalls learning in everything before it.
why:
Read this sentence: "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big." What was too big? You know immediately: the trophy. Change one word, "because it was too small", and "it" now means the suitcase. To understand "it", you had to look back at other words, decide which ones were relevant, and pull their meaning into your reading of "it". Every word in a sentence is like this to some degree: "bank" means different things next to "river" and "loan", and a verb's meaning depends on its subject several words away.

Before 2017 the dominant language models were recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which read text one token at a time and carried a single running summary vector forward (dl7 covers them). They had two problems. Information from far back had to survive being squeezed through hundreds of summary updates, so long-range links were weak. And because step 500 needed the result of step 499, training could not use the thousands of parallel arithmetic units of a GPU; it crawled along the sequence. Researchers had already found a patch, attention: let the model, at each step, look directly back at all earlier positions and take a weighted average of what it finds, with the weights decided by how relevant each position is.

In 2017 Vaswani and colleagues at Google asked what happens if you keep the attention and throw the recurrence away. The answer, the transformer, trained faster and translated better, and every large language model since is built on it. If you work with LLMs, self-attention is the operation you will be asked to explain, to compute by hand, to size in memory and to debug. It is also the source of the quadratic cost that limits context length, and of the KV cache that dominates inference memory.

This lesson builds self-attention from scratch: the idea of a soft lookup, queries, keys and values, the formula, one complete computation for three tokens with 2-dimensional vectors done by hand, why the scores are divided by √d_k, the causal mask that makes training parallel, multi-head attention, the cost, and what trained heads are found to do. The lab implements it in NumPy and checks it against PyTorch.
primer:
A soft lookup table

Think of a Python dictionary. You give it a key, it finds the exactly matching entry and returns that entry's value. Attention is a soft version of this. You give it a query vector. Instead of finding one exact match, it compares the query with every stored key vector, scores how similar each is, turns the scores into weights that sum to 1, and returns a weighted average of all the stored value vectors. A key that matches well contributes a lot of its value; a key that matches badly contributes almost nothing. Because everything is made of weighted sums, the whole lookup is differentiable, so the model can learn what to ask for and what to advertise by gradient descent.

In self-attention, the queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence of tokens. Every token produces all three, from its own current vector, using three learned matrices: the query says "what kind of information am I looking for?", the key says "what kind of information do I have, for others searching?", and the value is "what I will hand over if someone attends to me". Then every token runs the soft lookup against all tokens (in a language model, all earlier tokens and itself). The result is a new vector per token that mixes in information from the tokens most relevant to it.

The analogy, and where it breaks

Picture a conference where everyone wears a badge describing their expertise (the key) and carries notes they will share (the value). You walk in with a question (the query), glance at every badge, and spend your time with people in proportion to how well their badge matches your question, coming away with a blend of their notes. Everyone does this at once. The analogy breaks in two useful ways. First, the "badge" and the "notes" are learned transformations of the same person, not separate things they bring. Second, the room has no seating plan: nothing in the lookup itself knows who arrived first, which is why transformers need separate positional information (lm4).

The whole thing in one line

Stack the n tokens' queries as rows of a matrix Q, keys as rows of K and values as rows of V. Then

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q Kᵀ / √d_k ) V

Read it from the inside out. Q Kᵀ computes every query's dot product with every key: an n × n table of similarity scores. Dividing by √d_k, where d_k is the length of the query and key vectors, keeps the scores at a sensible size (section 5 of the body explains exactly why). The softmax, applied to each row, turns each query's scores into weights that are positive and sum to 1. Multiplying by V replaces each row of weights by the weighted average of the value vectors. Everything else in this lesson is detail around this line.

That is the correct mental model: a learned, content-based, weighted average over the sequence, computed for every position at once.
body:
1. The vectors attention starts from

Attention operates on one vector per token. In the first layer of a language model these are the token embeddings from lm1 (plus positional information, which lm4 covers; ignore it for now). In later layers they are the outputs of the previous layer. Each vector has the model's width, d_model: 512 in the original transformer, 4,096 in a typical 7-billion-parameter model. We write the n token vectors as the rows of a matrix X of shape n × d_model. Nothing about attention depends on what the vectors "mean"; it is a general operation that lets rows of X exchange information.

2. Three projections: query, key, value

A single vector per token cannot play three roles well at once. What a token is looking for ("I am a pronoun; I need my antecedent") is different from what it advertises ("I am a singular noun, an animal") and different again from the information it should pass along when chosen. So attention learns three weight matrices, W_Q and W_K of shape d_model × d_k, and W_V of shape d_model × d_v, and computes for every token

q = x W_Q      (query, length d_k)
k = x W_K      (key,   length d_k)
v = x W_V      (value, length d_v)

or, for all tokens at once, Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V. These are ordinary matrix multiplications, and the three matrices are the attention layer's learned parameters (along with an output projection, section 7). Queries and keys must have the same length d_k because they will be dotted together; values can in principle have a different length, though in practice d_v = d_k.

3. Scores, weights, output

The score of query i against key j is their dot product, q_i · k_j: the sum of element-wise products, which is large and positive when the two vectors point in a similar direction. For every pair of positions, that is the matrix product QKᵀ, of shape n × n: row i holds query i's scores against every key. Each score is divided by √d_k (section 5). Then, for each row separately, the softmax turns scores s_1 … s_n into weights

w_j = exp(s_j) / Σ_m exp(s_m)

which are positive and sum to 1, with larger scores getting exponentially more weight. Finally the output for position i is the weighted average of the values, o_i = Σ_j w_ij v_j, which for all positions at once is the matrix product of the n × n weight matrix with V. That is the whole formula: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V.

4. One complete attention step by hand

Take a three-token sequence, "the cat sat", with toy 2-dimensional vectors (d_model = d_k = 2) so the arithmetic fits on paper:

x₁ ("the") = [1, 0]      W_Q = [[1, 0],      W_K = [[1, 1],      W_V = [[1, 0],
x₂ ("cat") = [0, 1]             [1, 1]]             [0, 1]]             [0, 2]]
x₃ ("sat") = [1, 1]

Project. A row vector times a matrix: q₁ = [1, 0]W_Q = first row of W_Q = [1, 0]; q₂ = second row = [1, 1]; q₃ = sum of both rows = [2, 1]. Likewise k₁ = [1, 1], k₂ = [0, 1], k₃ = [1, 2], and v₁ = [1, 0], v₂ = [0, 2], v₃ = [1, 2].

Score. Every query against every key. For the third token, q₃ = [2, 1]: q₃·k₁ = 2·1 + 1·1 = 3; q₃·k₂ = 2·0 + 1·1 = 1; q₃·k₃ = 2·1 + 1·2 = 4. The full matrix QKᵀ is

          k₁   k₂   k₃
q₁  [     1    0    1 ]
q₂  [     2    1    3 ]
q₃  [     3    1    4 ]

Scale. d_k = 2, so divide by √2 ≈ 1.414. Row 3 becomes 2.121, 0.707, 2.828.

Mask. In a language model, a token may not look at tokens after it (section 6). So in row 1, the scores for k₂ and k₃ are replaced by −∞, and in row 2 the score for k₃ is. Row 3 is untouched: "sat" may look at all three.

Softmax. Row 3: exp(2.121) = 8.342, exp(0.707) = 2.028, exp(2.828) = 16.919; the sum is 27.289; the weights are 8.342/27.289 = 0.306, 2.028/27.289 = 0.074 and 16.919/27.289 = 0.620. Row 2 has only two allowed scores, 1.414 and 0.707: exp gives 4.113 and 2.028, sum 6.141, weights 0.670 and 0.330. Row 1 has a single allowed score, so its weight is 1: the first token can only attend to itself.

Weighted sum. Output for "sat": 0.306·[1, 0] + 0.074·[0, 2] + 0.620·[1, 2] = [0.306 + 0.620, 0.148 + 1.240] = [0.926, 1.389]. For "cat": 0.670·[1, 0] + 0.330·[0, 2] = [0.670, 0.660]. For "the": [1, 0], its own value. Each token now carries a mixture of information from the tokens its query matched; with trained weights, the mixture would be the context it needs.

5. Why divide by √d_k

The scaling factor has an exact justification, given in a footnote of the original paper. Suppose, as at initialisation, the components of a query and a key are independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product is a sum of d_k products, each with mean 0 and variance 1, so the sum has mean 0 and variance d_k, and standard deviation √d_k. With d_k = 64 the raw scores typically range over about ±8 and beyond; with d_k = 512, over about ±23.

Softmax is very sensitive to the spread of its inputs. If one score exceeds the others by 10, its weight is e¹⁰ ≈ 22,000 times larger, so the output is effectively one-hot: the query attends to a single key. A one-hot softmax is saturated: small changes to the scores barely change the output, so the gradient flowing back through it is close to zero (the same failure as a saturated sigmoid in dl3). The lab measures this: with 8 keys and unit-variance components, the largest weight averages 0.53 at d_k = 4, 0.88 at d_k = 64 and 0.96 at d_k = 512 without scaling, but stays near 0.35-0.37 at every d_k with scaling. Dividing by √d_k restores unit standard deviation regardless of head size, so the softmax starts training in its responsive range and the model can learn sharper patterns where it needs them.

6. The causal mask and parallel training

A decoder-only language model, the GPT design used by nearly all chat LLMs, is trained to predict each token from the tokens before it. If position t could attend to position t + 1, it could simply read the answer. The causal mask prevents this: before the softmax, every score where the key's position is after the query's is set to −∞, and exp(−∞) = 0, so those weights are exactly zero. The weight matrix becomes lower-triangular, as in the figure.

The mask is what makes training efficient. A single forward pass over a 2,048-token training sequence produces, at every position, a prediction of the next token that used only legitimate context, so one pass yields 2,048 training examples, all computed in parallel as large matrix multiplications. An RNN would need 2,048 sequential steps for the same thing. At generation time the model produces one token at a time anyway, and future tokens do not exist yet; the new token's query attends over the keys and values of all previous tokens, which are stored rather than recomputed (the KV cache, lm5). Encoder models such as BERT, which read a whole text to classify or embed it, use no causal mask: every token sees every other. A padding mask, applied the same way, stops tokens attending to the padding added to make sequences in a batch the same length.

7. Multi-head attention

A single attention computation gives each query one set of weights, so one head must average every relationship the token cares about into one distribution. "Sat" might need its subject ("cat"), the previous word, and the tense of an earlier verb, at the same time. Multi-head attention runs h attention computations in parallel, each with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V projecting to a smaller size d_k = d_model / h, so each head can learn a different pattern. The h outputs, each of length d_k, are concatenated back to length d_model and multiplied by an output matrix W_O (d_model × d_model) that mixes them.

In the original transformer, d_model = 512 and h = 8, so each head has d_k = d_v = 64. Because the heads split the width rather than copy it, the projection matrices together are still d_model × d_model each, and the attention layer has 4·d_model² weights (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O), about 1 million at d_model = 512 and 67 million at d_model = 4,096. In code, the "split into heads" step is just a reshape of the n × d_model projection into h × n × d_k, which is why multi-head attention is no more expensive than single-head attention of the same width.

8. Self-attention versus cross-attention

Everything above is self-attention: Q, K and V are all computed from the same sequence. The original transformer was an encoder–decoder for translation. Its decoder also had cross-attention layers, in which the queries come from the target sentence being generated and the keys and values come from the encoder's output for the source sentence, so each target word can look up the relevant source words. Decoder-only LLMs dropped the encoder and use only causal self-attention: the "source" (your prompt) is simply the beginning of the same sequence. Cross-attention survives in some multimodal and speech models, where text queries look up image or audio features.

9. What it costs

For one head with n tokens, the score matrix QKᵀ needs n² dot products of length d_k, and the weighted sum another n² × d_v multiply-adds: O(n²·d) arithmetic for the layer, and O(n²) memory if the score matrix is stored. At 8,192 tokens, one head's score matrix in 16-bit floating point (2 bytes per number) is 8,192² × 2 bytes = 128 MiB; at 32,768 tokens, 2 GiB, per head, per layer. A naive implementation writes this matrix to GPU memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the weights, and reads them again to multiply by V, so it is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic (gpu2 explains this "memory-bound" regime). FlashAttention (gpu7) computes exactly the same result in tiles that stay in fast on-chip memory, using a running maximum and sum so the softmax can be computed in pieces, and never stores the full matrix.

The quadratic term is not the whole story. Per token, the four projections cost 4·d_model² multiply-adds and the feed-forward block that follows (lm3) another 8·d_model², while attention's scores and weighted sum cost about 2·n·d_model. The attention term only dominates once n is several times d_model, about 24,000 tokens for d_model = 4,096. That is why attention's cost matters most for long-context models, and why short-context workloads are dominated by the matrix multiplications in the projections and MLPs.

10. From formula to code: shapes and batching

Real implementations process a batch of B sequences at once and all heads at once, so the tensors carry four dimensions. Writing the shapes out is the fastest way to catch bugs, and interviewers often ask for it:

X                    (B, n, d_model)          batch of token vectors
Q = X W_Q            (B, n, d_model)          one big projection for all heads
reshape + transpose  (B, h, n, d_k)           split the width into h heads
S = Q Kᵀ / √d_k      (B, h, n, n)             one score matrix per head per sequence
S + mask             (B, h, n, n)             −∞ above the diagonal (and on padding)
W = softmax(S, -1)   (B, h, n, n)             normalise along the key axis
O = W V              (B, h, n, d_k)
transpose + reshape  (B, n, d_model)          concatenate the heads
Y = O W_O            (B, n, d_model)          mix the heads

Three details trip people up. The softmax runs along the last axis, the keys: each query's weights sum to 1, not each key's. The three projections are usually fused into one d_model × 3·d_model matrix multiplication and split afterwards, which is faster on a GPU because one big multiplication keeps the hardware busier than three small ones. And the transpose of K swaps only the last two axes, so each head's queries meet only that head's keys. In PyTorch the middle five lines collapse into one call, torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True), which picks a fused FlashAttention-style kernel when it can; the lab checks a NumPy implementation against it.

11. Attention during generation

When a trained model generates text, it produces one token per step. At step t, the newest token is the only new query; it needs the keys and values of every earlier token, but those were already computed at earlier steps and do not change, because a token's key and value depend only on itself and (through earlier layers) on tokens before it. So inference engines keep each layer's past keys and values in memory and, at each step, compute just one new query, key and value, append the new key and value, and run one row of attention: a 1 × t score vector, a softmax, and a weighted sum of t values. That stored memory is the KV cache, the subject of lm5. It turns each generation step's attention from O(t²) into O(t) work, at the price of memory that grows with every token generated, and it is the main reason serving long conversations is expensive.

12. What trained heads turn out to do

Nothing in the architecture tells a head what to look for; roles emerge from training. Researchers inspecting trained models have found recurring types. Positional heads attend mostly to the previous token or a fixed offset, which lets later layers combine neighbouring tokens into phrases. Syntactic heads link verbs to their subjects or objects, or modifiers to the nouns they modify, with accuracy well above simple baselines when compared against grammatical annotations. Coreference heads connect pronouns to their antecedents, as the transformer paper's own visualisations of "its" suggest. Induction heads, described in the deep section, find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it. Many other heads have no clean interpretation, and some can be removed after training with little effect. These findings are useful intuition, but they come with the caveat in this lesson's myths: a weight pattern is a hint about information flow, not proof of what the model used.

13. Why it won

Vaswani et al. compared layer types on three properties: arithmetic per layer, how many operations must happen one after another, and the longest path a signal travels between two positions. Self-attention needs O(1) sequential operations and has path length O(1): any two tokens interact directly in every layer. A recurrent layer needs O(n) sequential steps and has path length O(n). Short paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn, and the absence of sequential steps lets training use the full parallel width of a GPU. Those two properties, more than any single accuracy number, are why attention displaced recurrence.
deep:
Attention as a kernel smoother, and its limits

Formally, each output is a weighted average of values with weights given by a similarity kernel, exp(q·k/√d_k), normalised over the allowed positions. This explains two properties. First, an attention output always lies in the convex hull of the value vectors: it can interpolate between them but never extrapolate beyond them, so a single head cannot, for example, compute a sum that grows with the number of matches; the averaging normalises it away. Second, because weights are normalised, attention struggles to say "nothing here is relevant": the weights must go somewhere. Trained models handle this by dumping weight onto a fixed position, usually the first token, whose value vector is near zero. These attention sinks are why streaming implementations that drop the oldest tokens must keep the first few, or quality collapses.

Multi-head as low-rank factorisation

For one head, the score between positions i and j is x_i W_Q W_Kᵀ x_jᵀ: a bilinear form with the d_model × d_model matrix W_Q W_Kᵀ, whose rank is at most d_k. Likewise the value path W_V W_O (restricted to that head's slice) is a rank-d_k map. So a head is a low-rank "which positions" circuit plus a low-rank "what to move" circuit, and h heads give h independent such circuits for the price of one full-rank one. This view, from mechanistic interpretability, explains why heads specialise and why pruning many heads after training often barely hurts: several are redundant. It also motivates sharing keys and values across heads to save inference memory, which lm5 develops as multi-query and grouped-query attention.

Why queries and keys need separate projections

One could imagine using the same projection for queries and keys, so the score is just the similarity of two tokens' vectors. That score would be symmetric: token i would attend to j exactly as strongly as j to i, and every token would score itself highest (a vector is most similar to itself). Real relationships are asymmetric. A pronoun should attend strongly to its antecedent noun, while the noun has no particular reason to attend back to the pronoun, and a verb looks for its subject but the subject is not looking for the verb in the same way. Separate W_Q and W_K make the bilinear form W_Q W_Kᵀ non-symmetric, so "what I am looking for" and "what I offer" can be different features. The separate value projection decouples a third thing: the features used to find a token need not be the ones worth copying from it, so a head can locate the subject of a sentence by its grammatical role while moving its meaning.

Logit growth and stabilisation at scale

The √d_k argument holds at initialisation, but during training the norms of queries and keys can grow, pushing scores back into the saturated regime; in large models this shows up as training-loss spikes. Two common remedies: QK-norm, which applies a normalisation (lm3 explains layer normalisation) to queries and keys before the dot product so their scale is controlled, and logit soft-capping, which squashes scores with c·tanh(s/c) so they never exceed ±c. Both trade a small amount of expressiveness for stability. In mixed precision (gpu4), large scores also risk overflow in 16-bit formats, which is why kernels subtract the row maximum before exponentiating.

Induction heads and in-context learning

Olsson et al. identified a two-layer circuit that appears suddenly during training. A previous-token head in an early layer copies into each position some information about the token before it. An induction head in a later layer forms its query from the current token and its keys from that "previous token" information, so it attends to positions that came right after an earlier occurrence of the current token, and copies what is there. On "Mr Dursley ... Mr", it attends to "Dursley" and boosts it as the next prediction. The authors found that the appearance of induction heads coincides with a sharp improvement in the model's ability to use earlier context, and argue they are a major mechanism of in-context learning. This is the kind of concrete answer interviewers are looking for when they ask "what do attention heads learn?".

Faster and approximate attention

Many variants trade exactness for cost. Sliding-window attention lets each token attend only to the previous w tokens, making cost O(n·w); stacking layers still lets information travel further, w positions per layer. Sparse patterns combine local windows with a few global tokens. Linear attention replaces exp(q·k) with a product of feature maps φ(q)·φ(k), so the sum over keys can be precomputed and cost becomes O(n); it behaves like a recurrent state of fixed size and is weaker at exact recall of earlier tokens. FlashAttention is different in kind: it is exact, and wins by reducing memory traffic rather than arithmetic. In production LLMs, exact attention with FlashAttention-style kernels plus memory savings in the KV cache has been the default, sometimes interleaved with sliding-window layers.

Numerics of the masked softmax

Implementations never compute exp of raw scores: they subtract each row's maximum first, which leaves the softmax unchanged (the factor cancels) and avoids overflow. Masking uses −∞ or a large negative number; with −∞, a row in which every entry is masked would produce 0/0 = NaN, which happens with left-padding in a batch if a padded query row is fully masked. Libraries guard this case, and it is a classic source of NaN losses in hand-written attention code. FlashAttention's online softmax keeps a running maximum m and running sum l per row and rescales the partial output whenever m increases, which is the same trick applied block by block.
prod:
The public case: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017)

The transformer paper is short, and its claims are concrete enough to check. The base model uses d_model = 512, h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = 64, 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, and has 65 million parameters; the big model uses d_model = 1,024 with 16 heads and has 213 million. The authors justify the √d_k scaling in a footnote with exactly the variance argument above. They trained on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs: the base model for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours, and the big model for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days.

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation benchmark the big model scored 28.4 BLEU (a 0–100 measure of overlap with human reference translations), more than 2 BLEU above the best previous results including ensembles of models, and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French, a new single-model state of the art, at a small fraction of the training cost of competing models. The paper's Table 1 is the argument in miniature: self-attention has O(1) sequential operations and O(1) maximum path length, against O(n) for recurrent layers. Its attention visualisations (figures 3-5) show heads in layer 5 following long-distance dependencies and apparently resolving which noun "its" refers to. Within two years the encoder half became BERT and the decoder half became GPT; the attention formula in every modern LLM is the one on page 4.

Failure modes in practice

NaNs from fully masked rows. Custom attention code that pads sequences on the left and masks with −∞ produces NaN for any query row with no allowed key. Symptom: loss becomes NaN only for certain batches. Fix: guard the row, or use library kernels such as PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention.

Mask bugs that leak the future. An off-by-one in the causal mask (allowing the diagonal plus one) gives a model that reaches suspiciously low training loss and then generates nonsense, because at inference the "future" it learned to copy is not there. A quick test, as in the lab: change only the last token and assert that all earlier outputs are unchanged.

Memory blow-ups at long context. A model that runs at 4K tokens and fails with out-of-memory errors at 32K is often using an attention path that materialises the n × n matrix, for example because a custom mask disabled the fused kernel. Check which attention backend is actually running; profilers (gpu11) show a huge allocation per layer.

Precision issues. Computing the softmax in 16-bit precision without max subtraction overflows; computing it in FP16 with long rows loses precision in the sum. Kernels accumulate in 32-bit; hand-written code should too.

What to watch

During training, track the maximum attention logit per layer: steady growth precedes loss spikes, and is the signal for adding QK-norm or lowering the learning rate. Attention entropy per head (how spread out the weights are) helps spot heads that have collapsed to one position. At serving time, attention's share of step time grows with context length; latency that rises with prompt length faster than linearly is a sign that attention, not the projections, has become the bottleneck.
myths: Attention weights tell you why the model produced its output.

An attention weight says how much one position's value vector contributed to one head's output in one layer. The output then passes through other heads, MLP layers and dozens more layers, mixed by residual connections. Studies have built models with very different attention patterns and the same predictions. Attention maps are a useful hint about information flow, not an explanation; attribution methods such as activation patching test causal influence directly.
Self-attention understands word order.

On its own it does not. Attention is a weighted sum over a set: the lab shows that permuting the inputs of unmasked attention just permutes its outputs. 'Dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would get the same per-token results. Order has to be injected separately, with positional information (lm4); the causal mask adds only the weak signal of how many tokens each position can see.
Dividing by √d_k is just a normalisation constant that could be any number.

It is chosen so that the scores have unit variance when queries and keys have unit-variance components: a dot product of d_k such terms has variance d_k, so dividing by √d_k restores standard deviation 1. Without it, at d_k = 512 the lab's scores have a standard deviation near 23, softmax puts about 96% of the weight on one key, and gradients through the softmax nearly vanish.
Multi-head attention multiplies the parameters and compute by the number of heads.

The heads split the model width rather than copying it: with d_model = 512 and 8 heads, each head works in 64 dimensions, so the four projection matrices are still 512 × 512 each, exactly as for one big head. What changes is that the model gets 8 independent attention patterns instead of one averaged pattern.
The causal mask is something you add at inference to stop the model cheating.

It is used during training, and it is what makes training efficient: with the mask, one forward pass over a 2,048-token sequence gives 2,048 next-token predictions in parallel, each seeing only its own past. At inference the future tokens do not exist yet, so the mask is trivially satisfied; what matters there is reusing past keys and values (the KV cache, lm5).
Attention is slow because of the n² multiply-adds.

For typical context lengths most of a transformer's arithmetic is in the projection and MLP matrices, which grow with n, not n². The naive attention kernel was slow mainly because it wrote the n × n score matrix to GPU memory and read it back, which is bandwidth-bound; FlashAttention computes the same result without materialising that matrix (gpu7). The n² term does dominate at long contexts.
lab:
Goal: implement causal scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention in NumPy, reproduce the hand-worked example, check against PyTorch, and verify three properties: causality, order-blindness without positions, and the saturation that √d_k prevents. NumPy only; the cross-check runs if torch is installed. Takes about a second.

import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)                 # subtract the row max: same result, no overflow
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, causal=True):
    d = Q.shape[-1]
    S = Q @ np.swapaxes(K, -1, -2) / np.sqrt(d)           # (..., n, n) scores
    if causal:
        n = S.shape[-1]
        S = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((n, n), bool), 1), -np.inf, S)
    W = softmax(S)
    return W @ V, W

# ---- 1. the lesson's worked example: 3 tokens, 2-dim vectors
X = np.array([[1., 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]])
WQ = np.array([[1., 0], [1, 1]]); WK = np.array([[1., 1], [0, 1]]); WV = np.array([[1., 0], [0, 2]])
out, W = attention(X @ WQ, X @ WK, X @ WV)
print("attention weights (causal):\n", W, "\noutputs:\n", out)

# ---- 2. multi-head attention on random data, checked against PyTorch if it is installed
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d_model, h = 6, 16, 4; dk = d_model // h
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d_model))
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (rng.normal(0, d_model ** -0.5, (d_model, d_model)) for _ in range(4))
def mha(X, causal=True):
    split = lambda M: (X @ M).reshape(n, h, dk).transpose(1, 0, 2)   # (h, n, dk)
    o, W = attention(split(Wq), split(Wk), split(Wv), causal)
    return o.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, d_model) @ Wo, W
Y, Wh = mha(X)
print("\nmulti-head output shape", Y.shape, " weights shape", Wh.shape, " rows sum to 1:", np.allclose(Wh.sum(-1), 1))
try:
    import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
    t = lambda M: torch.tensor((X @ M).reshape(n, h, dk).transpose(1, 0, 2))
    ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(t(Wq), t(Wk), t(Wv), is_causal=True).numpy()
    print("matches torch scaled_dot_product_attention:", np.allclose(ref.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, d_model) @ Wo, Y))
except ImportError:
    print("(torch not installed - skipped cross-check)")

# ---- 3. causality and permutation
X2 = X.copy(); X2[-1] += 10                                   # change only the last token
print("earlier outputs unchanged when the last token changes:", np.allclose(mha(X2)[0][:-1], Y[:-1]))
perm = rng.permutation(n); Yb = mha(X, causal=False)[0]
print("without mask or positions, permuting inputs just permutes outputs:", np.allclose(mha(X[perm], causal=False)[0], Yb[perm]))

# ---- 4. why divide by sqrt(d_k): score spread and softmax saturation
print("\n d_k   std(q.k)  max weight unscaled  max weight scaled")
for d in (4, 64, 512):
    q = rng.normal(size=(2000, d)); k = rng.normal(size=(2000, 8, d))
    s = np.einsum("bd,bjd->bj", q, k)
    print(f"{d:4d}  {s.std():8.2f}  {softmax(s).max(-1).mean():19.3f}  {softmax(s / np.sqrt(d)).max(-1).mean():17.3f}")

# ---- 5. memory of the full score matrix for one head, one layer, fp16
for ctx in (2048, 8192, 32768):
    print(f"context {ctx:6d}: score matrix {ctx*ctx*2/2**20:8.0f} MiB per head")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1 prints the weight matrix [[1, 0, 0], [0.670, 0.330, 0], [0.306, 0.074, 0.620]] and outputs [1, 0], [0.670, 0.660], [0.926, 1.389]: the lesson's hand calculation.
  2. Section 2 runs 4 heads on 6 random tokens: weights of shape (4, 6, 6), each row summing to 1, and True for the match against PyTorch's fused kernel.
  3. Section 3 prints True twice: changing the last token leaves every earlier output unchanged (the mask works), and without mask or positions a permuted input gives the same outputs, permuted (attention is order-blind).
  4. Section 4 shows the score standard deviation growing as √d_k (2.0, 8.0, 22.8) and the average largest weight rising to 0.96 without scaling but staying near 0.35-0.37 with it.
  5. Section 5 prints 8, 128 and 2,048 MiB for one head's score matrix at 2K, 8K and 32K tokens.

recap: Self-attention lets every token build its new representation as a weighted average of information from other tokens, with weights computed from the tokens themselves.
Each token's vector x is projected three ways: a query q = xW_Q (what this position is looking for), a key k = xW_K (what it offers to be found by) and a value v = xW_V (what it hands over).
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V: query–key dot products give an n × n score matrix, each row is softmaxed into weights summing to 1, and the output is those weights times the values.
In the worked example the third token's scaled scores 2.121, 0.707, 2.828 give weights 0.306, 0.074, 0.620, and its output is 0.306·[1, 0] + 0.074·[0, 2] + 0.620·[1, 2] = [0.926, 1.389].
Dividing by √d_k keeps scores at unit variance, because a dot product of d_k unit-variance terms has variance d_k; without it the softmax saturates to nearly one-hot and its gradient vanishes.

A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to −∞ before the softmax, so position t sees only positions up to t; this lets training compute every next-token prediction of a sequence in one parallel pass.

Multi-head attention splits d_model into h heads of size d_model/h, runs attention in each, concatenates and projects with W_O; the original transformer used 8 heads of 64 dimensions at d_model = 512.
Attention has no notion of order by itself: without positional information it treats the input as a set, so positions must be added (lm4).
The score matrix costs O(n²) memory and the scores O(n²·d) arithmetic per layer; at 8,192 tokens one head's fp16 score matrix is 128 MiB, which FlashAttention avoids storing by computing in tiles.

Attention replaced recurrence because it connects any two positions in one step and computes all positions in parallel; Vaswani et al.'s transformer reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English–German after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs.
glossary: One independent attention computation with its own query, key and value projections; multi-head attention runs several in parallel and concatenates their outputs.
The softmax of one row of scores: how much each position's value contributes to one query's output. Each row sums to 1.
A machine-translation score (0-100) that measures overlap of word sequences between a system's translation and human reference translations.
A mask that sets the scores of all later positions to −∞ before the softmax, so each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions.
Attention in which queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another, such as a decoder attending to an encoder's output.
The dimension of query and key vectors in one head; the scores are divided by its square root.
The width of the vectors that flow between a transformer's layers, such as 512 in the original transformer or 4,096 in a 7B model.
Sum of element-wise products of two vectors; large when they point in similar directions and have large length.
A circuit of two attention heads that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and predicts the token that followed it there; a mechanism behind in-context copying.
The vector a position exposes to be matched against queries: k = xW_K.
The stored keys and values of all earlier tokens, kept during generation so each new token only computes its own query, key and value; covered in lm5.
Large language model: a transformer trained to predict the next token on very large text corpora.
Multi-layer perceptron: here, the feed-forward block of two linear layers with a nonlinearity that follows attention in each transformer layer (lm3).
An unnormalised score fed into a softmax.
Running h attention heads, each on a d_model/h slice, concatenating their outputs and mixing them with an output projection W_O.
A mask that stops positions attending to padding tokens added to make sequences in a batch the same length.
A function where reordering the inputs reorders the outputs the same way and changes nothing else; attention without positional information is one.
The vector a position uses to search other positions: q = xW_Q.
Recurrent neural network: a model that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward (dl7).
The running vector per position that each layer reads from and adds its output back to; covered fully in lm3.
The n × n matrix QKᵀ/√d_k of every query's similarity to every key, before masking and softmax.
Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence.
When one input to a softmax is much larger than the others, the output is nearly one-hot and its gradient with respect to the inputs is nearly zero.
The vector a position contributes to the output when it is attended to: v = xW_V.
The output projection that mixes the concatenated head outputs back into a d_model-wide vector.
drill:
Work it out — head size and memory

A model has d_model = 4,096 and 32 attention heads. Compute (a) the per-head dimension, (b) the scaling factor, (c) the attention layer's parameter count, and (d) the size of the score matrix for one head at an 8,192-token context in fp16, and for all heads of one layer.

Answer

(a) d_k = 4,096 / 32 = 128.

(b) √128 ≈ 11.3. Without it, scores at initialisation would have a standard deviation of about 11 and the softmax would be nearly one-hot.

(c) Four d_model × d_model matrices: 4 × 4,096² = 67.1 million parameters per attention layer, independent of the number of heads.

(d) 8,192² = 67.1 million entries × 2 bytes = 128 MiB per head, × 32 heads = 4 GiB for one layer of one sequence. That is the matrix FlashAttention never stores: it tiles the computation in on-chip memory so the memory cost is linear in n.

Diagnose — the model that was too good

A colleague's hand-written GPT reaches a training loss far below a reference implementation within a few hundred steps, but at generation it produces repetitive nonsense. What do you suspect, and how do you test it in one minute?

Answer

A broken causal mask. If positions can see the next token, the model learns to copy it, so training loss collapses; at generation the next token does not exist yet, so the learned shortcut has nothing to copy and the output is garbage. Common causes: building the mask with triu(..., 0) instead of triu(..., 1) in the wrong convention, applying it after the softmax, or broadcasting it along the wrong axis. Test: run the model on a sequence, change only the last token, rerun, and assert that the outputs (logits) at all earlier positions are unchanged, exactly as the lab's section 3 does. If they change, information is flowing backwards.
qa: E
Explain self-attention in plain words.

Each token asks a question (its query), every token advertises what it has (its key), and the match between a query and each key, turned into weights by a softmax, decides how much of each token's content (its value) flows into the asking token's new representation. So every output is a weighted average of value vectors, with weights computed from the data itself. That lets 'it' in a sentence pull in information from 'animal' twenty words earlier in one step.
E
Write the attention formula and give the shapes.

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V. With n tokens and head dimension d_k, Q and K are n × d_k, QKᵀ is n × n, the softmax is applied to each row, and multiplying by V (n × d_v) gives n × d_v. For multi-head attention the h head outputs are concatenated to n × d_model and multiplied by W_O.
E
What does the causal mask do and why is it needed?

It sets every score where the key position is after the query position to −∞ before the softmax, so those weights are exactly zero. A decoder-only language model is trained to predict each next token from earlier ones; without the mask, position t could read token t + 1, the answer it is supposed to predict. With the mask, a single forward pass gives a valid prediction at every position in parallel.
M
Why divide by √d_k?

If query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product is a sum of d_k such products, with variance d_k. At d_k = 128 the scores would have a standard deviation of about 11, so the softmax would put almost all weight on one key, and the gradient through a saturated softmax is close to zero. Dividing by √d_k brings the standard deviation back to 1, keeping the softmax in its sensitive range at initialisation.

Follow-up: Is that enough at large scale? — Not always; learned query and key norms can still grow during training, so some models add QK-normalisation (normalising q and k before the dot product) or cap the logits.
M
Compute one attention row by hand for scores 2.121, 0.707, 2.828 and values [1, 0], [0, 2], [1, 2].

Exponentiate: 8.342, 2.028, 16.919, total 27.289. Divide: weights 0.306, 0.074, 0.620. Output = 0.306·[1, 0] + 0.074·[0, 2] + 0.620·[1, 2] = [0.926, 1.389]. The largest score dominates but does not take everything, and the weights sum to 1.

Follow-up: How would you compute this stably in code? — Subtract the row maximum before exponentiating; it leaves the softmax unchanged and prevents overflow, and masked −∞ scores become exactly zero weight.
M
What does multi-head attention buy you over one head of full width?

One head produces one set of weights per query, so it must average all the relationships it needs into one pattern. Several heads with their own projections can attend to different things at once, one tracking the previous token, another the subject of the verb, another an earlier copy of the current token, and their results are concatenated. Because each head works in d_model/h dimensions, the parameters and arithmetic stay roughly the same as one full-width head.
M
Compare self-attention with an RNN for modelling a 1,000-token sequence.

An RNN passes information through 999 sequential steps, so distant tokens interact only through a compressed state and training cannot parallelise over time. Self-attention connects any two positions in one layer (path length 1) and computes all positions at once, which suits GPUs. The price is O(n²) score computation and memory per layer and the need to add positional information, while the RNN is O(n) and order-aware by construction.

Follow-up: When does the RNN's profile win? — At inference with very long streams, because it keeps a fixed-size state while attention must keep keys and values for all past tokens; that is why recurrent and state-space designs are being revisited.
M
What is the difference between self-attention and cross-attention?

In self-attention, queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another; in the original encoder–decoder transformer the decoder's queries attend over the encoder's outputs, which is how the translation conditions on the source sentence. Decoder-only LLMs use only causal self-attention; multimodal models often use cross-attention from text to image features.
M
What are induction heads?

A two-head circuit found in trained transformers. A first head (a previous-token head) writes into each position information about the token before it; a second head then uses the current token as a query to find earlier positions whose previous token matches, and copies the token that came next. Given '... Harry Potter ... Harry', it predicts 'Potter'. They are a concrete mechanism for in-context copying and pattern completion and appear abruptly during training.
H
How much memory does the score matrix take, and why does it matter?

n² entries per head per layer: at 8,192 tokens in fp16, 8,192² × 2 bytes = 128 MiB per head, or 4 GiB for 32 heads in one layer of one sequence. A naive kernel writes this to GPU memory and reads it back for the softmax and the multiplication by V, so it is bandwidth-bound and limits context length. FlashAttention computes the same result in tiles that stay in on-chip memory, with a running softmax, so memory becomes linear in n.

Follow-up: Does FlashAttention change the arithmetic? — No: it does the same O(n²·d) multiply-adds (slightly more, because it recomputes in the backward pass); it is faster because it moves far fewer bytes.
H
At what context length does attention dominate the FLOPs of a layer?

Per token, the projections and MLP cost about 24·d_model² FLOPs per layer (forward, for a standard 4× MLP), while the attention scores and weighted sum cost about 4·n·d_model. They are equal when n ≈ 6·d_model: about 24,000 tokens for d_model = 4,096. Below that, attention's quadratic term is a minority of the arithmetic, although its memory traffic can still matter.
Follow-up: Where does 24·d² come from? — Q, K, V and O projections are 4·d² multiply-adds and the MLP 8·d², so 12·d² multiply-adds, which is 24·d² FLOPs.
H
Why are attention weights not a faithful explanation of model behaviour?

Each weight describes one head in one layer mixing value vectors; the head's output is projected, added to a residual stream that other heads and MLPs also write to, and transformed by later layers. Value vectors can be small, so a large weight can carry little information, and different attention patterns can produce the same output. To test whether a token matters, intervene: ablate or patch activations and measure the change in output.

Follow-up: What is activation patching? — Run the model on two inputs, copy one component's activation from one run into the other, and measure how much the output moves; that measures causal contribution.
H
Without any positional information, what can a causal transformer still tell about order?

With a causal mask, position t attends over exactly t tokens, so it can in principle infer how far into the sequence it is, for example from how diluted an average becomes; studies find such models can learn some positional information. But it cannot directly tell 'A then B' from 'B then A' among earlier tokens, and an unmasked encoder cannot tell order at all, which is why explicit positional schemes (lm4) are standard.

t: The transformer block, end to end
sum: A token's whole path through a decoder-only model: embedding, the residual stream, pre-norm blocks of attention and MLP, RMSNorm and SwiGLU, the LM head, and a parameter count of GPT-2 small and Llama 2 7B done by hand.
prereq: lm2
Self-attention mixes information between positions: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V with a causal mask, split into heads, with four d_model × d_model projection matrices per layer.
lm1
Text becomes token IDs; each ID selects a row of the embedding table, and the model's final layer scores every vocabulary entry.
dl4
LayerNorm rescales each vector to zero mean and unit variance and then applies a learned scale and shift; RMSNorm skips the mean and divides by the root mean square.
dl3
Residual (skip) connections add a layer's input to its output, giving gradients a path with derivative 1 so very deep networks stay trainable.
dl2
Activation functions such as ReLU, GELU and SiLU (x·sigmoid(x)) supply the nonlinearity between linear layers; gated linear units multiply one linear projection by an activated other.
gpu3
A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, and weight memory is parameters × bytes per parameter.
why:
Model cards read like this: "32 layers, hidden size 4,096, 32 attention heads, intermediate size 11,008, vocabulary 32,000, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE". An engineer who cannot turn that into a picture of the computation is stuck taking every downstream number on trust. How much GPU memory will the weights need? How many floating-point operations per generated token? Which parts would you quantise, shard across GPUs or replace with experts? Why did the team's fine-tune diverge after they changed one normalisation layer? All of these are questions about what is inside a single transformer block and how blocks are stacked.

The previous lesson (lm2) explained self-attention, the operation that lets tokens exchange information. But attention is only about a third of each layer's weights. Around it sit the pieces that make a deep stack trainable and give it most of its capacity: residual connections, normalisation, the feed-forward (MLP) sub-layer, the embedding at the bottom and the LM head at the top. These pieces look like plumbing, and they are the subject of a surprising number of interview questions precisely because they decide parameter counts, memory, compute, stability and where knowledge is stored.

There is also a practical career reason. When something goes wrong with a model in production, whether a port to a new inference engine produces subtly worse text, a fine-tune diverges, or a memory estimate is off by a factor of two, the debugging happens at this level: comparing the residual stream layer by layer against a reference, checking a normalisation's epsilon, recounting the parameters of a modified architecture. Knowing the block well enough to draw it from memory is what turns those incidents from mysteries into checklists.

This lesson follows one token from its ID to a probability distribution over the next token. It introduces the residual stream as the organising idea, builds a block piece by piece (normalisation, attention, MLP), explains why modern models settled on pre-norm, RMSNorm and SwiGLU, counts the parameters of GPT-2 small and Llama 2 7B by hand to the exact published totals, and converts parameters into memory and FLOPs. The lab builds a two-block model from scratch in NumPy and the same parameter calculator.
primer:
A stack of identical blocks

A decoder-only language model has three parts. At the bottom, the embedding turns each token ID into a vector of length d_model (lm1). In the middle, L identical blocks (also called layers; 12 in GPT-2 small, 32 in Llama 2 7B, 80 in Llama 2 70B) each refine every position's vector using context. At the top, a final normalisation and the LM head, a linear layer, turn each position's vector into one score (logit) per vocabulary entry; a softmax over the scores gives the probability of each possible next token.

Each block does two things, in order. Attention lets each position read from earlier positions: this is where "it" picks up information from "the animal". The MLP (multi-layer perceptron, also called the feed-forward network) then processes each position's vector on its own: it expands the vector to a wider hidden size, applies a nonlinearity and projects it back. A useful slogan: attention moves information between tokens; the MLP thinks about each token individually. Each of the two is wrapped in a normalisation layer and a residual connection.

The residual stream: a shared whiteboard

The organising idea is the residual stream. Picture each token position as having a whiteboard. It starts with the token's embedding written on it. Each sub-layer in turn reads the whiteboard (through a normalisation that rescales what it sees), computes something, and adds its result to the board; it never erases. After 32 blocks, the board holds the embedding plus 64 contributions, and the LM head reads the final board to make a prediction. In code it is two lines per block:

x = x + attention(norm1(x))     # read the stream, add what other positions contribute
x = x + mlp(norm2(x))           # read the stream, add per-position processing

The analogy holds well: information written early stays readable later, and later layers can refine or cancel it by adding a correction. It breaks in one respect: the "board" has only d_model numbers, so contributions share space, and a lot of interpretability research is about how many features models pack into that space.

Why stack identical blocks at all?

Why not one enormous layer? Because each block can only do a limited amount of work: one round of information exchange between positions, then one round of per-position processing. Many linguistic and reasoning steps need several rounds. To resolve "it" in a long sentence, a model may first need to work out which words form noun phrases (one round), then which noun phrase is the subject (another), then match the pronoun to it (a third). Stacking blocks gives the model as many rounds as it has layers, and because every block has the same shape, depth is a simple dial: GPT-2 came in versions with 12, 24, 36 and 48 blocks of the same design. Each block has its own weights, so different depths learn different jobs, and interpretability studies find early blocks handling local, surface patterns and later blocks more abstract ones.

Numbers to hold on to

Llama 2 7B: d_model = 4,096, 32 blocks, 32 heads, MLP hidden width 11,008, vocabulary 32,000, for 6.74 billion parameters, 13.5 GB in 16-bit precision, about 13.5 billion floating-point operations per token in a forward pass. About two thirds of each block's weights are in the MLP. The rest of the lesson shows where each of those numbers comes from.
body:
1. From IDs to the residual stream

The input is a sequence of n token IDs. The embedding table, a matrix of shape vocabulary × d_model, turns each ID into its row: for Llama 2 7B, a 32,000 × 4,096 matrix, and each token becomes a vector of 4,096 numbers. The result is the n × d_model matrix X, one row per position. Attention by itself cannot tell positions apart (lm2 showed it treats its input as a set), so position information must be added. GPT-2 does it here, by adding a second learned table indexed by position (1,024 rows of 768). Llama instead rotates queries and keys inside every attention layer (rotary embeddings). lm4 is devoted to the options; for this lesson it is enough that each block's attention knows token order.

That matrix X is the initial residual stream. From here on, every position's row will be added to, block by block, and its shape never changes: n × d_model from the first block to the last. This constant shape is what lets you stack as many blocks as you like.

2. Normalisation: keeping the numbers in range

Before each sub-layer reads the stream, it normalises it. The reason is scale. The stream is a sum of many contributions, and its magnitude varies across positions and grows with depth; a matrix multiplication applied to vectors of wildly different sizes produces outputs of wildly different sizes, which makes training unstable. Normalisation rescales each position's vector to a standard size before the sub-layer sees it (dl4 covers normalisation in general).

LayerNorm, used in the original transformer and GPT-2, subtracts the vector's mean, divides by its standard deviation, then multiplies by a learned per-feature scale γ and adds a learned shift β. RMSNorm, used by Llama and most recent models, skips the mean and the shift: it divides by the root mean square and multiplies by γ. Worked by hand for x = [1, −2, 3, 0]: the mean of squares is (1 + 4 + 9 + 0)/4 = 3.5, the RMS is √3.5 = 1.871, so RMSNorm(x) = [0.535, −1.069, 1.604, 0] (with γ = 1). LayerNorm first subtracts the mean 0.5, giving [0.5, −2.5, 2.5, −0.5], whose standard deviation is 1.803, so LayerNorm(x) = [0.277, −1.387, 1.387, −0.277]. RMSNorm is cheaper (one reduction instead of two, no shift) and was found to work as well, which at billions of tokens per day is reason enough.

3. The attention sub-layer

The first sub-layer is causal multi-head self-attention from lm2: project the normalised stream to queries, keys and values, compute softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) with the causal mask per head, take the weighted sum of values, concatenate heads and project with W_O. Its output, n × d_model, is added to the stream. This is the only place in the block where position i's vector is influenced by position j's. Its weights are four d_model × d_model matrices: 4 × 4,096² = 67.1 million for Llama 2 7B. (Models that share keys and values across heads, covered in lm5, have smaller W_K and W_V.)

4. The MLP sub-layer

The second sub-layer is applied to each position independently, with the same weights at every position. The classic version is two linear layers with a nonlinearity between: expand from d_model to a hidden width d_ff (usually 4·d_model), apply an activation such as ReLU or GELU, project back to d_model:

MLP(x) = GELU(x W₁ + b₁) W₂ + b₂          W₁: d × 4d,  W₂: 4d × d   → 8·d² weights

Why expand and contract? The expansion gives the layer many hidden units, each of which can respond to a particular pattern in its input; the nonlinearity lets it represent functions that a single matrix cannot; the contraction writes the combined result back in the stream's size. Interpretability work (Geva et al.) found that a useful way to read it is as a large key-value memory: each column of W₁ is a key that fires on some input pattern, and the matching row of W₂ is a value written into the stream when it fires, often one that promotes the tokens that tend to follow that pattern.

Modern LLMs use a gated variant, SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020). It computes two projections of the input, applies the SiLU activation (x·sigmoid(x), a smooth ReLU) to one, multiplies them element by element so one acts as a learned gate on the other, and projects back:

SwiGLU(x) = ( SiLU(x W₁) ⊙ (x W₃) ) W₂     W₁, W₃: d × d_ff,  W₂: d_ff × d   → 3·d·d_ff weights

With three matrices instead of two, keeping the same parameter count as a 4·d MLP requires d_ff = (2/3)·4·d = 8d/3. For d = 4,096 that is 10,923, which Llama rounds up to a multiple of 256: 11,008. That odd-looking number in every Llama 2 7B config comes straight from this rule. Shazeer found the gated variants reached lower perplexity than ReLU and GELU MLPs at the same parameters and compute; nobody has a complete theory of why, and the paper itself says so.

5. Residual connections and pre-norm

The two sub-layers are joined by residual connections: each adds its output to its input rather than replacing it. Residuals were introduced for very deep image networks (dl3) and matter for the same reason here. The derivative of x + f(x) with respect to x is 1 + f′(x), so during backpropagation every layer receives the gradient from the loss through a path that multiplies by exactly 1, no matter how many layers sit above. Without them, a 32- or 80-block stack would suffer vanishing or exploding gradients.

Where the normalisation goes relative to the residual matters. The original transformer used post-norm: x ← LayerNorm(x + f(x)). The residual path then passes through a normalisation at every layer, so the identity path is broken, and Xiong et al. (2020) showed that at initialisation the gradients near the output are large, which is why post-norm transformers need a learning-rate warm-up (a gradual ramp of the learning rate over the first thousands of steps) or they diverge. GPT-2 switched to pre-norm, x ← x + f(LayerNorm(x)), which normalises only what each sub-layer reads; the stream itself is a pure sum. Pre-norm needs one extra normalisation at the very top, before the LM head, because the raw stream is never normalised otherwise; GPT-2 added exactly that. Xiong et al. showed pre-norm transformers can train without warm-up, and almost every large model since is pre-norm.

6. The top: final norm, LM head, loss

After L blocks, the stream is normalised one last time and multiplied by the LM head, a d_model × vocabulary matrix, giving n × vocabulary logits: a score for every possible next token at every position. Some models tie the LM head to the embedding table (use its transpose), so the same vector represents a token going in and coming out; GPT-2 does, Llama does not.

In training, the causal mask means position t's logits depend only on tokens 1 … t, so they are a legitimate prediction of token t + 1. The loss is the cross-entropy at every position, −log p(correct next token), averaged over the n − 1 positions that have a next token. One forward pass therefore yields n − 1 training signals in parallel. At generation, only the last position's logits are needed; they are turned into a choice of next token by the decoding rules of lm8, the token is appended, and the process repeats.

7. A SwiGLU unit by hand

To see the gate at work, take one hidden unit with a 2-dimensional input x = [1, 2]. Suppose its column of W₁ is [0.5, 0.5] and its column of W₃ is [1, −1]. The gate pre-activation is x·[0.5, 0.5] = 1.5, and SiLU(1.5) = 1.5 × sigmoid(1.5) = 1.5 × 0.818 = 1.227. The other projection is x·[1, −1] = −1. The unit's value is their product, 1.227 × (−1) = −1.227, and it is written back to the stream through this unit's row of W₂. Now flip the input to x = [−1, −2]: the gate pre-activation is −1.5 and SiLU(−1.5) = −1.5 × 0.182 = −0.273, nearly closed, so even though the other projection is now +1 the unit outputs only −0.273. The gate decides whether this unit speaks; the other projection decides what it says. With 11,008 such units per layer, the MLP can switch on combinations of features that suit each input.

8. One token's trip, step by step

Put together, here is what happens to the token " sat" at position 3 of "the cat sat" in a Llama-style model. Its ID selects its row of the embedding table: a 4,096-number vector, the stream's starting value. Block 1: RMSNorm rescales a copy; attention projects it to a query, compares with the keys of " the", " cat" and itself (rotated for position), and adds a weighted mix of their values to the stream; RMSNorm rescales a copy again; the SwiGLU MLP expands it to 11,008 hidden units, gates them, projects back and adds the result. Blocks 2 to 32 repeat this with their own weights, each adding contributions. The final RMSNorm rescales the stream, and the LM head turns it into 32,000 logits; the softmax gives, say, a high probability to " on" and " down". During training the loss compares this distribution with the true next token; during generation one token is chosen and fed back in.

9. Counting parameters by hand: Llama 2 7B

A model card gives d = 4,096, L = 32 blocks, d_ff = 11,008, vocabulary V = 32,000, no bias terms, RMSNorm, untied embeddings. Counting:

attention per block   4 · d²             = 4 · 4,096²            =    67,108,864
MLP per block         3 · d · d_ff       = 3 · 4,096 · 11,008    =   135,266,304
norms per block       2 · d              = 2 · 4,096             =         8,192
one block                                                         =   202,383,360
32 blocks                                                         = 6,476,267,520
embedding + LM head   2 · V · d          = 2 · 32,000 · 4,096    =   262,144,000
final norm            d                                           =         4,096
total                                                             = 6,738,415,616

6.74 billion, the published count for Llama 2 7B. The MLP is 135.3 / 202.4 = 67% of each block. Run the same arithmetic for Llama 3 8B, whose attention shares keys and values across groups of heads (W_K and W_V are 4,096 × 1,024 rather than 4,096 × 4,096, explained in lm5), MLP width 14,336 and vocabulary 128,256, and you get 8,030,261,248; there the MLP is 81% of each block and the embeddings alone are 1.05 billion.

10. Counting GPT-2 small

GPT-2 small is the older recipe: d = 768, 12 blocks, d_ff = 3,072, LayerNorm (scale and shift, so 2·d each), bias terms everywhere, learned position embeddings for 1,024 positions, tied embeddings, V = 50,257:

attention per block   4·d² + 4·d (biases)        = 2,359,296 + 3,072   = 2,362,368
MLP per block         2·d·4d + 4d + d (biases)   = 4,718,592 + 3,840   = 4,722,432
LayerNorms per block  2 · 2·d                                          =     3,072
12 blocks                                                              = 85,054,464
token embedding       V · d   (tied: counted once)                     = 38,597,376
position embedding    1,024 · d                                        =    786,432
final LayerNorm       2 · d                                            =      1,536
total                                                                  = 124,439,808

Note how big the embedding is here: 38.6 million of 124.4 million, 31%. In small models the vocabulary is a major cost, which is why tying made sense for GPT-2; in a 7B model the same table is a few percent. (The GPT-2 paper's table lists this model as 117M; the weights as released count to 124M, the figure usually quoted. Published parameter counts often differ by such conventions and slips, which is why you should be able to recount.)
