11. From parameters to memory and FLOPs

Two conversions every interviewer expects (gpu3 derives them in detail). Memory: weights take parameters × bytes per parameter. In bf16 (2 bytes) Llama 2 7B is 6.74 × 10⁹ × 2 = 13.5 GB; in 8-bit, 6.7 GB; in 4-bit, about 3.4 GB plus a little for scaling factors (lm12). Compute: in a forward pass every weight takes part in one multiply-add per token, which is two floating-point operations (FLOPs), so a forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs per token: 13.5 GFLOP for Llama 2 7B. Attention adds a term that is not in the parameter count: computing scores and the weighted sum costs about 4·n·d FLOPs per layer per token for a context of n tokens, 2.1 GFLOP per token across 32 layers at n = 4,096 (about 15% extra) and more than the weights' term beyond about 24K tokens. Training costs roughly three times the forward pass (the backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights), so about 6N FLOPs per token, the rule lm7 uses for scaling-law budgets.

12. Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder

The same block appears in three arrangements. Encoder-only models such as BERT use attention without the causal mask, so every token sees the whole input; they are trained to fill in masked-out tokens and are used to produce representations for classification and retrieval (lm10 uses such embeddings). Encoder–decoder models such as the original transformer and T5 have an encoder stack for the input and a decoder stack that generates the output with causal self-attention plus cross-attention to the encoder. Decoder-only models, GPT and Llama, use one causal stack for everything: the prompt is just the start of the sequence. Decoder-only won for general LLMs largely because one simple objective (predict the next token of any text) scales to any data, and because the same model can then handle any task phrased as text.
deep:
The residual stream as a communication channel

Mechanistic interpretability treats the residual stream as the model's shared memory bus. Because every sub-layer reads from it with a linear map (after normalisation) and writes to it with a linear map, two sub-layers communicate whenever one writes in a direction the other reads. Different features occupy different directions, and since there are far more useful features than d_model dimensions, models pack many nearly-orthogonal features into the same space ("superposition"). This view explains why attention heads in later layers can depend on heads in earlier layers (the induction-head circuit from lm2 is exactly a previous-token head writing a feature that a later head reads), and why you can sometimes steer a model by adding a vector to the stream.

Why the residual stream grows, and what pre-norm does about it

Each sub-layer reads a normalised copy and adds an output of roughly constant scale, so the stream's norm tends to grow with depth, as the lab's tiny model shows (from 3.4 after block 1 to 4.4 after block 2 with random weights). Late sub-layers therefore change the stream by a smaller fraction, and studies find middle and late layers of large models are more redundant than early ones: some can be removed with modest damage. GPT-2 counters this at initialisation by scaling the output projections of residual layers by 1/√N, where N is the number of residual layers, so the sum of N contributions starts with a variance that does not grow with depth. Other schemes add learned per-layer scales or extra normalisations on sub-layer outputs.

Gated MLPs as multiplicative interactions

A standard MLP computes act(xW₁)W₂: each hidden unit's output is a fixed nonlinear function of a single linear feature. A gated MLP computes act(xW₁) ⊙ (xW₃): each hidden unit is the product of two features of the input, so it can express "A and B" style interactions (fire strongly only if both features are present) directly. That is a plausible reason for its consistent small advantage. The cost is a third weight matrix, absorbed by shrinking the hidden width to 8d/3, and slightly more memory traffic per token, which matters at inference when the MLP weights dominate the bytes read (gpu10).

Why no biases and why RMSNorm

Removing biases saves parameters and memory traffic, and makes every linear layer a pure matrix multiplication, which simplifies sharding across GPUs (tensor parallelism splits weight matrices across devices, dl9) and some quantisation schemes. RMSNorm's justification is empirical and practical: Zhang and Sennrich found that re-centring (subtracting the mean) contributed little, and dropping it removes one reduction over the vector per normalisation. At inference these small savings matter because normalisations are memory-bound element-wise operations that are fused into neighbouring kernels when possible (gpu6).

Parallel blocks and other variants

Some models compute attention and the MLP from the same normalised input and add both to the stream at once: x ← x + Attn(norm(x)) + MLP(norm(x)). This "parallel" formulation (used in GPT-J and PaLM) lets the two sub-layers' matrix multiplications be fused and run together, which PaLM's authors reported as roughly 15% faster training at large scale with small quality cost at small scale. Other common variations: QK-norm inside attention for stability (lm2), sliding-window attention in some layers, and mixture-of-experts MLPs (lm17). All keep the residual-stream skeleton.

Reading the stream mid-way: the logit lens

Because the LM head is a linear map applied to the (normalised) stream, you can apply it to the stream after any block, not just the last, and ask what the model "would predict" at that depth. This technique, known as the logit lens, shows predictions forming gradually: early layers often predict generic or copied tokens, middle layers converge on the right answer for easy cases, and late layers sharpen the distribution. It works because pre-norm models keep the stream in a roughly consistent basis from bottom to top; refined versions train a small linear translator per layer (the "tuned lens") to correct for drift. It is a cheap, practical tool when investigating where in the stack a fact is retrieved or a mistake is introduced, and it rests entirely on the residual-stream structure explained in this lesson.

Activation memory and the shape of training cost

During training each block must keep its intermediate activations for the backward pass: the normalised inputs, the queries, keys and values, the attention outputs, the MLP's wide hidden activations (n × d_ff per sequence, the largest), and the softmax statistics. Per token per layer this is a few tens of times d_model numbers, so for long sequences and large batches activation memory can exceed weight memory. That is why activation checkpointing (recomputing activations in the backward pass instead of storing them, gpu9) is standard, and why the MLP's width, which sets its hidden activation size, matters for training memory as well as parameters.

Depth versus width

For a fixed parameter budget you can have more, narrower blocks or fewer, wider ones. Width makes each matrix multiplication bigger, which uses GPUs more efficiently and parallelises well across devices; depth composes more sequential steps of computation, which helps tasks that need multi-step reasoning, but adds latency because blocks run one after another. Large models settle on aspect ratios d_model / L of roughly 50 to 200 (Llama 2 7B: 4,096 / 32 = 128). Kaplan et al.'s scaling study found loss depends mostly on total non-embedding parameters and only weakly on shape within a broad range, so shape is usually chosen for hardware efficiency.
prod:
The public case: GPT-2's block and the move to pre-norm

The GPT-2 paper (Radford et al., 2019) describes its architecture in one paragraph of section 2.3, and almost every change it lists is now standard. Layer normalisation "was moved to the input of each sub-block, similar to a pre-activation residual network"; "an additional layer normalization was added after the final self-attention block"; and "a modified initialization which accounts for the accumulation on the residual path with model depth is used", scaling residual-layer weights at initialisation by 1/√N. The same paragraph raises the vocabulary to 50,257 and the context from 512 to 1,024 tokens. The paper trained four sizes, with 12, 24, 36 and 48 layers at widths 768 to 1,600; the largest, 1.5 billion parameters, still underfit its training data.

Xiong et al. (2020) later explained why the pre-norm move mattered: with post-norm, the expected gradients of the parameters near the output are large at initialisation, so a large learning rate makes training unstable unless it is warmed up; with pre-norm the gradients are well-behaved, and their experiments trained pre-norm transformers without warm-up in less time. LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023) then fixed the recipe most open models follow: pre-normalisation with RMSNorm, SwiGLU MLPs at width (2/3)·4d, rotary position embeddings, no biases. The lab's parameter counter reproduces the 124,439,808 parameters of GPT-2 small and the 6,738,415,616 of Llama 2 7B from these descriptions.

Failure modes in practice

Loss spikes and divergence. Large-model training runs show sudden loss spikes, often traced to growing activations in the residual stream or attention logits. Symptoms: gradient-norm spikes before the loss jumps. Remedies: lower learning rate, gradient clipping, QK-norm, restarting from a checkpoint and skipping the offending batches.

Mismatched architecture details at load time. Loading weights into an implementation with a different normalisation epsilon, a different SwiGLU ordering (which of W₁ and W₃ is gated) or a different rotary convention gives a model that runs but produces degraded text. Always validate a ported model by comparing logits on a fixed input with the reference implementation to a tight tolerance.

Memory estimates that forget something. Weights are only the start: inference also needs the KV cache (lm5) and activations, training needs gradients, optimiser states and activations (gpu9). A 7B model whose weights are 13.5 GB needs on the order of 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam training, over 100 GB, before activations.

Silent quality loss from the wrong MLP width. Architecture variants built by hand sometimes use 4·d for a SwiGLU MLP instead of 8d/3, giving a model 50% larger in its MLPs than intended; it trains, but compute and memory budgets are off and comparisons with published baselines are no longer fair. Recount parameters from the code, not from the plan, before launching a run.

Precision in norms and softmax. Normalisations and softmaxes computed in 16-bit lose precision; implementations upcast to float32 inside these operations. A custom kernel that does not is a common source of slowly degrading quality.

What to monitor

In training: loss, gradient norm, the norm of the residual stream per layer and the largest activation values, which warn of instabilities early. In serving: whether the fused kernels (attention, normalisation plus matrix multiplication) are actually in use, and the weight bytes read per generated token, which sets the floor on decode latency (gpu10).
myths: Attention is where most of a transformer's parameters live.

In a standard block, attention has 4·d² weights and the MLP 8·d², so the MLP holds two thirds of each layer: 135 million against 67 million per layer in Llama 2 7B. Grouped-query attention shrinks attention further (Llama 3 8B: 42 million against 176 million). This is why mixture-of-experts designs replace the MLP, and why quantising MLP weights saves the most memory.
Each layer replaces the token's representation with a new one.

Each sub-layer adds to it. The residual connection means x ← x + f(norm(x)), so the vector flowing up the model (the residual stream) is the embedding plus the sum of every attention and MLP output so far. Information written by layer 2 is still directly readable at layer 30 unless a later layer writes something to cancel it.
The MLP is just a nonlinearity; the clever part is attention.

Attention is the only part that moves information between positions, but it is a weighted average and largely linear in the values. The MLP is where most of the computation per token happens and, according to interpretability work such as Geva et al., where much factual association is stored: its first matrix detects input patterns and its second writes out what tends to follow them.
Pre-norm and post-norm are cosmetic variants.

They change what the gradient sees. Post-norm (the original transformer) normalises after the residual addition, so every layer's gradient passes through every normalisation above it; deep post-norm models need careful learning-rate warm-up or they diverge. Pre-norm normalises only the sub-layer's input, leaving a clean identity path through the stream; Xiong et al. showed pre-norm transformers train without warm-up. Nearly all modern LLMs are pre-norm.
A 7B model needs 7 GB of memory.

7 billion parameters in 16-bit precision take 2 bytes each: about 13.5 GB for Llama 2 7B's 6.74 billion weights, before the KV cache, activations and framework overhead. 8-bit and 4-bit quantisation (lm12) bring it to about 7 and 3.5 GB.
The model computes a next-token prediction only for the last position.

During training every position's output is used: a causal transformer computes logits at all n positions in one pass and averages the cross-entropy of all n − 1 next-token predictions. At generation only the last position's logits are needed, so engines skip the LM head for the others.
lab:
Goal: count parameters of real models from their configs, normalise a vector by hand, and build a two-block pre-norm decoder (RMSNorm, causal multi-head attention, SwiGLU, LM head) from scratch to see the residual stream in action. NumPy only, under a second.

import numpy as np

# ---- 1. parameter counts from a config, layer by layer
def count(name, d, L, vocab, d_ff, n_heads, n_kv=None, gated=True, bias=False, tied=False, pos=0, norm_params=1):
    n_kv = n_kv or n_heads; hd = d // n_heads
    attn = d * d * 2 + d * (n_kv * hd) * 2 + (4 * d if bias else 0)            # W_Q, W_O full; W_K, W_V may be smaller (lm5)
    mlp = (3 if gated else 2) * d * d_ff + ((d_ff + d) if bias else 0)
    norms = 2 * norm_params * d                                                   # two norms per block (LayerNorm has scale+shift)
    emb = vocab * d * (1 if tied else 2) + pos * d
    total = L * (attn + mlp + norms) + emb + norm_params * d
    print(f"{name:13s} attn/layer {attn/1e6:7.2f}M  mlp/layer {mlp/1e6:7.2f}M  layers {L*(attn+mlp+norms)/1e9:6.3f}B"
          f"  embeddings {emb/1e9:6.3f}B  total {total:,}  (MLP share of layers {mlp/(attn+mlp):.0%})")
    return total
count("GPT-2 small", 768, 12, 50257, 3072, 12, gated=False, bias=True, tied=True, pos=1024, norm_params=2)
n7 = count("Llama 2 7B", 4096, 32, 32000, 11008, 32)
n8 = count("Llama 3 8B", 4096, 32, 128256, 14336, 32, n_kv=8)
print(f"weights in bf16: 7B -> {n7*2/1e9:.1f} GB, 8B -> {n8*2/1e9:.1f} GB;  forward FLOPs/token ~ 2N = {2*n7/1e9:.1f} GFLOP")

# ---- 2. RMSNorm and LayerNorm by hand
x = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 3.0, 0.0])
rms = np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean())
print("\nx =", x, " RMS =", round(rms, 4), " RMSNorm(x) =", np.round(x / rms, 4))
mu, sd = x.mean(), x.std()
print("mean", mu, "std", round(sd, 4), " LayerNorm(x) =", np.round((x - mu) / sd, 4))

# ---- 3. a tiny pre-norm decoder (2 blocks) built from scratch, random weights
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
V, d, h, dff, L, n = 50, 16, 4, 43, 2, 7
def rmsnorm(x, g): return g * x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-6)
def softmax(z): z = z - z.max(-1, keepdims=True); e = np.exp(z); return e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
silu = lambda z: z / (1 + np.exp(-z))
P = {"emb": rng.normal(0, 0.02, (V, d)), "out": rng.normal(0, 0.02, (d, V)), "gf": np.ones(d)}
for l in range(L):
    for k, shape in [("q", (d, d)), ("k", (d, d)), ("v", (d, d)), ("o", (d, d)), ("w1", (d, dff)), ("w3", (d, dff)), ("w2", (dff, d))]:
        P[f"{k}{l}"] = rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5 if k != "w2" else dff ** -0.5, shape)
    P[f"g1{l}"], P[f"g2{l}"] = np.ones(d), np.ones(d)
def forward(ids, trace=False):
    x = P["emb"][ids]                                                     # (n, d): the residual stream
    for l in range(L):
        a = rmsnorm(x, P[f"g1{l}"])
        q, k, v = (a @ P[f"{w}{l}"] for w in "qkv")
        sp = lambda t: t.reshape(len(ids), h, d // h).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        s = sp(q) @ sp(k).transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d // h)
        s = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((len(ids),) * 2, bool), 1), -np.inf, s)
        att = (softmax(s) @ sp(v)).transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(len(ids), d) @ P[f"o{l}"]
        x = x + att                                                       # write attention's result into the stream
        m = rmsnorm(x, P[f"g2{l}"])
        mlp = (silu(m @ P[f"w1{l}"]) * (m @ P[f"w3{l}"])) @ P[f"w2{l}"]   # SwiGLU, per position
        x = x + mlp
        if trace: print(f"  block {l}: |attn out| {np.linalg.norm(att, axis=1).mean():.3f}  |mlp out| {np.linalg.norm(mlp, axis=1).mean():.3f}  |stream| {np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1).mean():.3f}")
    return rmsnorm(x, P["gf"]) @ P["out"]                                 # logits (n, V)
ids = rng.integers(0, V, n)
print(f"\ntiny model: {sum(p.size for p in P.values()):,} parameters"); logits = forward(ids, trace=True)
p = softmax(logits[-1])
print("logits shape", logits.shape, " next-token distribution sums to", round(p.sum(), 6), " top token", p.argmax())
ids2 = ids.copy(); ids2[-1] = (ids2[-1] + 1) % V
print("changing the last token leaves earlier logits unchanged:", np.allclose(forward(ids2)[:-1], logits[:-1]))
nll = -np.log(softmax(logits[:-1])[np.arange(n - 1), ids[1:]]).mean()
print(f"untrained loss {nll:.3f} vs uniform ln(V) = {np.log(V):.3f}")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1 prints exactly 124,439,808 for GPT-2 small, 6,738,415,616 for Llama 2 7B and 8,030,261,248 for Llama 3 8B, with the MLP share of each block (67%, 67%, 81%), 13.5 GB and 16.1 GB of bf16 weights, and about 13.5 GFLOP per token for the 7B forward pass.
  2. Section 2 reproduces the hand calculation: RMS 1.8708, RMSNorm [0.5345, −1.069, 1.6036, 0]; LayerNorm [0.2774, −1.3868, 1.3868, −0.2774].
  3. Section 3 traces the tiny model: each sub-layer's output norm and the stream's norm, which grows block by block because sub-layers add. The next-token distribution sums to 1, changing the last token leaves earlier logits unchanged (the causal mask works through the whole stack), and the untrained loss (3.93) is close to ln 50 = 3.91, the loss of a uniform guess.

Try next. Switch the block to post-norm and compare stream norms; replace SwiGLU with a GELU MLP of width 4d and confirm the parameter count is about the same as SwiGLU at 8d/3.
recap: A decoder-only LLM is: token embedding, a stack of L identical blocks, a final normalisation, and an LM head that turns each position's vector into a score for every vocabulary entry.
The residual stream is the per-position vector that flows up the stack; every block reads it through a normalisation and adds its result back, x ← x + Attention(norm(x)), then x ← x + MLP(norm(x)).
Attention is the only operation that moves information between positions; the MLP processes each position independently and holds about two thirds of a standard layer's weights (4·d² versus 8·d²).

Modern LLMs use pre-normalisation with RMSNorm (divide by the root mean square: x = [1, −2, 3, 0] has RMS 1.871 and normalises to [0.535, −1.069, 1.604, 0]), a SwiGLU MLP, rotary positions, and no bias terms.
SwiGLU uses three matrices instead of two, so to keep the parameter count of a 4·d MLP its hidden width is about 8d/3: Llama 2 7B uses 11,008 for d = 4,096.
Llama 2 7B by hand: 32 layers × (67.1M attention + 135.3M MLP + 8K norm) = 6.476B, plus 2 × 32,000 × 4,096 = 0.262B of embeddings and LM head, totals 6,738,415,616 parameters.
GPT-2 small (d = 768, 12 layers, tied embeddings, learned positions, biases, LayerNorm) counts to 124,439,808 parameters, of which the token embedding is 38.6M.
A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (13.5 GFLOP per token for a 6.74B model), plus an attention term that grows with context; weights take parameters × bytes (13.5 GB in bf16).
Training computes next-token losses at every position in one pass thanks to the causal mask; generation uses only the last position's logits, one token at a time.
GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block, added a final LayerNorm and scaled residual-layer initialisation by 1/√N; pre-norm became standard because it trains stably without warm-up.
glossary: The constant vector added after a matrix multiplication (y = xW + b). Most modern LLMs omit them in attention and MLP layers.
A transformer with causal self-attention only and no encoder, trained to predict the next token; the GPT and Llama design.
A transformer with bidirectional self-attention, used to produce representations of a whole text (BERT); it is not used for generating text left to right.
A transformer whose encoder reads the input bidirectionally and whose decoder generates output with causal self-attention plus cross-attention to the encoder (the original transformer, T5).
One floating-point operation; a multiply-add counts as two.
Gaussian error linear unit, a smooth ReLU-like activation x·Φ(x) used in GPT-2 and BERT.
Stored keys and values of earlier tokens kept during generation so they are not recomputed; its memory is covered in lm5.
Normalises a vector to zero mean and unit variance across its features, then applies a learned per-feature scale and shift.
The final linear layer that maps each d_model vector to one logit per vocabulary entry; also called the unembedding.
The raw scores the LM head produces, one per vocabulary entry; softmax turns them into next-token probabilities.
The per-position block in each layer: expand the vector to a wider hidden size, apply a nonlinearity, project back to d_model.
The original transformer arrangement, x ← norm(x + f(x)): normalise after the residual addition.
The modern arrangement, x ← x + f(norm(x)): normalise only the input to each sub-layer, leaving the residual path untouched.
The per-position vector that runs from the embedding to the final norm; each sub-layer reads it and adds its output to it.
Root-mean-square normalisation: divide a vector by the square root of the mean of its squares, then apply a learned per-feature scale; no mean subtraction and no shift.
The activation x·sigmoid(x), a smooth version of ReLU.
One of the two components of a block, attention or MLP, each wrapped in a normalisation and a residual connection.
A gated MLP: (SiLU(xW₁) ⊙ xW₃)W₂, where ⊙ is element-wise multiplication; three weight matrices instead of two.
One layer of a transformer: an attention sub-layer and an MLP sub-layer, each with normalisation and a residual connection.
Using the same matrix for the input embedding and the LM head (transposed), which saves vocabulary × d_model parameters.
Starting training with a small learning rate and increasing it over the first steps, needed by post-norm transformers to avoid divergence.
Brain floating point: a 16-bit format with float32's exponent range and fewer mantissa bits, the usual format for LLM weights (gpu4).
drill:
Work it out — size a model from its config

A config says: d_model 5,120, 40 layers, 40 heads, MLP width 13,824 (SwiGLU), vocabulary 32,000, untied embeddings, no biases. Estimate the parameters, the bf16 weight memory and the forward FLOPs per token at short context.

Answer

Attention per layer: 4 × 5,120² = 104.9M. MLP: 3 × 5,120 × 13,824 = 212.3M. Norms: 10,240. Per layer ≈ 317.2M; × 40 = 12.69B. Embeddings: 2 × 32,000 × 5,120 = 0.33B. Total ≈ 13.0B; this is the Llama 2 13B shape. Check: 13,824 ≈ 8 × 5,120 / 3 = 13,653 rounded up to a multiple of 256.

Memory: 13.0B × 2 bytes ≈ 26 GB of weights in bf16, so it does not fit a 24 GB GPU unquantised, and an 80 GB GPU has room for weights plus KV cache.

FLOPs: about 2 × 13.0B ≈ 26 GFLOP per token in a forward pass at short context, plus about 4 × n × 5,120 × 40 for attention at context n (about 3.4 GFLOP at n = 4,096).

Diagnose — the ported model that rambles

You port a Llama-style checkpoint into your own inference code. It runs without errors and produces fluent-ish but noticeably worse text than the reference. Where do you look?

Answer

Compare logits with the reference on one fixed input, layer by layer: feed the same tokens to both, and compare the residual stream after the embedding, after each block, and the final logits, to find the first point of divergence. Usual culprits: RMSNorm epsilon or computing the norm in 16-bit instead of float32; swapped W₁/W₃ in SwiGLU (which matrix is gated); a different rotary-embedding convention (interleaved versus split halves, lm4); a wrong causal mask; or a chat template or tokeniser mismatch (lm1) before the model is even reached. A model that is wrong but still fluent usually has a small numerical or convention mismatch rather than a crash-level bug, which is why layer-by-layer comparison beats reading the code.
qa: E
Describe one transformer block in a modern decoder-only LLM.

Two sub-layers, each wrapped as x ← x + f(norm(x)). The first is causal multi-head self-attention, which lets each position gather information from earlier positions; the second is an MLP applied to each position separately, which expands the vector to a wider hidden size, applies a gated nonlinearity such as SwiGLU and projects back. The norms are usually RMSNorm, and the additions are the residual connections that carry the residual stream up the stack.
E
What is the residual stream?

The per-position vector that starts as the token embedding and flows up through every block to the final norm and LM head. Each attention and MLP sub-layer reads a normalised copy of it and adds its output back. Because sub-layers add rather than overwrite, information written early stays available later, and gradients have a direct path from the loss to every layer.
E
Where does the next-token probability come from?

After the last block, the final normalisation is applied to each position's vector and the LM head, a d_model × vocabulary matrix, produces one logit per vocabulary entry. A softmax over the last position's logits gives the distribution for the next token, which is then sampled or chosen (lm8).
M
Count the parameters of Llama 2 7B from its config.

d = 4,096, 32 layers, MLP width 11,008, vocabulary 32,000, no biases, untied embeddings. Attention per layer is 4 × 4,096² = 67.1M; the SwiGLU MLP is 3 × 4,096 × 11,008 = 135.3M; two RMSNorm scales add 8,192. That is 202.4M per layer and 6.476B for 32 layers. Embedding and LM head add 2 × 32,000 × 4,096 = 262M and the final norm 4,096, for 6,738,415,616 in total.
Follow-up: How much memory and compute does that imply? — In bf16 the weights are 13.5 GB; a forward pass is about 2 × 6.74B ≈ 13.5 GFLOP per token, plus attention over the context.
M
Why do the MLPs hold about two thirds of the parameters?

Attention has four d × d projections, 4·d². A standard MLP expands to 4·d and back, two matrices of d × 4d, so 8·d². The MLP is therefore two thirds of each layer; SwiGLU's three matrices at width 8d/3 keep the same total. With grouped-query attention, which shrinks the key and value projections, the MLP share rises further, 81% in Llama 3 8B.
Follow-up: What design exploits this? — Mixture of experts (lm17) replaces the MLP with several MLPs and routes each token to a few, growing parameters without growing per-token compute.
M
Pre-norm versus post-norm: what is the difference and why did pre-norm win?

Post-norm computes norm(x + f(x)), so the residual path itself passes through a normalisation at every layer; pre-norm computes x + f(norm(x)), leaving the residual path as a pure sum. In pre-norm the gradient reaches early layers through an identity path, so deep models train stably; post-norm models have large gradients near the output at initialisation and need a learning-rate warm-up. Xiong et al. showed pre-norm transformers train without warm-up, and GPT-2 onwards adopted it.

Follow-up: Does pre-norm have a cost? — The residual stream's magnitude grows with depth, so later layers' contributions are relatively smaller; models add a final norm before the LM head, and some research adds extra norms or scaling to counter this.
M
What is SwiGLU and why does Llama use an MLP width of 11,008?

SwiGLU is a gated MLP: compute two projections of the input, apply SiLU to one, multiply them element-wise, then project back: (SiLU(xW₁) ⊙ xW₃)W₂. It uses three matrices instead of two, so to match a standard 4·d MLP's parameters the hidden width is reduced to about two thirds of 4·d, 8d/3 = 10,923 for d = 4,096, which Llama rounds up to a multiple of 256, giving 11,008. Shazeer found gated variants gave lower perplexity than ReLU or GELU MLPs at equal parameters and compute.
M
What is weight tying and when is it worth it?

Using the transposed input embedding matrix as the LM head, so token vectors are read and written with the same matrix. It saves vocabulary × d_model parameters, 38.6M for GPT-2 small, which is 31% of that model, so it matters for small models with large vocabularies. Large models usually untie the matrices because the saving is a small share and separate matrices give slightly more flexibility.
M
Why do modern LLMs drop bias terms?

At scale they add almost nothing to quality, cost parameters and memory traffic, and complicate some optimisations and sharding schemes; some reports also find training more stable without them. Llama-style models drop biases in attention and MLP projections. GPT-2 still had them.
H
How does the forward FLOP count of a decoder-only model depend on parameters and context?

Each weight is used in one multiply-add per token, so the matrix multiplications cost about 2N FLOPs per token for N non-embedding parameters. Attention adds work that is not in the parameter count: per layer, scores and the weighted sum cost about 4·n·d FLOPs per token for context length n. For Llama 2 7B at n = 4,096 that is 32 × 4 × 4,096 × 4,096 ≈ 2.1 GFLOP per token on top of about 13 GFLOP, so roughly 15%; at 32K context the attention term exceeds the weights' term.
Follow-up: And training? — Backward costs about twice the forward, so training is about 6N FLOPs per token, the basis of compute estimates in lm7.
H
Why might a later layer of a pre-norm model contribute relatively little, and what does that imply?

The residual stream is a sum that grows as layers add to it, while each sub-layer reads a normalised copy and adds an output of roughly fixed scale. Late layers therefore change the stream proportionally less, and measurements find that removing some late or middle layers costs less than removing early ones. It implies redundancy that layer pruning and early-exit methods try to exploit, and motivates normalisation and scaling schemes that keep late layers effective.
H
What do the MLP layers appear to store, according to interpretability work?

Geva et al. showed an MLP can be read as a key-value memory: each row of the first matrix acts as a key that fires on a textual pattern in the input, and the corresponding row of the second matrix is a value that, projected through the LM head, raises the probability of tokens that tend to follow that pattern. Lower layers' keys respond to shallow patterns (specific words), upper layers' to semantic ones. Editing methods use this to locate and change individual facts.

Follow-up: Why does that matter in practice? — It explains why factual knowledge is spread across MLP weights and why fine-tuning on a small dataset can overwrite or fail to update facts, which bears on hallucination (lm15) and fine-tuning (lm11).
H
The GPT-2 paper's table lists the small model at 117M parameters, but counting the weights gives 124M. Why might counts disagree, and how do you count reliably?

Published counts differ by convention: whether embeddings, position embeddings, biases and norms are included, whether tied matrices are counted once, and plain errors. GPT-2 small has a 38.6M token embedding, 0.8M position embedding, 85.1M in blocks and a final norm, 124.4M in total. Count from the config layer by layer, as in the lab, and cross-check with the loaded model's parameter tensors.

t: Positional information: sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi
sum: Attention ignores order, so position has to be injected: sinusoidal and learned absolute embeddings, RoPE's rotations worked by hand, ALiBi's distance penalty, and how RoPE models are stretched to longer contexts with interpolation, base changes and YaRN.
prereq: lm2
Self-attention scores are query–key dot products followed by a softmax; without extra information, permuting the inputs just permutes the outputs, so attention cannot see order.
lm3
Each block reads the residual stream through a normalisation and adds back attention and MLP outputs; the embedding at the bottom is the stream's starting value.
ml13
Vectors can be rotated by multiplying with a rotation matrix; rotation changes direction but not length, and the dot product of two vectors depends only on their lengths and the angle between them.
why:
Take two sentences: "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog". Same five words, very different news. Now recall how self-attention works (lm2): each token's new vector is a weighted average of other tokens' values, with weights from query–key similarity. Nothing in that computation looks at where a token is. If you shuffle the words, every token gets exactly the same attention weights over the same set of other tokens, and the outputs are simply shuffled along with them. To a transformer with no positional information, both sentences are the same bag of words.

So position has to be put in deliberately, and how it is put in turns out to matter far more than it first appears. It decides whether a model can run at all on text longer than it was trained on. It decides how expensive it is to grow a model's context window from 4,000 tokens to 128,000, which is one of the main things LLM vendors have competed on since 2023. And it explains a family of strange behaviours: models that read long documents fluently but miss facts in the middle, models whose quality falls off a cliff at exactly their training length, and models whose output degrades subtly after someone changes a "rope_theta" setting in a config file.

It also matters in day-to-day engineering. When you choose a model for a long-document feature, the advertised context window tells you what the model accepts, not how well it uses what it accepts; understanding how the window was obtained (trained natively, or extended with interpolation from something shorter) tells you what to test before you trust it.

This lesson starts from why attention is order-blind, then walks through the four schemes you will be asked about. Sinusoidal and learned embeddings label each position with a vector. RoPE, the scheme used by Llama and most open models, rotates queries and keys so attention depends on relative distance; you will rotate one by hand. ALiBi subtracts a penalty proportional to distance. The last part covers context extension: why RoPE models fail past their training length, and how position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN and base changes stretch them, with Meta's position-interpolation paper as the real-world case.
primer:
The problem in one sentence

Attention scores come from dot products of content vectors, so they are the same whatever order the tokens arrive in. Positional information is any trick that makes a token's position affect the computation. There are two broad families. Absolute schemes give each position its own signature, "this is token number 17", and let the model work out relationships. Relative schemes make attention depend directly on the distance between two tokens, "this key is 3 tokens before this query", which is closer to how language works: the link between a verb and its subject does not care whether the sentence begins at token 5 or token 5,000.

An analogy: clocks with many hands

Picture labelling each position in a sequence with the reading of a clock that has many hands, each spinning at a different speed. A seconds hand changes noticeably from one position to the next, so it distinguishes neighbours; an hour hand barely moves between neighbours but separates positions that are hundreds apart. The original sinusoidal encoding writes down the angles of all the hands as a position label. RoPE goes one step further: it physically turns each query and key by its clock's angles, so that when a query compares itself with a key, what matters is the difference between their clock readings, the distance between them. The analogy breaks in an instructive place: a clock's hands come back round, so two positions exactly one revolution apart look identical on that hand. Using many hands at different speeds is what keeps positions distinguishable, and what happens when you go beyond the slowest hand's trained range is the whole problem of context extension.

Two places to put position

There are two natural places to inject position, and the four schemes split between them. The first is the input: add a position vector to each token's embedding before the first block, so the residual stream itself carries "I am token 17" and every layer can read it. The original transformer and GPT-2 do this. The second is inside attention, the only place where tokens interact: leave the residual stream alone and make the attention score between two tokens depend on their positions. RoPE (by rotating queries and keys) and ALiBi (by adding a penalty to the scores) do this. Putting position inside attention has a structural advantage: the score between a query and a key can be made to depend directly on their distance, in every layer, without the position signal being diluted as the stream accumulates other information.

What "extrapolation" means and why it matters

A model is trained on sequences up to some maximum length, its training context: 1,024 tokens for GPT-2, 2,048 for the first LLaMA, 4,096 for Llama 2. Running it on longer inputs is called extrapolation. With some schemes the model cannot even run (there is no learned vector for position 1,025); with others it runs but quality collapses; with others it degrades gently. Because training on long sequences is expensive (attention cost grows with the square of length), the industry's path to long-context models has been to pretrain mostly at moderate length and then extend, which is why the second half of this lesson is about extension methods.
