recap: In a decoder, each token's keys and values in every layer depend only on that token and earlier ones, so once computed they never change; the KV cache stores them so each new token computes only its own query, key and value.

Generation has two phases: prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and fills the cache; decode then produces one token per step, appending one key and value per layer and attending over the cache.
Without a cache, generating T tokens recomputes past keys and values about T²/2 times (500,500 projections for 1,000 tokens); with it, T times.
Cache bytes per token = 2 (key and value) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per number: Llama 2 7B (32 × 32 × 128, fp16) needs 512 KiB per token, 2 GiB for a 4,096-token sequence.
Llama 2 70B with 8 KV heads needs 320 KiB per token; with standard multi-head attention (64 KV heads) it would need 2.5 MiB, eight times more, and 10 GiB per 4,096-token sequence.
Decode is memory-bound: each step reads all weights plus every active sequence's cache, so at large batch or long context the cache, not the weights, dominates step time and limits batch size.
Multi-query attention (MQA) shares one key and value head across all query heads; grouped-query attention (GQA) shares one per group, interpolating between MQA and multi-head attention (MHA).

The GQA paper uptrained T5-XXL from MHA using 5% of pretraining compute: GQA-8 reached an average of 47.1 against 47.2 for MHA and 46.6 for MQA, with 0.28 s per sample against 1.51 s for MHA and 0.24 s for MQA.

Llama 2 adopted GQA with 8 KV heads for its 34B and 70B models, and Llama 3 for all sizes; an MHA checkpoint can be converted by mean-pooling each group's key and value heads and briefly continuing training.
Further cache savings come from storing it in 8-bit, from paging and sharing it across requests (lm13), and from compressing keys and values into a latent vector (multi-head latent attention).
glossary: Producing text one token at a time, each token conditioned on all previous ones and appended before the next step.
The generation phase that produces one token per step per sequence, reading all weights and the sequence's KV cache each step.
Binary units: 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB, 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB (about 1.074 × 10⁹ bytes).
One floating-point operation; a multiply-add counts as two. TFLOP/s means 10¹² per second.
Attention in which query heads are divided into groups and each group shares one key head and one value head.
High-bandwidth memory: the GPU's main memory, where weights and the KV cache live; 80 GB at about 3.35 TB/s on an H100 SXM.
The size of one head's query, key and value vectors, usually 128 in current LLMs.
The stored key and value vectors of all previous tokens in every layer, kept during generation so they are not recomputed.
One key projection and one value projection; MHA has as many as query heads, GQA fewer, MQA one.
Limited by how fast data can be read from memory rather than by arithmetic speed.
Standard attention in which every head has its own query, key and value projections.
DeepSeek's scheme that caches a small compressed latent vector per token per layer and reconstructs keys and values from it.
Attention in which all query heads share a single key head and a single value head.
The first phase of a request: one parallel forward pass over the whole prompt that fills the KV cache and produces the first output token.
Splitting each weight matrix across several GPUs so they compute one layer together; attention is usually split by heads.
The time of one decode step as seen by a user: the gap between successive generated tokens.
The delay from sending a request to receiving the first generated token, dominated by queueing and prefill.
Continuing to train an existing checkpoint after changing its architecture, such as converting MHA to GQA, using a small fraction of the original compute.
drill:
Estimate — how many users fit?

You serve Llama 3 70B (80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128) in bf16 on one node of 8 × 80 GB GPUs with tensor parallelism. Average conversations are 6,000 tokens. How many can be served concurrently, and what would the number be if the model used MHA?

Answer

Memory available: 8 × 80 = 640 GB; at 90% usable, 576 GB. Weights: about 70.6B × 2 bytes ≈ 141 GB. Free for cache ≈ 435 GB (ignoring activation overhead, which is small at decode).

Cache per conversation: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB per token; × 6,000 = 1.97 GB.

Concurrency: 435 ÷ 1.97 ≈ 220 conversations.

With MHA (64 KV heads): 2.5 MiB per token, 15.7 GB per conversation, about 27 conversations: eight times fewer. Each decode step would also read eight times more cache bytes, so it would be slower at the same batch.

Caveats to mention: conversations vary in length, so paged allocation matters; the latency target may cap the batch below the memory limit, because each step reads all active caches (220 × 1.97 GB ≈ 433 GB, about 16 ms per step at 8 × 3.35 TB/s aggregate on top of the weights); and an 8-bit cache would double capacity.

Diagnose — the assistant that slows down over time

Users report that a chat assistant's answers stream quickly at the start of a conversation but noticeably slower after an hour of back-and-forth. GPU compute utilisation is low. What is happening and what are your options?

Answer

Each decode step reads the whole conversation's KV cache, so time per output token grows linearly with conversation length; after an hour the context may be tens of thousands of tokens, making cache reads dominate each step. Low compute utilisation confirms the step is memory-bound. As the caches of long conversations grow, the server can also batch fewer users, so per-user throughput falls further, and it may be evicting and recomputing caches. Options: summarise or truncate older turns to bound the context; enable prefix caching so the system prompt is shared; quantise the cache to 8-bit; serve a GQA model or one with sliding-window layers; and check engine metrics for preemptions, which add recomputation stalls.
qa: E
What is the KV cache and why is it needed?

During generation, every new token must attend to the keys and values of all earlier tokens in every layer. Those keys and values never change once computed, because of the causal mask, so the model stores them and each step computes only the new token's query, key and value. Without the cache, generating T tokens would recompute past keys and values about T²/2 times instead of T times.
E
What exactly is stored, and what is not?

For each layer, each KV head and each past token: one key vector and one value vector of the head dimension. Queries are not stored, because each is used only by its own token at its own step; attention scores and weights are recomputed each step for the new query.
E
Write the formula for KV-cache size.

Bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per element. Multiply by context length for one sequence and by the number of concurrent sequences for a batch. For Llama 2 7B in fp16: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 524,288 bytes, 512 KiB per token, 2 GiB per 4,096-token sequence.
M
Compute the KV cache of a 70B model with and without GQA at a 4,096-token context and batch 32.

Llama 2 70B has 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128. With GQA: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 320 KiB per token, 1.25 GiB per sequence, 40 GiB for 32 sequences. With MHA it would have 64 KV heads: 2.5 MiB per token, 10 GiB per sequence and 320 GiB for the batch, which would not fit on a node of 8 × 80 GB GPUs alongside the 138 GB of weights.

Follow-up: How would you get the batch of 32 to fit in the MHA case? — Shorter contexts, an 8-bit cache, paged allocation so short requests do not reserve the maximum length, or fewer concurrent sequences; architecturally, GQA is the fix.
M
Why is the decode phase memory-bound, and how does the cache change that?

Each decode step does one new token per sequence, so every weight read from memory is used for only batch-size multiply-adds, far below the arithmetic a GPU can do per byte. The cache adds more bytes: each step reads every active sequence's whole cache to compute one row of attention, with only a couple of FLOPs per byte read. On an H100, Llama 2 7B's weights take about 4 ms to read, but 27 sequences of 4,096 tokens add about 17 ms of cache reads per step.
Follow-up: So what helps decode most? — Reading fewer bytes: GQA or MQA, cache quantisation, weight quantisation, and batching to amortise weight reads.
M
Compare MHA, MQA and GQA.

MHA gives every query head its own key and value heads: best quality, largest cache. MQA shares one key and value head across all query heads: cache smaller by the head count (64× for 64 heads), fastest decode, but some quality loss and training instability. GQA shares one key and value head per group of query heads, typically 8 KV heads: about 8× smaller cache than MHA in a 64-head model, quality close to MHA, speed close to MQA. Most current LLMs use GQA.
M
What happens in prefill versus decode, and why do they behave so differently?

Prefill runs the whole prompt in one forward pass: thousands of tokens share each weight read, so it is compute-bound and fills the cache for all prompt tokens at once; it determines time to first token. Decode generates one token per step: each step reads all weights and the cache for a single new token per sequence, so it is memory-bound; it determines time per output token. Serving systems schedule the two differently because one is limited by FLOPs and the other by bytes.
M
How does the GQA paper convert an existing multi-head model?

Group the query heads, build each group's single key and value projection by mean-pooling the key and value projection matrices of the heads in that group, then continue pretraining (uptrain) the converted model for a small fraction of the original compute; they used 5% for T5-XXL. Mean-pooling worked better than picking one head or random initialisation.
M
Why does GQA work well with tensor parallelism?

Attention is usually split across GPUs by heads. With 8 KV heads and 8 GPUs, each GPU holds one KV head and its group of query heads, so nothing is duplicated. With MQA's single KV head, every GPU needs a copy of it, so the cache per GPU is the same as GQA-8 anyway; the Llama 2 paper points this out as one reason it chose GQA for the models it serves on 8-GPU nodes.
H
Your service runs out of GPU memory at 20 concurrent users with 8K-token conversations on a 13B MHA model. Diagnose and fix.

Llama 2 13B has 40 layers, 40 heads, head dimension 128: 2 × 40 × 40 × 128 × 2 = 800 KiB per token, so 8,192 tokens is 6.25 GiB per conversation and 20 users need 125 GiB, far more than an 80 GB GPU has after 26 GB of weights. Options in order of effort: paged KV allocation so conversations only hold what they use (lm13), an 8-bit cache (halves it), prefix sharing for common system prompts, capping context or summarising old turns, tensor parallelism over more GPUs, and switching to a GQA model, which at 8 KV heads would cut the cache 5× for this shape.

Follow-up: What metric would have warned you? — KV-cache utilisation and preemption or eviction counts from the serving engine, alongside queue time; they rise before out-of-memory errors or latency spikes.
H
Why does the KV cache make long-context serving expensive even with FlashAttention?

FlashAttention removes the n × n score matrix from memory but cannot remove the cache: each decode step must still read every cached key and value of the sequence, so step time grows linearly with context, and capacity falls inversely with it. A 128K-token conversation on Llama 3 8B (128 KiB per token) holds 16 GiB of cache, more than the model's 16 GB of weights, for a single user.

Follow-up: What architectural ideas attack this? — Fewer KV heads (GQA, MQA), compressed latent caches (MLA), sliding-window layers that only keep recent tokens, cache quantisation, and offloading cold parts of the cache to CPU memory.
H
What is multi-head latent attention and how does it differ from GQA?

GQA reduces the number of distinct key and value heads. MLA, introduced in DeepSeek-V2, instead projects each token's hidden state down to a small latent vector, caches only that latent, and reconstructs per-head keys and values from it with up-projection matrices; position information is handled with a small separate rotary component. It can make the cache smaller than GQA while keeping per-head keys and values distinct, at the cost of extra computation and more complex kernels.
Follow-up: Why is the extra computation acceptable? — Decode is memory-bound, so trading bytes read for FLOPs is usually a win.
H
How would you estimate the maximum batch size for a model on one GPU?

Free memory = GPU memory × usable fraction − weights − activation and framework overhead. Cache per sequence = bytes per token × (prompt + output length). Maximum concurrent sequences ≈ free memory ÷ cache per sequence. For Llama 3 8B on an 80 GB GPU at 90% usable: 72 − 16.1 ≈ 55.9 GB free; at 128 KiB per token and 4,096 tokens per sequence, about 104 sequences. Then check the latency target: each step reads weights plus all those caches, so step time rises with batch.

t: How a chat model is made: pretraining, SFT, RLHF, DPO
sum: The three stages that turn a text predictor into an assistant: pretraining, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, and preference tuning with a reward model and RL or with DPO, including the Bradley–Terry and DPO losses worked by hand and what each stage can and cannot fix.
prereq: lm3

A decoder-only transformer outputs, at every position, a probability for every next token; the probability of a whole response is the product of its tokens' probabilities, so its log-probability is a sum.
ml5
Cross-entropy loss is −log of the probability given to the correct answer; training minimises its average over the data.
ml6
Logistic regression models a probability as sigmoid(score); the loss −log sigmoid(score) pushes the score of the observed outcome up.
dl11
Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained network on a smaller task-specific dataset, usually with a lower learning rate, reusing what it learned.
dl5
Optimisers such as AdamW take gradient steps on the loss; the learning rate controls how far each step moves the weights.
why:
In 2020 OpenAI released GPT-3, a 175-billion-parameter model that had read a large slice of the internet. It could write poetry, translate and complete code. It was also frustrating to use. Ask it "Explain the moon landing to a six-year-old" and it might produce a list of similar prompts, as if continuing a web page of writing exercises. Ask it a question and it might answer, or ramble, or invent a confident falsehood, or produce something offensive it had picked up from its training data. It knew a great deal; it simply was not trying to help you, because nothing in its training had asked it to.

Two years later the same company published InstructGPT, and the result surprised people: human raters preferred the answers of a 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, a model more than 100 times larger. The difference was not more data or a better architecture. It was what happened after pretraining: a stage of imitating example answers written by people, and a stage of optimising against people's preferences between answers. ChatGPT, launched later that year, was built the same way, and every chat assistant since follows some version of this pipeline.

For an AI engineer this pipeline matters in three practical ways. It explains the behaviour of the models you use: why they are helpful and polite, why they sometimes flatter you or refuse harmless requests, and why no amount of tuning makes them stop hallucinating. It is the toolkit you reach for when you adapt a model to your own domain or style. And it is a standard interview topic, usually with a request to write down and explain a loss.

This lesson starts from what pretraining produces and why it is not an assistant, then covers supervised fine-tuning, preference data, the reward model (with the Bradley–Terry loss worked by hand), RLHF with its KL penalty and the reward-hacking problem it guards against, the closed-form optimum that makes DPO possible, and DPO itself with one pair's loss computed by hand. It ends with what each stage can and cannot fix. The lab builds a toy world of five candidate responses, trains a reward model on simulated comparisons, and shows that DPO lands on exactly the policy RLHF would.
primer:
Three stages, three teachers

Think of training an assistant the way you might train a new employee who has read every book in the library but has never had a job. Pretraining is the reading: the model sees trillions of tokens of text and learns to predict the next token, absorbing language, facts, styles and reasoning patterns. It comes out knowledgeable but aimless. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shadowing: the employee studies thousands of examples of good answers to customer requests, written by experienced colleagues, and learns to imitate them, absorbing the format, the tone and the habit of actually answering. Preference tuning is feedback: the employee drafts several answers, a supervisor says which ones are better, and the employee adjusts towards what gets approved. The supervisor does not need to be able to write the perfect answer, only to recognise a better one.

The analogy shows what each stage can fix. Reading gives knowledge; shadowing gives format and manners; feedback polishes judgement on whatever the supervisor can assess. None of the later stages adds knowledge the reading did not provide, and feedback teaches whatever the supervisor rewards, including bad habits if the supervisor is easily impressed by long, confident answers. Where the analogy breaks: a model has no intentions to correct, and "adjusting towards approval" is a precise mathematical operation on probabilities, which the body of this lesson writes down.

The pipeline in one picture

Why not just pretrain on better data?

A natural question is why the assistant behaviour is not simply baked into pretraining by choosing better text. The answer is scale and specificity. Pretraining needs trillions of tokens, far more than anyone could write in an assistant's voice, so it uses whatever text exists, and most text on the internet is not an assistant helping a user. The post-training stages are tiny by comparison (thousands to hundreds of thousands of examples) but highly specific: every example is exactly the behaviour you want. This division of labour is the reason the pipeline exists. Pretraining buys general competence cheaply per token; post-training spends expensive human attention where it has the most effect, on the model's default behaviour. It also explains why companies can release many differently behaving products, a coding assistant, a customer-service bot, a cautious medical assistant, from the same base model: they share the expensive stage and differ only in the cheap ones.

What "preference" means in numbers

The preference stage works with comparisons: a prompt, two responses, and a label saying which one a rater preferred. From many such comparisons, the training either fits a reward model, a network that gives any response a score, and then optimises the chat model to earn high scores (RLHF), or skips the reward model and adjusts the chat model's probabilities directly so that preferred responses become more likely relative to rejected ones (DPO). Both keep the model close to its starting point, measured by a quantity called KL divergence, so it does not forget how to write well in pursuit of a score.
body:
1. What pretraining produces

Pretraining trains a decoder-only transformer (lm3) to predict the next token on an enormous corpus, typically trillions of tokens of web pages, books, code and papers, filtered and deduplicated. The objective is plain cross-entropy: at every position, −log of the probability the model gave to the actual next token, averaged over everything. This is self-supervised (ml1): the labels come from the text itself, so the data scales without human labelling, which is why pretraining can use so much of it and why it consumes almost all of a model's training compute. Llama 3, for example, was pretrained on about 15 trillion tokens.

The result, a base model, is remarkably capable and remarkably unhelpful. To minimise next-token loss on the internet it has had to learn grammar, facts, the structure of arguments, code, arithmetic patterns and many styles of writing. But its behaviour is to continue a document in the way such documents tend to continue. A question might be followed by an answer, or by another question, or by a forum signature. It has no default persona, no notion of a user, no habit of stopping when the answer is complete, and no preference for truth over plausible fiction, because the internet contains both.

2. Prompting a base model, and why it is not enough

You can coax a base model into answering by writing the start of a document in which an answer naturally follows, for example a few question–answer pairs and then your question ("few-shot prompting"). GPT-3's paper was largely about this. But it is fragile: results depend on the exact examples, the model still drifts, and there is no way to express "be concise, be honest, refuse harmful requests" except by more examples. Engineers want a model that treats any instruction as an instruction. That requires changing the model's weights so that the assistant role becomes its default behaviour.

3. Supervised fine-tuning

SFT continues training the base model on a dataset of demonstrations: prompts paired with high-quality responses, written by people or curated from good existing answers, formatted as conversations with the model's chat template (lm1). The loss is the same next-token cross-entropy as pretraining, with one change: it is usually computed only on the tokens of the assistant's response. The prompt tokens are fed in so the model can condition on them, but their predictions are excluded from the loss, because the goal is to learn to produce answers, not to imitate user messages.

A worked view of the loss: suppose the response is "Paris." (two tokens, "Paris" and "."). If after the prompt the model gives "Paris" probability 0.6 and then "." probability 0.9, the SFT loss on this example is −(ln 0.6 + ln 0.9)/2 = (0.511 + 0.105)/2 = 0.308 per token. Gradient descent raises those probabilities. Over thousands of examples, the model learns the format (answer directly, use the template's end-of-turn token), the style (structured, polite, concise or detailed as demonstrated), and the general habit of doing what the instruction says. InstructGPT's SFT dataset had about 13,000 training prompts, written by labellers or taken from early API usage. The LIMA study (Zhou et al., 2023) fine-tuned a 65B LLaMA on only 1,000 carefully curated examples and found its responses equivalent to or preferred over GPT-4's in 43% of cases, which the authors took as evidence that almost all knowledge comes from pretraining and SFT mainly teaches the format to express it.

4. What SFT can and cannot do

SFT is efficient at teaching anything that can be demonstrated: formats, tone, tool-call syntax (lm16), domain conventions, refusing certain requests. Its limits follow from imitation. The model can only be as good as its demonstrations, and writing excellent demonstrations is slow and expensive. It learns to imitate the surface of answers it may not be able to back up: if a demonstration states a fact the model does not know, SFT teaches it to state facts of that kind confidently, which is one root of hallucination (lm15). And imitation gives no signal about which of two imperfect answers is better; every token in the demonstration is treated as equally correct.

5. Why comparisons

People are much better at judging than at producing. Most of us cannot write a perfect explanation of quantum tunnelling for a child, but we can usually say which of two attempts is clearer. Comparisons are also more consistent across raters than absolute scores ("is this a 6 or a 7?"), which vary with each rater's personal scale. So the preference stage collects, for many prompts, several responses sampled from the SFT model and asks raters which they prefer. InstructGPT showed labellers between 4 and 9 responses per prompt and asked for a ranking, which yields up to K(K − 1)/2 pairwise comparisons per prompt (36 for K = 9); its reward-model dataset had about 33,000 training prompts.

6. The reward model and the Bradley–Terry loss

A reward model takes a prompt and a response and outputs one number, its score. In practice it is an LLM (InstructGPT used a 6B model initialised from SFT) with its vocabulary output layer replaced by a single scalar output read at the last token. It is trained with the Bradley–Terry model of comparisons, which says the probability that response A is preferred to B is the logistic sigmoid of the difference of their scores:

P(y_w ≻ y_l | x) = σ( r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l) )        σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z))
loss = −log σ( r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l) )

where y_w is the chosen ("winning") response and y_l the rejected one. This is exactly logistic regression (ml6) on the score difference. By hand: if the reward model gives the chosen response 1.5 and the rejected 0.3, the difference is 1.2, the predicted probability that the chosen one wins is σ(1.2) = 1/(1 + e^(−1.2)) = 1/(1 + 0.301) = 0.769, and the loss is −ln 0.769 = 0.263. If the scores were reversed the loss would be −ln σ(−1.2) = −ln 0.231 = 1.463, a much larger penalty. Note that only differences matter: adding 10 to every score changes nothing, so reward values have no absolute meaning. In the lab, a reward model fitted to 4,000 simulated comparisons recovers the hidden true rewards [0, 1, 2, 1.2, −2] as [0, 1.09, 2.16, 1.14, −1.96].

7. RLHF: optimising against the reward with a leash

With a reward model, the chat model (now called the policy, in reinforcement-learning language) can be optimised to produce high-scoring responses. The objective is

maximise  E_{x ~ prompts, y ~ π(·|x)} [ r(x, y) ]  −  β · KL( π(·|x) ‖ π_ref(·|x) )

The first term rewards high scores. The second is the KL divergence between the policy π and the frozen reference π_ref (the SFT model): a measure of how differently the two assign probability to responses, zero when they are identical. For one response it is estimated by log π(y|x) − log π_ref(y|x), summed over the response's tokens, and InstructGPT subtracts β times this per-token quantity from the reward. The coefficient β sets the trade-off. Because responses are generated by sampling, with no gradient through the choice of tokens, the optimisation uses a policy-gradient RL algorithm, typically PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization): sample responses for a batch of prompts, score them, estimate which tokens contributed to above-average reward, and nudge their probabilities up, with a clipping rule that limits how far any single update can move the policy. PPO needs four models in memory at once (policy, reference, reward model and a value model that estimates expected reward), which makes it heavy to run.

8. Reward hacking and why the leash matters

The reward model is trained on responses from the SFT model. As the policy moves away, it produces responses unlike anything the reward model saw, and there the reward model's scores are unreliable. Optimising hard finds those errors: if raters slightly preferred longer answers, the policy learns to pad; if a phrasing happens to score well, it repeats it. This is reward hacking, an instance of Goodhart's law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"). The lab shows it in miniature. A proxy reward over-rates a "verbose" response. As β falls (weaker leash), the proxy reward of the optimised policy rises from 0.81 to 2.15, but its true reward peaks at 1.28 and then falls to 1.20, while with an accurate reward model the true reward would have reached 2.00. The KL penalty keeps the policy in the region where the reward model is trustworthy; early stopping on independent evaluations does the same from the other side.

9. The optimum of the RLHF objective

For a fixed prompt, the KL-regularised objective has an exact solution. The best policy is the reference policy reweighted by the exponentiated reward:

π*(y | x) = π_ref(y | x) · exp( r(x, y) / β ) / Z(x)

where Z(x) is the normalising constant that makes the probabilities sum to 1. Read it as: start from what the SFT model would say, and multiply each response's probability by e^(reward/β). With a large β the multipliers are all near 1 and the policy barely changes; with a small β the highest-reward response dominates. In the lab's toy world, with β = 10 the policy is almost the reference (KL 0.007), at β = 1 the best response's probability rises from 0.10 to 0.35, at β = 0.3 it reaches 0.88 and at β = 0.1 the policy puts all its mass on it (KL 2.27). For a real LLM this formula cannot be used directly, because Z(x) sums over every possible response, which is why RLHF uses RL to approach it. But it is the key to DPO.

10. DPO: the reward model was hiding in the policy

Rafailov et al. (2023) noticed that the formula can be turned around. Take logs and rearrange: r(x, y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x). Any reward can be written in terms of its optimal policy, plus a term that depends only on the prompt. Now substitute this expression into the Bradley–Terry loss. The loss uses only the difference of the rewards of the chosen and rejected responses to the same prompt, so the troublesome β·log Z(x) term cancels. What remains is a loss on the policy itself:

L_DPO = −log σ( β · [ (log π(y_w|x) − log π_ref(y_w|x)) − (log π(y_l|x) − log π_ref(y_l|x)) ] )

Training the policy with this loss on preference pairs is equivalent to fitting a reward model and then solving the KL-regularised RL problem exactly, but there is no reward model, no sampling and no RL: just a forward pass of the policy and the frozen reference on both responses of each pair, and a classification-style loss. The quantity β·log(π/π_ref) is called the implicit reward: how much more likely the tuned model has made a response than the reference made it. The lab trains a tabular policy with this loss on the same 4,000 comparisons and lands on exactly the RLHF optimum, [0.109, 0.327, 0.348, 0.207, 0.009] in both cases.

11. One DPO loss by hand

Take β = 0.1 and one pair. Log-probabilities of whole responses are sums over their tokens. Suppose the policy gives the chosen response a log-probability of −12.0 and the rejected −15.0, while the frozen reference gave −13.0 and −14.0. The chosen log-ratio is −12.0 − (−13.0) = +1.0 (the policy made it e¹ ≈ 2.7 times more likely), the rejected log-ratio is −15.0 − (−14.0) = −1.0 (the policy made it 2.7 times less likely). The margin is β × (1.0 − (−1.0)) = 0.2. The loss is −log σ(0.2) = −log 0.550 = 0.598. At the start of training the policy equals the reference, both log-ratios are 0, the margin is 0 and the loss is −log 0.5 = ln 2 = 0.693. The gradient on this pair is proportional to σ(−0.2) = 0.450: pairs the model already ranks correctly with a large margin contribute little, so training concentrates on pairs it still gets wrong.

12. DPO versus RLHF in practice

DPO's appeal is operational: one trainable model plus a frozen copy, a loss as simple as supervised learning, no generation in the loop, and stable training. Rafailov et al. reported that on the Reddit TL;DR ("too long; didn't read") summarisation task, judged against reference summaries by GPT-4, DPO reached a win rate of about 61% at sampling temperature 0, against 57% for PPO at its best temperature, and was more robust to the sampling temperature; in a human evaluation DPO samples were preferred 58% of the time over PPO's. The limitations come from DPO being offline: it learns only from the fixed pairs it is given and cannot try new responses and see how they score. If the pairs were sampled from a different model, or are noisy, DPO can over-fit them, and it has been observed to lower the probability of both chosen and rejected responses while widening the gap between them. Online and iterative variants generate new pairs from the current policy and label them (with humans, a reward model or a judge model), recovering some of RL's exploration. Large labs use RL with reward models, DPO-style methods, or both in sequence.

13. Variants worth knowing

Rejection sampling (best-of-n) fine-tuning: sample n responses per prompt, keep the one the reward model scores highest, and do SFT on those; simple and stable, used in Llama 2's pipeline alongside PPO. RLAIF and Constitutional AI: replace some human labels with labels from a model prompted with a written set of principles, as in Anthropic's Constitutional AI, which made harmlessness training cheaper and more transparent. RL with verifiable rewards: for maths and code, the reward can be computed by checking the answer or running tests, which removes reward-model errors on those tasks; this is central to recent reasoning-focused training. All of them sit on the same foundation: start from a good SFT model, optimise towards a preference or reward signal, and stay close to the reference.

14. What each stage can and cannot fix

StageSignalFixesCannot fix
Pretrainingnext token of web-scale textknowledge, language, skillsassistant behaviour, safety
SFTdemonstrationsformat, instruction following, stylequality beyond the demonstrations; missing knowledge
RLHF / DPOcomparisonshelpfulness and harmlessness as raters judge themmissing knowledge; rater biases (length, sycophancy); adversarial misuse

The practical rule follows: if a model lacks knowledge, give it the knowledge at inference time (retrieval, lm9) or continue pretraining; if it has the knowledge but uses the wrong format, use SFT; if it produces acceptable answers but not the best ones by criteria people can judge, use preference tuning.
deep:
Deriving the optimal policy

For one prompt, maximise Σ_y π(y)r(y) − β Σ_y π(y) log(π(y)/π_ref(y)) over distributions π. Rewrite it as −β Σ_y π(y) log(π(y) / (π_ref(y) e^{r(y)/β})). Define π*(y) = π_ref(y)e^{r(y)/β}/Z with Z = Σ_y π_ref(y)e^{r(y)/β}; the objective becomes −β·KL(π ‖ π*) + β log Z. KL is never negative and is zero only when π = π*, so π* is the unique maximiser. This two-line argument is worth being able to reproduce: it explains both why RLHF's solution is "reference times exponentiated reward" and why DPO's reparameterisation is exact rather than an approximation. The catch in practice is that the policy is a neural network that may not be able to represent π* exactly, and both methods optimise from finite data.

PPO in a little more detail

Policy-gradient methods estimate the gradient of expected reward as E[∇log π(y|x)·A], where A, the advantage, is how much better a response (or token) did than expected. PPO estimates expected reward with a learned value model and computes per-token advantages; it then maximises a clipped surrogate objective in which the ratio π_new/π_old for each token is clipped to a band such as [0.8, 1.2], so that no update moves the policy far from the one that generated the samples. This stabilises training but brings many hyperparameters (clip range, value-loss weight, KL coefficient, number of epochs per batch) and the cost of generating fresh samples every iteration. InstructGPT also mixed in pretraining gradients ("PPO-ptx") to reduce the "alignment tax", the drop on standard NLP benchmarks after RLHF, finding it worked better than simply increasing the KL coefficient.

Reward-model over-optimisation as a curve

Studies that train policies against a learned "proxy" reward while measuring a separate "gold" reward find a characteristic shape: as the policy moves away from the reference (measured by KL), the proxy reward keeps rising, while the gold reward rises, peaks and then declines. Larger reward models and more preference data push the peak further out but do not remove it. This is the quantitative version of reward hacking, and it is why practitioners treat KL (or DPO's β) as a budget and pick checkpoints by independent evaluation rather than by training reward. The lab's last table is a five-response version of this curve.

Failure modes of DPO

Because DPO's loss depends only on the difference of log-ratios, it can be satisfied by pushing both responses' probabilities down, the rejected one more. Observers have reported exactly this: the chosen response's likelihood falls during training, mass moves to responses outside the dataset, and generations can lengthen or degrade. Remedies include adding an SFT term on the chosen responses, using pairs sampled from the policy being trained (so the data is "on-policy"), filtering noisy pairs, and tuning β (higher β keeps the policy closer to the reference). Variants change the loss shape (IPO, identity preference optimisation, adds a regulariser that stops margins growing without bound) or drop the need for pairs (KTO, Kahneman–Tversky optimisation, uses single responses labelled good or bad). The common thread is controlling how far, and in which direction, the policy moves away from data it was trained on.

Why β means the same thing in RLHF and DPO

In RLHF, β multiplies the KL penalty: larger β, stronger leash. In DPO, β multiplies the log-ratios inside the sigmoid. These are the same parameter, because DPO's loss was derived from the RLHF objective with that β. Intuitively, a larger β means a given difference in log-ratios produces a larger margin, so the loss is satisfied with smaller moves away from the reference; a smaller β requires larger log-ratio changes to reach the same margin, letting the policy drift further. Typical values in DPO practice are around 0.1, and the DPO authors note they barely tuned it, which is one reason published DPO numbers may understate what careful tuning achieves.

Who the raters are matters

InstructGPT's own discussion stresses that the model was aligned to the preferences of a particular group: about 40 contractors following OpenAI's instructions, plus the researchers who wrote those instructions, not to "human values" in general. Rater demographics, instructions and incentives shape the reward. Raters under time pressure favour longer, well-formatted answers that look thorough; raters without domain expertise cannot detect subtle factual errors, so the model learns to be convincing rather than correct in those domains. This is why high-stakes domains use expert raters, why rubrics are explicit, and why preference data is audited for systematic biases such as length.

Where the knowledge comes from: superficial alignment

LIMA's authors proposed a "superficial alignment hypothesis": a model's knowledge and capabilities are learned almost entirely during pretraining, and alignment teaches which sub-distribution of formats and styles to use when interacting with users. The evidence is that small, high-quality SFT sets produce strong assistants, and that post-training rarely improves knowledge benchmarks. The hypothesis is not the whole story, since preference tuning measurably changes behaviours such as refusal, honesty and multi-step reasoning, and RL with verifiable rewards can substantially improve maths and coding. But it is the right default expectation for an engineer deciding whether fine-tuning will fix a problem.
prod:
The public case: InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., OpenAI, 2022)

InstructGPT is the paper that defined the modern pipeline, and its numbers are worth knowing. OpenAI hired a team of about 40 contractors to label data. Step 1, SFT: labellers wrote demonstrations for prompts, many taken from the OpenAI API, giving an SFT dataset of about 13,000 training prompts. Step 2, reward model: labellers ranked between 4 and 9 sampled responses per prompt; the reward-model dataset had about 33,000 training prompts, and the authors used 6B reward models because 175B reward-model training was unstable. Step 3, RL: the SFT model was optimised with PPO against the reward model on about 31,000 prompts, with a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model and, in the "PPO-ptx" variant, pretraining gradients mixed in. All models used the GPT-3 architecture at 1.3B, 6B and 175B parameters.

The headline results: labellers preferred outputs of the 1.3B InstructGPT model to those of the 175B GPT-3, despite its having over 100 times fewer parameters; the 175B InstructGPT was preferred to 175B GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time and to few-shot-prompted GPT-3 71 ± 4% of the time. On TruthfulQA it generated truthful and informative answers about twice as often as GPT-3. When prompted to be respectful it generated about 25% fewer toxic outputs, but it showed no improvement on bias benchmarks. Labellers held out from training preferred it at about the same rate. The authors also reported an "alignment tax" on some public NLP datasets, mitigated by PPO-ptx, and they were explicit that the model was aligned to their labellers' and researchers' preferences, not to a universal standard. A year later DPO (Rafailov et al.) showed the same objective could be optimised without the reward model and RL loop, and open-model pipelines adopted it widely.

Failure modes in production

Length creep. After preference tuning, answers get longer and more padded. Cause: rater or reward-model preference for length. Detect with response-length tracking and length-controlled win rates; fix with length penalties, rubric changes or pairs that prefer concise answers.

Over-refusal. Safety-focused preference data teaches the model to refuse borderline but legitimate requests ("how do I kill a Python process?"). Track refusal rates on a benign-but-edgy evaluation set alongside harmful-request refusal.

Sycophancy. The model agrees with users' incorrect claims or changes correct answers when challenged. Measure with paired prompts that state a wrong view; counter with data that rewards respectful correction.

Capability regressions. Fine-tuning on a narrow domain degrades general skills, such as coding after a customer-service fine-tune. Keep a broad regression suite and mix in general data.

Template mismatch. SFT and preference data formatted with a different chat template from the one used at inference silently degrades the model (lm1). Validate the full serving path on held-out conversations.

What to track during a preference-tuning run

Training reward or DPO loss and accuracy (fraction of pairs ranked correctly), the KL to the reference or the chosen and rejected log-ratios, response length, held-out win rate against the SFT model judged by humans or a strong model with a fixed rubric, and task-specific checks such as factual accuracy and policy compliance. Pick the checkpoint by the held-out evaluations, not by the training reward.
myths: RLHF teaches the model new knowledge.

Preference tuning reweights behaviours the model already has: which of the answers it could give it actually gives. LIMA's authors fine-tuned a 65B model on only 1,000 curated examples and concluded that almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining. If the base model does not know a fact, SFT and RLHF can teach it to say so politely, or to state a fluent guess; they cannot add the fact.
The reward model knows what humans want.

It is a learned approximation trained on a finite set of comparisons, and it has blind spots: it may prefer longer answers, confident tone or particular phrasings regardless of correctness. Optimising hard against it finds those blind spots. That is reward hacking, and it is why RLHF adds a KL penalty and why the lab's policy, trained on a reward that over-rates verbosity, gains reward while its true quality falls.
DPO is a different objective from RLHF.

DPO optimises the same KL-regularised objective. Rafailov et al. show that the optimal RLHF policy is the reference policy reweighted by exp(reward/β), invert that to write the reward in terms of the policy, and substitute it into the reward model's loss. The result trains the policy directly on preference pairs, with no separate reward model and no sampling. The lab's DPO policy and the closed-form RLHF optimum agree to three decimals.
SFT and preference tuning are interchangeable.

They use different signals. SFT imitates demonstrations, so it can only be as good as the people writing them, and it teaches format and style efficiently. Preference tuning uses comparisons, which are easier to give than perfect answers and can push the model beyond the demonstrators' quality on what raters can judge. Most pipelines use SFT first, then preference tuning.
The KL penalty is a minor regulariser that can be set to zero.

Without it, the policy drifts to whatever the reward model scores highest, including degenerate outputs it has never been trained to judge, and loses the language quality of the SFT model. β sets the trade: in the lab's toy problem, β = 10 barely moves the policy (KL 0.007) while β = 0.1 collapses onto one response (KL 2.27).
Preference tuning makes models more truthful.

It makes them more like what raters prefer, which correlates with helpfulness and truthfulness but also with confidence and agreeableness. InstructGPT improved on TruthfulQA, but sycophancy (agreeing with the user's stated view) is a documented side effect of optimising for approval. Truthfulness needs targeted data and evaluation (lm15).
lab:
Goal: compute the Bradley–Terry and DPO losses by hand, fit a reward model to simulated comparisons, see the RLHF optimum for different β, show that DPO trained directly on the comparisons reaches the same policy, and watch reward hacking happen. A toy world with one prompt and five candidate responses; NumPy only, a few seconds.

import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
softmax = lambda z: np.exp(z - z.max()) / np.exp(z - z.max()).sum()

# ---- 1. the two losses for one preference pair, by hand
r_w, r_l = 1.5, 0.3                                         # reward model scores: chosen, rejected
print(f"reward-model (Bradley-Terry) loss: -log sigmoid({r_w} - {r_l}) = {-np.log(sig(r_w - r_l)):.3f}  (P(chosen) = {sig(r_w - r_l):.3f})")
beta = 0.1
lp_w, lr_w, lp_l, lr_l = -12.0, -13.0, -15.0, -14.0         # log-probs of whole responses: policy / reference
margin = beta * ((lp_w - lr_w) - (lp_l - lr_l))
print(f"DPO: implicit reward margin = {beta} x ((({lp_w}) - ({lr_w})) - (({lp_l}) - ({lr_l}))) = {margin:.2f};"
      f" loss = -log sigmoid({margin:.2f}) = {-np.log(sig(margin)):.3f}; at the start (policy = reference) loss = ln 2 = {np.log(2):.3f}")
print(f"gradient weight sigmoid(-margin) = {sig(-margin):.3f}  (how 'wrong' the model still is on this pair)")

# ---- 2. a toy world: one prompt, 5 candidate responses, hidden true rewards; the SFT model is the reference
names = ["curt", "helpful", "great", "verbose", "rude"]
true_r = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 1.2, -2.0])
ref = softmax(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5]))           # SFT model's probability of each response
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pairs = []
for _ in range(4000):                                        # labellers compare two sampled responses
    a, b = rng.choice(5, 2, replace=False)
    pairs.append((a, b) if rng.random() < sig(true_r[a] - true_r[b]) else (b, a))   # (winner, loser)
W, L = np.array(pairs).T
print("\nresponses:", names, "\nreference (SFT) policy:", ref)

# ---- 3. fit a reward model to the comparisons (one scalar per response, gradient descent on BT loss)
r = np.zeros(5)
for _ in range(2000):
    g = sig(-(r[W] - r[L]))                                  # d loss / d margin, per pair
    grad = np.zeros(5); np.add.at(grad, W, -g); np.add.at(grad, L, g)
    r -= 0.5 * grad / len(W)
print("learned rewards (shifted to curt = 0):", (r - r[0]).round(2), " true:", true_r)

# ---- 4. RLHF's optimum in closed form: pi*(y) proportional to ref(y) * exp(r(y) / beta)
def kl(p, q): return float((p * np.log(p / q)).sum())
print("\n beta   policy over responses                   E[true reward]  KL to ref")
for b in (10.0, 1.0, 0.3, 0.1):
    pi = ref * np.exp((r - r.max()) / b); pi /= pi.sum()
    print(f"{b:5.1f}  {pi}   {pi @ true_r:6.2f}        {kl(pi, ref):6.3f}")

# ---- 5. DPO: train the policy directly on the comparisons, no reward model, no sampling
beta = 1.0; logits = np.log(ref).copy(); lref = np.log(ref)
for step in range(3000):
    lp = logits - np.log(np.exp(logits).sum())               # log pi_theta
    m = beta * ((lp[W] - lref[W]) - (lp[L] - lref[L]))
    gm = -sig(-m) * beta                                     # d loss / d margin
    g_lp = np.zeros(5); np.add.at(g_lp, W, gm); np.add.at(g_lp, L, -gm)
    pi = np.exp(lp); g_logits = g_lp - pi * g_lp.sum()       # chain rule through log-softmax
    logits -= 2.0 * g_logits / len(W)
dpo = softmax(logits)
target = ref * np.exp(r / beta); target /= target.sum()
print(f"\nDPO policy (beta=1):        {dpo}\nRLHF optimum with learned r: {target}\nsame answer: {np.allclose(dpo, target, atol=0.01)}")

# ---- 6. reward hacking: a proxy reward that over-rates 'verbose'
proxy = r.copy(); proxy[3] += 1.5
print("\n beta  E[proxy reward]  E[true reward]  | E[true reward] if the reward model were right")
for b in (3.0, 1.0, 0.3, 0.1):
    pi = ref * np.exp((proxy - proxy.max()) / b); pi /= pi.sum()
    ok = ref * np.exp((r - r.max()) / b); ok /= ok.sum()
    print(f"{b:5.1f}  {pi @ proxy:12.2f}  {pi @ true_r:13.2f}    | {ok @ true_r:6.2f}")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1: reward-model loss 0.263 (P = 0.769); DPO margin 0.20 and loss 0.598, against ln 2 = 0.693 at the start; gradient weight 0.450.
  2. Section 3: the learned rewards [0, 1.09, 2.16, 1.14, −1.96] closely match the hidden true rewards [0, 1, 2, 1.2, −2], recovered from comparisons alone.
  3. Section 4: as β falls from 10 to 0.1 the policy moves from the reference to all mass on "great"; expected true reward rises from 0.49 to 2.00 while KL grows from 0.007 to 2.27.
  4. Section 5: the DPO policy equals the RLHF optimum, [0.109, 0.327, 0.348, 0.207, 0.009], and prints True.
  5. Section 6: with a proxy reward that over-rates "verbose", the proxy reward keeps rising as β falls (0.81 → 2.15), but the true reward stalls at about 1.2-1.3, while an accurate reward model would have reached 2.00: reward hacking.
recap: A chat model is built in stages: pretraining on trillions of tokens of text with next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstration conversations, and preference tuning with human or AI comparisons.

A pretrained base model is a text continuer: it knows a great deal but has no notion of answering, following instructions or stopping; SFT teaches the format and behaviour of an assistant by imitating thousands of example responses, with the loss on response tokens only.
Preference data asks raters which of two responses is better, which is easier and more consistent than writing perfect answers; InstructGPT collected rankings of 4 to 9 responses per prompt.
A reward model scores a (prompt, response) pair and is trained with the Bradley–Terry loss −log σ(r_chosen − r_rejected); scores 1.5 and 0.3 give P(chosen) = 0.769 and loss 0.263.

RLHF then maximises E[reward] − β·KL(policy ‖ reference) with an RL algorithm such as PPO, sampling responses from the policy, scoring them and updating; the KL term keeps the policy close to the SFT model and limits reward hacking.
The optimum of that objective is π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β); a small β concentrates the policy on the highest-reward responses, a large β keeps it near the reference.

DPO rewrites the reward as β·log(π/π_ref) and plugs it into the Bradley–Terry loss, so the policy is trained directly on pairs: loss = −log σ(β[(log π(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w)) − (log π(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))]).

Worked DPO example: with β = 0.1 and log-probability gains of +1 on the chosen and −1 on the rejected response, the margin is 0.2 and the loss 0.598, down from ln 2 = 0.693 when policy equals reference.
InstructGPT used about 13k SFT prompts, 33k reward-model prompts and 31k PPO prompts; labellers preferred its 1.3B model to the 175B GPT-3, and its 175B model to GPT-3 85% of the time.

Each stage fixes different things: pretraining gives knowledge and skill, SFT gives format and instruction following, preference tuning gives helpfulness and harmlessness as raters judge them; none of them adds knowledge the base model lacks.
glossary: A loss of performance on standard benchmarks caused by alignment training; InstructGPT reduced it by mixing pretraining gradients into PPO.
A model after pretraining only: a next-token predictor that continues text rather than following instructions.
A model of pairwise comparisons in which P(A beats B) = σ(score_A − score_B); the standard way to train reward models.
The preferred (y_w) and dispreferred (y_l) responses in one preference pair.
Anthropic's method of using a written list of principles and AI-generated critiques and preferences in place of most human harmlessness labels.
Direct Preference Optimization: trains the policy on preference pairs with a classification-style loss derived from the KL-regularised RLHF objective, with no reward model or RL loop.
Large language model: a transformer trained on very large text corpora to predict the next token.
Supervised fine-tuning on many (instruction, response) examples so the model learns to follow instructions.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another; here, how far the tuned policy has moved from the reference model.
In RL language, the model being trained: it maps a prompt to a probability distribution over responses.
Proximal Policy Optimization: a policy-gradient RL algorithm that limits how much each update changes the policy, used in InstructGPT's RLHF.
Any training stage that uses comparisons between responses (RLHF, DPO and variants).
The first and most expensive stage: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of general text.
The frozen copy of the starting policy (usually the SFT model) that the KL penalty, or DPO's log-ratios, measure against.
When a policy optimised against a learned reward finds outputs the reward model scores highly but humans would not, such as excessive length or flattery.
A network, usually an LLM with a scalar output head, trained on comparisons to score how good a response is for a prompt.
Reinforcement learning from AI feedback: preference labels produced by a model rather than by humans.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human comparisons, then optimise the policy against it with RL under a KL penalty.
Supervised fine-tuning: training on demonstration (prompt, ideal response) pairs with the ordinary next-token loss, usually applied to response tokens only.
A tendency of preference-tuned models to agree with or flatter the user, because raters often prefer agreement.
The coefficient on the KL penalty (RLHF) or log-ratio (DPO) that sets how far the policy may move from the reference.
drill:
Diagnose — the model got worse while the reward went up

Your team runs PPO on a support assistant. The reward-model score climbs steadily for 2,000 steps. Human reviewers say answers after step 1,200 are worse: longer, repetitive, and full of apologies. What happened, and what do you change?

Answer

Reward hacking. The policy has moved into regions the reward model was not trained on and found features it over-rates, here length and apologetic phrasing (likely because raters slightly preferred thorough, polite answers). The training reward is a proxy; past some KL distance from the reference, proxy and true quality diverge.

Immediate fix: choose the checkpoint by held-out human or independent-judge evaluation (around step 1,200), not by training reward.

Structural fixes: increase the KL coefficient β or cap KL; add a length penalty or evaluate length-controlled; collect new comparisons on the policy's current outputs, including pairs where the concise answer wins, and retrain the reward model; consider a reward-model ensemble and stop when members disagree. Track KL, length and held-out win rate in the run dashboard so the divergence is visible next time.

Choose — SFT, DPO or retrieval?

Three requests arrive: (a) the model should answer in your company's JSON format; (b) it should know your product's 2026 pricing; (c) it gives correct answers but users prefer a competitor's tone and structure. Which technique for each?

Answer

(a) SFT on a few hundred to a few thousand examples in the target format (or constrained decoding, lm16): format is exactly what demonstrations teach. (b) Retrieval (lm9): post-training does not reliably add knowledge, and pricing changes; put the current price list in the context at inference time. (c) Preference tuning (DPO with pairs where the preferred answer has the desired tone and structure), because raters can judge it easily even if writing ideal answers is slow; start from a model already SFT-tuned for your domain and track helpfulness and accuracy so tone gains do not cost correctness.
qa: E
What are the stages of building a chat model, and what does each one contribute?

Pretraining: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens, which gives knowledge, language and reasoning skill but only a text-continuing behaviour. Supervised fine-tuning: training on example conversations, which teaches the assistant format, instruction following and when to stop. Preference tuning (RLHF or DPO): training on comparisons between responses, which shifts the model towards responses people prefer, more helpful and less harmful. Most of the compute is in pretraining; most of the visible 'assistant' behaviour comes from the last two.
E
Why doesn't a pretrained model just answer questions?

Its objective is to continue text in the way documents on the internet continue. Given 'What is the capital of France?', a plausible continuation might be another quiz question, a forum reply or a list of capitals, not necessarily an answer. It has the knowledge but no reason to use it in the assistant role; SFT supplies examples of that role.
E
How is the SFT loss different from the pretraining loss?

It is the same next-token cross-entropy, but computed on conversations formatted with the chat template, and usually only on the assistant's response tokens: the prompt tokens are fed in but their predictions are masked out of the loss, so the model learns to produce answers rather than to imitate user messages.
M
How is a reward model trained?

Start from an LLM (often the SFT model) and replace its output layer with a single scalar head. For each comparison of a chosen and a rejected response to the same prompt, compute both scores and minimise −log σ(r_chosen − r_rejected), the Bradley–Terry loss, so the chosen response's score rises relative to the rejected one. With scores 1.5 and 0.3, the model's probability that the chosen one wins is σ(1.2) = 0.769 and the loss is 0.263.
Follow-up: Why train on comparisons rather than absolute scores? — Raters disagree about absolute scales but agree more on which of two is better, and only score differences are identified anyway.
M
What is the RLHF objective and what does the KL term do?

Maximise the expected reward of the policy's responses minus β times the KL divergence from the reference (SFT) model. The reward pulls the policy towards high-scoring responses; the KL term charges for moving away from the reference, which keeps the language natural, preserves capabilities, and stops the policy from exploiting the reward model's errors on responses unlike anything it was trained on. InstructGPT applies the KL penalty per token during PPO.

Follow-up: What happens with β too small? — The policy collapses onto whatever the reward model rates highest, often verbose, repetitive or sycophantic text, and quality as judged by humans falls even as the reward rises.
M
Explain DPO and how it relates to RLHF.

The KL-regularised RLHF objective has a closed-form optimum: π*(y|x) = π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β)/Z(x). Rearranged, any reward can be written as β·log(π*/π_ref) plus a term that depends only on the prompt. Substituting this into the Bradley–Terry loss, the prompt term cancels between chosen and rejected, leaving a loss on the policy alone: −log σ(β[(log π(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w)) − (log π(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))]). So DPO solves the same problem without a reward model, without sampling and without RL.
Follow-up: What is DPO's implicit reward? — β·log(π(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)): how much more likely the tuned model makes a response than the reference did.
M
Compute the DPO loss for one pair.

Take β = 0.1. The policy assigns log-probability −12 to the chosen response and −15 to the rejected one; the reference assigned −13 and −14. The chosen log-ratio is +1, the rejected −1, so the margin is 0.1 × (1 − (−1)) = 0.2 and the loss is −log σ(0.2) = −log 0.550 = 0.598. At initialisation the policy equals the reference, the margin is 0 and the loss is ln 2 = 0.693.
Follow-up: How large is this pair's gradient? — Proportional to σ(−margin) = 0.450: pairs the model already ranks confidently contribute little, so training focuses on pairs it gets wrong.
M
What are DPO's practical advantages and disadvantages compared with PPO-based RLHF?

Advantages: one model to train plus a frozen reference, no reward model, no generation inside the training loop, a simple supervised-style loss, and stable training; it is much cheaper to run. Disadvantages: it learns only from a fixed dataset of pairs (offline), so it cannot explore and correct its own new mistakes; its quality depends heavily on how the pairs were produced; and it can push down the likelihood of both responses or over-fit when pairs are noisy. Online variants generate fresh pairs from the current model to recover some of RL's benefits.
M
What did InstructGPT show?

That a much smaller model tuned with SFT and RLHF on human data could be preferred to a much larger base model: labellers preferred outputs of the 1.3B InstructGPT model to the 175B GPT-3, and the 175B InstructGPT to GPT-3 85% of the time (71% against few-shot GPT-3). It also generated truthful and informative answers about twice as often on TruthfulQA and about 25% fewer toxic outputs when asked to be respectful, with no improvement on bias.
H
What is reward hacking and how do teams limit it?

The policy finds outputs the reward model scores highly but people would not, because the reward model is only accurate near the data it was trained on. Common symptoms are growing response length, hedging or flattery, and formulaic structure. Limits: a KL penalty to the reference model, early stopping based on held-out human or strong-model evaluations rather than reward, reward-model ensembles, length penalties or length-controlled evaluation, retraining the reward model on the policy's new outputs, and using verifiable rewards (tests, exact answers) where possible.

Follow-up: How would you detect it? — Track true quality (human or independent judge win rates) against the training reward; when reward keeps rising and judged quality flattens or falls, you are over-optimising, as the lab's proxy-reward table shows.
H
Why might a model become sycophantic after preference tuning?

If raters, on average, prefer responses that agree with them, validate their views or sound confident, the reward model learns that preference and the policy is optimised towards it. The effect grows with optimisation strength. Mitigations include rater guidelines that reward honest disagreement, targeted data where the correct answer contradicts the user, evaluations that measure sycophancy directly, and principles-based AI feedback that encodes honesty explicitly.
H
Design a preference-tuning stage for a customer-support model.

Start from a good SFT model trained on high-quality support transcripts. Collect prompts from real traffic, sample several responses from the SFT model, and have trained raters (or a strong model with a rubric, spot-checked by humans) choose the better of pairs according to explicit criteria: correct, policy-compliant, concise, polite. Run DPO with a held-out set to tune β, or PPO with a reward model if you have the infrastructure and want online exploration. Evaluate on held-out human win rate, factual accuracy against the knowledge base, policy violations and response length, and check for regressions on capabilities you care about.

Follow-up: How many pairs do you need? — Thousands to tens of thousands are typical for a narrow domain; InstructGPT's reward model used 33k prompts, each with several ranked responses. Quality and coverage matter more than raw count.
H
What can't post-training fix, and what does that imply for a product?

It cannot add knowledge the base model lacks, make the model reliable on facts outside its training data, or remove capabilities completely: it changes which behaviours are likely. Safety behaviours from preference tuning can be bypassed by adversarial prompts (lm18), and hallucination persists (lm15). For a product this means retrieval for knowledge (lm9), tools for exact work (lm16), guardrails outside the model, and evaluation (lm14), rather than expecting fine-tuning to solve everything.

t: Scaling laws and the Chinchilla correction
sum: Why loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute; the C ≈ 6ND budget; Kaplan's laws and Chinchilla's correction to about 20 tokens per parameter, worked for a 10²⁴-FLOP budget; the replication that fixed Chinchilla's fit; and why modern small models are deliberately over-trained.
prereq: lm3
A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token and training about 6, so training compute is roughly 6 × parameters × tokens.
ml5
The pretraining loss is the average cross-entropy, −log p(next token), in nats; lower is better, and its exponential is the perplexity.
ml2
Error has parts due to a model being too small to represent the target (bias) and parts due to too little data to pin it down (variance); more parameters and more data attack different parts.
gpu12
Training cost in GPU-hours is total FLOPs ÷ (peak FLOP/s × utilisation achieved), times the price per hour.
dl9

why:
Imagine you have been given a budget of a few tens of millions of dollars of GPU time to train a language model. That buys a fixed number of floating-point operations, perhaps 10²⁴. You must decide, before you start, how big the model should be and how many tokens of text to train it on. You get one shot: the run will take a couple of months on thousands of GPUs, and if you choose badly there is no budget for a second. Make the model too big and you will run out of compute before it has seen enough data; make it too small and it will saturate, learning nothing more from extra text. How do you choose?

In 2020 the answer seemed to be "as big as possible". Researchers at OpenAI had found that loss falls predictably as models grow, and their analysis said most of any extra compute should go into parameters. GPT-3 (175B parameters), Gopher (280B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B, from Microsoft and NVIDIA) were all trained on roughly 300 billion tokens. Then in 2022 DeepMind published a study of over 400 training runs that reached a different conclusion: model size and data should grow together, about 20 tokens for every parameter, which meant the giants of the day were badly undertrained. To prove it, they trained Chinchilla, a 70B model, on 1.4 trillion tokens, using the same compute as their own 280B Gopher. The smaller model won almost everywhere, and it was four times cheaper to run.

That result changed how every lab plans its training runs, and it is a favourite interview topic because it combines a clean estimate (C ≈ 6ND), a surprising empirical finding and a trade-off that keeps evolving: today's small open models are trained far past Chinchilla's ratio on purpose, because the cost of serving them matters more than the cost of training them.

This lesson builds up from what a power law is and why loss follows one, through the 6ND compute estimate, Kaplan's original laws, Chinchilla's three methods and its parametric loss model, a worked compute-optimal sizing for a 10²⁴-FLOP budget, the 2024 replication that corrected Chinchilla's fit, and the shift to inference-aware over-training. The lab evaluates the fitted laws, finds compute-optimal sizes by walking along an iso-FLOP curve, and shows how to recover an exponent from small runs.
primer:
Three knobs and one budget

Three quantities describe a pretraining run. N is the number of parameters (model size). D is the number of training tokens the model sees. C is the total compute in floating-point operations (FLOPs). They are tied together by a simple estimate: every parameter takes part in about 2 FLOPs per token in the forward pass and about 4 in the backward pass (lm3 and gpu3 derive this), so

C ≈ 6 · N · D

A compute budget therefore fixes the product N·D. You can have a large model that sees few tokens or a small model that sees many, but not both. The question scaling laws answer is where on that curve to sit.

An analogy: a student and a library

Think of N as the size of a student's brain and D as the number of books they read. Study time is limited (the budget), and a bigger brain takes longer per book. A huge brain that reads three books will not have learned much; a tiny brain that reads the whole library will forget most of it. The best outcome for a fixed amount of study time comes from matching the two. Chinchilla's finding is that for language models the match is roughly linear: double the brain, double the books. The analogy breaks in one respect that turns out to matter commercially: in the real world you pay not only for the student's studying but for every exam they sit afterwards, and a smaller student is cheaper to examine, which is why modern small models read far more than Chinchilla's ratio.

Why "laws"

The surprising empirical fact is that loss falls smoothly and predictably as N, D or C grow, following a power law: loss ∝ X^(−k) for a small exponent k. On a graph with logarithmic axes, a power law is a straight line, and that line has held across many orders of magnitude of compute. This is what makes scaling laws useful: you can train a series of small, cheap models, fit the line, and predict how a model 100 or 1,000 times larger will do before spending the money. A pretraining loss is measured in nats per token (the cross-entropy with natural logarithms, ml5); differences that look tiny, such as 1.99 versus 1.94, correspond to clearly different model quality.

What a small difference in loss means

Scaling-law plots show losses like 2.00 and 1.94 and it is easy to dismiss the gap. Convert to perplexity, e^loss, which is roughly "how many equally likely next tokens the model is choosing between": e^2.00 = 7.39 and e^1.94 = 6.96, about 6% fewer effective choices at every single token. Because the irreducible part of the loss (the genuinely unpredictable text) is large, the reducible part is a fraction of the total, and a 0.06 drop is a substantial share of what is left to learn. In practice such gaps show up as clear differences on benchmarks: the 0.06-nat gap between Gopher and Chinchilla corresponded to 7.5 points on MMLU.
body:
1. Power laws, from scratch

A power law has the form y = a·x^k. Take logarithms of both sides: log y = log a + k·log x. So if you plot log y against log x you get a straight line with slope k. For language-model loss the exponent is small and negative, which means each tenfold increase in x multiplies the (reducible) loss by the same factor 10^k. With k = −0.05, every tenfold increase in compute cuts loss by about 11% (10^−0.05 = 0.891). That is a slow but extremely regular improvement, and its regularity is the useful part: three or four points on a straight line in log-log space let you extrapolate. The lab generates nine noisy "runs" from a known law with exponent −0.05 between 10¹⁸ and 10²² FLOPs, fits a straight line in log space and recovers −0.0499, predicting the loss at 10²⁴ FLOPs within 0.003 of the truth.

2. Why loss should follow a power law at all

There is no complete theory, but an intuition helps. Language contains patterns at every level of frequency: a few extremely common ones (grammar, frequent words), and a long tail of rarer ones (specific facts, unusual constructions), whose frequencies themselves follow roughly power-law distributions. A larger model has room to store more of the tail; more data shows it more examples of rare patterns. Each increment of scale picks off the next slice of the tail, which is rarer and therefore worth less loss than the last, giving a smooth, diminishing return. Whatever the explanation, the empirical regularity has held for model families across architectures and labs, and that is what engineers rely on.

3. The compute estimate C ≈ 6ND, worked

From lm3, each parameter takes part in one multiply-add per token in the forward pass: 2 FLOPs. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights, roughly twice the forward work: 4 FLOPs. Total: about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token. (Attention adds a term that grows with context length; for typical contexts it is a modest correction and is usually ignored in these estimates.) Some examples: GPT-3, 6 × 175 × 10⁹ × 300 × 10⁹ = 3.15 × 10²³ FLOPs. Gopher, 6 × 280 × 10⁹ × 300 × 10⁹ = 5.0 × 10²³ (the Chinchilla paper quotes Gopher's budget as 5.76 × 10²³, which includes details such as attention). Chinchilla, 6 × 70 × 10⁹ × 1.4 × 10¹² = 5.9 × 10²³. Llama 3 405B, 6 × 405 × 10⁹ × 15.6 × 10¹² = 3.8 × 10²⁵, the figure Meta reports.

Turning FLOPs into time and money uses the hardware's delivered throughput (gpu12). An H100 has a dense bf16 peak of about 989 TFLOP/s; a well-tuned large run achieves perhaps 40% of that as model FLOPs utilisation (MFU), about 4 × 10¹⁴ useful FLOP/s per GPU. A 10²⁴-FLOP run therefore needs 10²⁴ / (4 × 10¹⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁹ GPU-seconds, about 700,000 GPU-hours: roughly 29 days on 1,000 H100s.

4. Kaplan et al. (2020): the first laws

Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI trained many transformer language models and fitted three separate laws, each holding when the other factors are not the bottleneck. Loss versus non-embedding parameters: L(N) = (N_c/N)^0.076. Loss versus data: L(D) = (D_c/D)^0.095. Loss versus compute, when compute is allocated optimally: L(C) ∝ C^−0.050. They also found that architecture details such as depth versus width mattered much less than total parameters within a wide range. Their most consequential conclusion was about allocation: as compute grows, the optimal model size should grow as about C^0.73, much faster than the data. Ten times more compute should buy a model about 5.4 times bigger but only about 1.8 times more data. Following that advice, the large models of 2020-2021 grew enormously in parameters while staying near 300 billion training tokens.

5. Hoffmann et al. (2022): the Chinchilla study

DeepMind revisited the question with more than 400 models from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters, trained on 5 to 500 billion tokens, and three independent methods for finding the compute-optimal allocation:

  1. Training curves: for each model size, train with several token budgets and record the lowest loss achieved at each compute level; read off which size wins at each compute.
  2. Iso-FLOP profiles: fix nine compute budgets; at each, train models of different sizes for exactly that budget (so smaller models see more tokens); the loss traces a valley, and its bottom is the optimal size for that budget.
  3. Parametric fit: fit a formula for loss as a function of both N and D to all the runs, then minimise it along C = 6ND.

All three said the same thing qualitatively: N and D should be scaled in roughly equal proportion. The exponents for N_opt ∝ C^a and D_opt ∝ C^b were a = 0.50, b = 0.50 (method 1), a = 0.49, b = 0.51 (method 2) and a = 0.46, b = 0.54 (method 3). Double the compute, and both the model and the data should grow by about √2. The paper's Table 3 turns this into a recipe: a 1B model should see about 20 billion tokens, a 67B model about 1.5 trillion, a 175B model 3.7 trillion. The ratio, about 20 tokens per parameter, is the famous rule of thumb.

6. Why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreed

The main culprit is the learning-rate schedule. Training uses a schedule that warms the learning rate up, then decays it (often along a cosine curve) to a small value by the end of training; loss improves sharply during that final decay. Kaplan et al. used a schedule of fixed length for all runs and compared models at intermediate points, so runs with fewer tokens were measured before their learning rate had decayed, understating how good short-trained (and so relatively small-for-their-compute) models can get. Chinchilla set each run's schedule to match its token count. The lesson generalises: scaling-law conclusions depend on every run being trained properly for its own budget, which is harder than it sounds.

7. The parametric loss model

Chinchilla's third method fits

L(N, D) = E + A / N^α + B / D^β

Each term has a meaning. E is the irreducible loss, the entropy of natural text: even a perfect model cannot predict every next token. A/N^α is the penalty for finite model size: what an infinitely trained model of N parameters still gets wrong. B/D^β is the penalty for finite data: what a model of unlimited size still gets wrong after seeing only D tokens. The published values were E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34, β = 0.28. Minimising this along C = 6ND balances the two shrinking terms: spending a FLOP on a bigger model should reduce loss exactly as much as spending it on more tokens. The formula is valuable as a mental model, but section 9 shows why its published constants should not be used as-is.

8. Sizing a 10²⁴-FLOP run by hand

Combine C = 6ND with the rule D = 20N:

C = 6 · N · (20 N) = 120 N²      →      N = √(C / 120),   D = 20 N
C = 10²⁴:  N = √(8.33 × 10²¹) = 9.13 × 10¹⁰ ≈ 91B parameters
           D = 20 × 9.13 × 10¹⁰ = 1.83 × 10¹² ≈ 1.8T tokens
check:     6 × 9.13 × 10¹⁰ × 1.83 × 10¹² = 1.0 × 10²⁴ ✓

For Gopher's budget, 5.76 × 10²³, the same calculation gives N ≈ 69B and D ≈ 1.4T: almost exactly Chinchilla. The rule also explains how far off the 2021 models were. Gopher, at 280B parameters, should have seen about 5.6T tokens to be compute-optimal for its size (and would have needed about 9.4 × 10²⁴ FLOPs, 16 times its actual budget); trained on 300B tokens it had about 1 token per parameter. GPT-3 had 1.7. These models were not too small; they were too big for the data they were given.

The lab walks along Gopher's iso-FLOP curve using the corrected fit from section 9: 280B parameters on 0.34T tokens gives loss 1.993; 140B, 1.979; 70B on 1.37T, 1.975 (the valley floor); 35B, 1.980; 10B on 9.6T, 2.015. The valley is shallow near the bottom, which is good news in practice: being within a factor of two of the optimal size costs very little loss, so the exact ratio matters less than avoiding the 15-fold mistakes of 2021.
