9. The replication that corrected the fit

In 2024 Besiroglu and colleagues at Epoch AI reconstructed Chinchilla's data points from the paper's figures and re-ran the third method. They found the published parametric estimates were inconsistent with the paper's own first two methods, fitted the extracted data poorly, and came with confidence intervals so narrow they would have required over 600,000 experiments where likely fewer than 500 were run. They traced the problems to the optimiser stopping before convergence because of a poor choice of loss scale, and to the rounding of the reported parameters, which substantially biases predictions. Their re-fit is L = 1.8172 + 482.01/N^0.3478 + 2085.43/D^0.3658, and it is compatible with the first two methods and with roughly 20 tokens per parameter.

You can see the difference in the lab. Minimised along iso-FLOP curves, the published constants put the optimum at 50 to 120 tokens per parameter (for Gopher's budget, a 32B model on 3T tokens), contradicting the Chinchilla model the paper itself trained. The re-fit puts it at 17 to 22 tokens per parameter across budgets from 10²¹ to 10²⁵ FLOPs (for Gopher's budget, 72B on 1.33T tokens), matching Chinchilla. The broader lesson is that fitted constants in scaling-law papers are fragile, and the qualitative conclusion (scale N and D together) is far more robust than any particular number.

10. Compute-optimal is not cost-optimal

Chinchilla optimises one thing: the loss reached for a fixed training budget. But a deployed model's lifetime cost includes inference, about 2N FLOPs per generated token (lm3), multiplied by every token it ever serves. A model used by millions of people can spend far more compute in inference than it did in training. Then it pays to train a smaller model for longer: its loss is a little higher than the compute-optimal model's at the same training cost, but every served token is cheaper. In the lab, for a 10²⁴-FLOP budget, the optimal 96B model reaches loss 1.960; a 48B model trained on 3.5T tokens reaches 1.964 with half the inference cost per token, and a 24B model on 7T tokens reaches 1.977 at a quarter. Sardana et al. made this precise and found that for expected demand of about a billion requests or more, models should be trained smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal, with quality still improving at ratios up to 10,000 tokens per parameter in their experiments. Meta's Llama 3 report says exactly this: the 405B flagship is approximately compute-optimal for its 3.8 × 10²⁵-FLOP budget, while the smaller models were trained "for much longer than is compute-optimal" and perform better than compute-optimal models at the same inference budget.

The same logic explains a pattern you will see across open model releases: a family of several sizes all trained on the same, very large token count. The largest member is near compute-optimal; the smaller ones are heavily over-trained, because they are the ones most people will run on their own hardware, where inference cost per token and memory are what users feel. When you compare models for deployment, tokens seen in training is as informative as parameter count: a well-trained 8B model can beat an under-trained model several times its size.

11. How scaling laws are used in practice

Teams training large models use scaling laws as planning tools. Before a big run they train a sweep of small models on the exact data mix, tokeniser and recipe, fit loss against compute and optimal size against compute, and choose N and D for the target budget. Llama 3's team did this with budgets from 6 × 10¹⁸ to 10²² FLOPs and then predicted downstream benchmark accuracy for the flagship by chaining two fits: compute to the model's loss on the benchmark's answers, and that loss to accuracy. During the run, the loss curve is compared against the prediction, and a run falling behind is investigated early. Scaling laws are also the standard way to compare data mixes or architectures: the better choice shifts the line down or makes it steeper, and you can see it with small runs.

12. A worked cost estimate for Chinchilla itself

It is worth doing the full chain once for a real model. Chinchilla: 6 × 70 × 10⁹ × 1.4 × 10¹² = 5.9 × 10²³ FLOPs. On modern H100s at 40% MFU (about 4 × 10¹⁴ useful FLOP/s each), that is 5.9 × 10²³ / 4 × 10¹⁴ = 1.5 × 10⁹ GPU-seconds, about 410,000 GPU-hours, or about 17 days on 1,000 GPUs. At a few dollars per GPU-hour that is on the order of one to two million dollars of compute for the final run, before the experiments, failed runs and evaluations that typically multiply it. Gopher's run cost about the same, which is the point: the same money bought a much better model once it was spent in the right shape. Serving tells the other half of the story: Chinchilla needs 140 GFLOP per generated token against Gopher's 560, and 140 GB of bf16 weights against 560 GB, so every deployment of the smaller model is about four times cheaper.

13. What scaling laws do not tell you

They predict pretraining loss on the training distribution. They do not directly predict whether a model can do a particular task, how it behaves after fine-tuning, or how it handles data unlike its training set. They assume the data is effectively unlimited and of constant quality; when high-quality unique data runs out and must be repeated, the effective value of extra tokens falls. They depend on the tokeniser (loss per token is not comparable across tokenisers, lm1), so fitted constants from one lab do not transfer to another. And they say nothing about inference-time compute such as generating long reasoning chains, which follows its own scaling behaviour. Treat them as a precise tool for one question, how to spend pretraining compute, and as a rough guide for everything else.
deep:
Deriving the compute-optimal exponents

Minimise L = E + A·N^(−α) + B·D^(−β) subject to 6ND = C. Substitute D = C/(6N) and set dL/dN = 0: αA·N^(−α−1) = βB·(C/6)^(−β)·N^(β−1). Solving gives N_opt ∝ C^(β/(α+β)) and D_opt ∝ C^(α/(α+β)). With the published α = 0.34 and β = 0.28, the exponents are 0.45 and 0.55, close to method 3's reported 0.46 and 0.54; with the re-fit's α = 0.348 and β = 0.366, they are 0.51 and 0.49, matching methods 1 and 2. The algebra shows why the split depends only on the ratio of the exponents: whichever resource the loss is more sensitive to (larger exponent) gets a smaller share of the growth, because it gives diminishing returns faster. The tokens-per-parameter ratio itself depends on A and B too, which is why it shifts with data quality and tokeniser.

Hyperparameters must scale too

A scaling law is only as good as the runs behind it, and runs at different sizes need different hyperparameters. The optimal learning rate generally falls as models grow, and the critical batch size, beyond which larger batches stop helping, grows as loss falls (Kaplan et al. fitted this too). A sweep that uses the same learning rate for all sizes will under-train some of them and bend the fitted line. Modern practice uses parameterisations designed so that hyperparameters tuned on small models transfer to large ones (for example maximal-update parameterisation), plus explicit scaling rules for learning rate and batch size, so that the small runs used for fitting are each near their own optimum.

Data-constrained scaling

Chinchilla assumes every token is fresh. Frontier runs now approach the amount of high-quality text that exists, so data gets repeated across epochs. Studies of data-constrained scaling find that a few epochs over the same data are nearly as valuable as new data, while returns decline steeply after many repetitions, and propose modifying D to an "effective data" term that saturates with repetition. Practical consequences: deduplication matters (accidental repetition wastes budget), data quality filtering effectively raises the value of each token, and synthetic and multimodal data become ways to keep D growing. These considerations are why data teams are as central to frontier training as infrastructure teams.

Loss is per token, and tokenisers differ

Scaling-law losses are cross-entropies per token. A tokeniser that packs more text into each token (lm1) raises per-token loss even if the model is equally good per character, because each token carries more information. So losses, and the constants of fitted laws, cannot be compared across models with different tokenisers; comparisons should use bits per byte or per character of a fixed evaluation set. The same caution applies to token counts in the tokens-per-parameter ratio: 20 tokens per parameter with a 32K vocabulary is less text than with a 128K vocabulary.

Inference-time scaling

A newer axis of scaling spends compute at inference rather than in training: sampling several answers and choosing among them, or letting a model generate long chains of reasoning before answering. Both show their own smooth relationships between compute and accuracy on tasks such as mathematics, and they change the economics: a smaller model that "thinks longer" can match a larger one on some tasks, at a per-query cost that depends on difficulty. This complements the over-training argument: both push the frontier towards models that are cheap per token, with quality bought by more training tokens or more inference tokens rather than by more parameters.

Why the valley is shallow

Near the compute-optimal point, loss as a function of model size along the iso-FLOP curve is flat to first order (that is what being at a minimum means), so small deviations cost only second-order amounts. In log terms: if the optimum is N*, choosing N = 2N* or N*/2 shifts both the parameter and data terms by factors of 2^α and 2^β in opposite directions, and the sum changes only slightly. The lab shows it: along Gopher's budget, 35B and 140B are within 0.005 nats of the 70B optimum, while 280B (a factor of four) is 0.019 worse and 10B (a factor of seven) 0.040 worse. This is why practitioners can deviate from the optimum for good reasons, such as inference cost or hardware fit, with little training-efficiency penalty, as long as they avoid order-of-magnitude mistakes.

Mixture-of-experts and other architectures

Scaling laws are architecture-specific. Mixture-of-experts models (lm17) decouple total parameters from per-token compute, so the C ≈ 6ND estimate uses active parameters, while memory depends on total parameters, and their laws involve both. Changes such as better attention variants or optimisers typically shift the curve by a constant factor in effective compute ("this change is worth 1.5× compute") rather than changing its slope, and that is the standard way such improvements are reported.
prod:
The public case: Chinchilla versus Gopher (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind, 2022)

DeepMind's paper states the problem in its first table: GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), Gopher (280B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) had all been trained on about 300 billion tokens. Fitting their 400-plus runs with three methods, the authors concluded that for compute-optimal training, "for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled", and that current large models were "considerably over-sized" for their budgets. Their Table 3 estimates, for example, that a 175B model should be trained on about 3.7T tokens and that a 280B model like Gopher would be optimal at a budget of about 10²⁵ FLOPs with about 5.9T tokens.

They then tested the prediction directly. For Gopher's compute budget (5.76 × 10²³ FLOPs), their analysis gave an optimal size around 70B; they trained Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens. Chinchilla "uniformly and significantly" outperformed Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B) and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream tasks. On MMLU it reached 67.5% average accuracy against Gopher's 60.0%, more than 7 percentage points better; on BIG-bench (a collection of 62 diverse tasks in this evaluation) 65.1% against 54.4%; on TruthfulQA it reached 43.6% zero-shot against Gopher's 29.5%. And because it is four times smaller, it is about four times cheaper for fine-tuning and inference. Two years later Epoch AI's replication corrected the paper's parametric fit while confirming its central conclusion, and subsequent open models adopted, then deliberately exceeded, its ratio.

How this goes wrong in practice

Mis-sized runs. A team picks a large model because "bigger is better", then cannot afford enough tokens; the result underperforms a smaller model that would have cost the same. Size with C = 6ND and the tokens-per-parameter target before committing.

Extrapolating from bad small runs. Small runs with untuned learning rates, mismatched schedules or a different data mix give a scaling law that does not describe the large run. Make sure each fitting run is trained properly for its own budget, on the same data and tokeniser.

Ignoring inference. A compute-optimal model chosen for training efficiency turns out too expensive to serve at the product's traffic. Include expected inference volume in the decision; for high-traffic products, train smaller and longer.

Running out of data. Planning 20 tokens per parameter for a large model may require more high-quality unique tokens than exist in the target domain or language. Check data availability and plan for repetition, filtering or synthetic data.

A modern decision: Llama 3's sizing

Meta's Llama 3 report is the clearest public example of scaling laws used for a real decision. The team ran iso-FLOP sweeps between 6 × 10¹⁸ and 10²² FLOPs, fitted the compute-optimal number of training tokens against compute, and extrapolated to their flagship budget of 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs, which suggested a 402B-parameter model on 16.55T tokens; they trained 405B on 15.6T, about 39 tokens per parameter, a reminder that the optimal ratio depends on the data and recipe (their fit gave more tokens per parameter than Chinchilla's 20). They also predicted the flagship's downstream benchmark scores from the small runs before training it. For the 8B and 70B models, they ignored compute-optimality on purpose and trained on about the same 15T tokens, because those models would be deployed widely and a smaller, longer-trained model is cheaper to serve at a given quality.

What to measure

For a scaling study: final loss of each small run at its own schedule end, the iso-FLOP valleys, the fitted exponents with honest uncertainty (bootstrap over runs), and a held-out prediction (fit on the smaller runs, predict the largest one before looking). For a production run: the loss curve against the scaling-law prediction, MFU (which converts FLOPs into calendar time and cost), and downstream evaluations at checkpoints.
myths: Bigger models are always better, so spend the budget on parameters.

For a fixed training budget, parameters and data trade off against each other: C ≈ 6ND. Chinchilla (70B on 1.4T tokens) used about the same compute as Gopher (280B on 300B tokens) and beat it on almost every benchmark, including 67.5% against 60.0% on MMLU. Gopher was too big for its data.
Chinchilla says every model should be trained on 20 tokens per parameter.

Chinchilla answers one question: which size minimises loss for a fixed training budget. It ignores the cost of using the model. If a model will serve billions of requests, a smaller model trained much longer reaches the same quality with cheaper inference; Llama 3 8B was trained on about 15T tokens, roughly 1,900 per parameter, on purpose, and Meta says its small models perform better than compute-optimal ones at the same inference budget.
Scaling laws predict what a model will be able to do.

They predict pretraining loss on the training distribution, smoothly. Downstream abilities relate to loss less simply: some benchmarks improve smoothly, others appear to jump. Llama 3's team predicted downstream accuracy with a two-step method (compute → loss on the task → accuracy), which needed its own fitting.
The fitted constants from a scaling-law paper apply to any model.

The exponents and constants depend on the data, tokeniser, architecture and training recipe. Chinchilla's published parametric fit (E = 1.69, α = 0.34, β = 0.28) even disagrees with its own other two methods: a 2024 replication found it was biased by a fitting problem and rounding, and the corrected fit is consistent with about 20 tokens per parameter. Re-fit scaling laws on your own setup.
Kaplan et al. were simply wrong.

Their power laws in parameters, data and compute hold up; what changed was the compute-optimal allocation. Kaplan et al. found model size should grow faster than data (N ∝ C^0.73), partly because their runs used a learning-rate schedule fixed regardless of the number of training tokens and were not trained to their schedules' ends at each size. Chinchilla, adjusting the schedule to each run's length, found the two should grow about equally.
Loss can go to zero with enough scale.

The fitted laws have an irreducible term E (1.69 nats in Chinchilla's published fit, 1.82 in the replication) representing the entropy of text itself: some next tokens are genuinely unpredictable. Scaling only shrinks the terms that depend on parameters and data.
lab:
Goal: apply C ≈ 6ND to real models, find compute-optimal sizes for several budgets with the rule of thumb and with both the published and corrected Chinchilla fits, walk along Gopher's iso-FLOP curve, recover a power-law exponent from small runs, and quantify the trade-off of over-training. NumPy only, instant.

import numpy as np

# Chinchilla's fitted loss (Hoffmann et al. 2022, eq. 10): L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta
loss = lambda N, D: 1.69 + 406.4 / N ** 0.34 + 410.7 / D ** 0.28
# Epoch AI's re-fit of the same data (Besiroglu et al. 2024), which found the published constants biased
loss2 = lambda N, D: 1.8172 + 482.01 / N ** 0.3478 + 2085.43 / D ** 0.3658

# ---- 1. the 6ND rule and tokens per parameter for real models
for name, N, D in [("GPT-3", 175e9, 300e9), ("Gopher", 280e9, 300e9), ("Chinchilla", 70e9, 1.4e12),
                   ("Llama 3 8B", 8.03e9, 15e12), ("Llama 3 405B", 405e9, 15.6e12)]:
    print(f"{name:13s} N={N/1e9:6.1f}B  D={D/1e12:5.2f}T  C=6ND={6*N*D:.2e} FLOPs  tokens/param={D/N:5.0f}  re-fit loss={loss2(N, D):.3f}")

# ---- 2. compute-optimal split for a budget: the 20-tokens-per-parameter rule vs minimising each fitted loss
def rule_of_thumb(C):                          # C = 6 N D and D = 20 N  ->  N = sqrt(C / 120)
    N = np.sqrt(C / 120); return N, 20 * N
def fitted_optimum(C, f):
    N = np.logspace(8, 13, 20001); D = C / (6 * N)     # walk along the iso-FLOP curve
    i = np.argmin(f(N, D)); return N[i], D[i]
print("\n budget C    rule: N, D          published fit: N, D, tok/param    re-fit: N, D, tok/param")
for C in (1e21, 1e23, 5.76e23, 1e24, 1e25):
    n1, d1 = rule_of_thumb(C); n2, d2 = fitted_optimum(C, loss); n3, d3 = fitted_optimum(C, loss2)
    print(f"{C:9.2e}  {n1/1e9:6.1f}B {d1/1e12:5.2f}T     {n2/1e9:6.1f}B {d2/1e12:5.2f}T {d2/n2:4.0f}"
          f"          {n3/1e9:6.1f}B {d3/1e12:5.2f}T {d3/n3:4.0f}")

# ---- 3. same compute, different splits (Gopher's budget, 5.76e23 FLOPs)
C = 5.76e23
print(f"\nGopher's budget {C:.2e} FLOPs, re-fit loss:")
for N in (280e9, 140e9, 70e9, 35e9, 10e9):
    D = C / (6 * N); print(f"  N={N/1e9:5.0f}B  D={D/1e12:5.2f}T  loss={loss2(N, D):.4f}")

# ---- 4. power laws are straight lines on log-log axes: recover an exponent from noisy small 'runs'
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Cs = np.logspace(18, 22, 9)
L_runs = 3.1 * (Cs / 1e18) ** -0.05 * np.exp(rng.normal(0, 0.005, Cs.size))
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log(Cs), np.log(L_runs), 1)
print(f"\nfitted exponent from 9 small runs: {slope:.4f} (true -0.05); "
      f"extrapolated loss at 1e24: {np.exp(intercept) * 1e24 ** slope:.3f} vs true {3.1 * 1e6 ** -0.05:.3f}")

# ---- 5. over-training for cheaper inference: smaller models at the same training compute
C = 1e24; n_opt, d_opt = fitted_optimum(C, loss2)
print(f"\nat C=1e24 (re-fit): optimum {n_opt/1e9:.0f}B on {d_opt/1e12:.1f}T tokens -> loss {loss2(n_opt, d_opt):.4f}")
for N in (n_opt / 2, n_opt / 4):
    print(f"  {N/1e9:4.0f}B on {C/(6*N)/1e12:4.1f}T tokens: loss {loss2(N, C/(6*N)):.4f};"
          f" inference {2*N/1e9:.0f} vs {2*n_opt/1e9:.0f} GFLOP per token")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1: training FLOPs of 3.15 × 10²³ (GPT-3), 5.0 × 10²³ (Gopher), 5.9 × 10²³ (Chinchilla), 7.2 × 10²³ (Llama 3 8B) and 3.79 × 10²⁵ (Llama 3 405B), with tokens per parameter of 2, 1, 20, about 1,870 and 39. (The predicted losses use Chinchilla's data and tokeniser, so only compare them with each other.)
  2. Section 2: the rule of thumb gives 91.3B on 1.83T tokens at 10²⁴ FLOPs. The published fit puts the optimum at 50-122 tokens per parameter, contradicting Chinchilla itself; the corrected re-fit gives 17-22, matching the rule.
  3. Section 3: the loss valley along Gopher's budget, lowest near 70B (1.9745), with 280B at 1.9933: Gopher's shape was wrong, and the valley is shallow near its floor.
  4. Section 4: the fitted exponent −0.0499 from nine noisy runs, extrapolating to within 0.003 at 100× the largest run.
  5. Section 5: at 10²⁴ FLOPs, halving the model from 96B to 48B costs 0.004 in loss but halves inference cost per token.
recap: Language-model loss falls smoothly as a power law in parameters N, training tokens D and compute C, across many orders of magnitude, so small runs can predict large ones.

Training compute is about C ≈ 6ND FLOPs: 2 per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass; Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) and Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) both used about 5-6 × 10²³.

Kaplan et al. (2020) fitted L(N) ∝ N^−0.076, L(D) ∝ D^−0.095 and L(C) ∝ C^−0.050, and concluded model size should grow faster than data (N ∝ C^0.73), which led to large models trained on about 300B tokens.
Hoffmann et al. (2022) trained over 400 models from 70M to over 16B parameters on 5B to 500B tokens and found N and D should grow equally (exponents near 0.5): double the model, double the data.
The rule of thumb is about 20 tokens per parameter: with C = 6ND and D = 20N, N = √(C/120); for C = 10²⁴ FLOPs that is about 91B parameters on 1.8T tokens.

Chinchilla, the predicted compute-optimal model for Gopher's budget, beat Gopher, GPT-3, Jurassic-1 and Megatron-Turing NLG, reaching 67.5% on MMLU against Gopher's 60.0%, while being four times cheaper to run.

Chinchilla's loss model L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β separates an irreducible term from model-size and data terms; Epoch AI's 2024 replication found the published constants biased and re-fitted them, recovering about 20 tokens per parameter.

Compute-optimal is not cost-optimal when inference matters: models expected to serve heavy traffic are trained smaller and longer; Llama 3 8B saw about 15T tokens, while the 405B flagship at 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs was roughly compute-optimal.
Scaling laws are used to choose model size, data and learning rate before a large run, to predict its loss from small runs, and to compare data mixes and architectures by how they shift the curves.
They predict loss on the training distribution, not specific capabilities; data quality, repetition and the tokeniser all move the curves, so they must be re-fitted for each setup.
glossary: DeepMind's 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens with the same compute as Gopher, used to test the compute-optimal allocation.
The total training FLOPs available for a run, C ≈ 6ND.
The choice of model size and token count that minimises training loss for a fixed compute budget.
A capability that appears to switch on abruptly as models scale; often an artefact of a discontinuous metric rather than of the underlying loss.
One floating-point operation; training budgets are quoted in total FLOPs, such as 10²⁴.
One GPU used for one hour; the unit cloud providers bill training in.
DeepMind's 280B-parameter model trained on 300B tokens, the comparison point for Chinchilla.
The constant term E in a scaling law: the part of the loss no model or dataset size removes, reflecting the inherent unpredictability of text.
A set of runs with the same compute but different splits between model size and tokens; its minimum marks the compute-optimal size.
Model FLOPs utilisation: the fraction of the hardware's peak FLOP/s a training run actually achieves on useful model arithmetic.
Massive Multitask Language Understanding: a benchmark of multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, reported as accuracy.
The unit of cross-entropy when the natural logarithm is used; a loss of 2 nats per token corresponds to a perplexity of e² ≈ 7.4.
Training a model on far more tokens than compute-optimal so that a smaller, cheaper-to-serve model reaches a given quality.
A formula such as L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β fitted to many runs to predict loss for any N and D.
A relationship y = a·x^k; on log-log axes it is a straight line with slope k.
An empirical power-law relationship between loss and parameters, data or compute.
D/N, the ratio of training tokens to parameters; about 20 at Chinchilla's compute-optimal point.
drill:
Estimate — size a training run

You have 2,048 H100 GPUs for 30 days and expect 40% MFU. How much compute is that, what is the compute-optimal model, and what would you actually train if the model will power a high-traffic product?

Answer

Compute: 2,048 GPUs × 30 × 86,400 s × 989 × 10¹² FLOP/s × 0.40 ≈ 2,048 × 2.592 × 10⁶ × 3.96 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 2.1 × 10²⁴ FLOPs.

Compute-optimal: N = √(C/120) = √(1.75 × 10²²) ≈ 132B parameters on D = 20N ≈ 2.6T tokens.

What to actually train: for heavy inference, a smaller model trained longer, for example about 30-40B parameters on 9-12T tokens (C/6N), if that much good data exists. Its loss is slightly higher than the 132B model's, but every served token costs about a quarter as much, and it fits on fewer GPUs at inference. Before committing, run a small-scale sweep on your data to confirm the curves, check that you have enough unique high-quality tokens (repetition beyond a few epochs loses value), and leave budget for failures, evaluation and the long-context and post-training stages.

Explain — the undertrained giant

A manager asks why a 280B model trained in 2021 was beaten by a 70B model trained with the same compute a year later. Explain in three sentences, with numbers.

Answer

A training budget fixes parameters × tokens (C ≈ 6ND), and the 280B Gopher spent it on size, seeing only 300B tokens, about one token per parameter. DeepMind's scaling study showed loss is minimised when size and data grow together, about 20 tokens per parameter, which for Gopher's budget means about 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens. Chinchilla, built exactly that way, scored 67.5% on MMLU against Gopher's 60.0% and costs a quarter as much to run.
qa: E
What is a scaling law for language models?

An empirical rule that pretraining loss falls as a power law in model size, training tokens or compute: L ∝ X^(−k) for some small exponent k, which is a straight line on log-log axes. The relationship holds over many orders of magnitude, so loss at a large scale can be predicted from a series of small runs.
E
Estimate the training compute of a 7B model on 2T tokens.

C ≈ 6ND = 6 × 7 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹² = 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs. The 6 is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and about 4 for the backward pass. On H100s at about 40% utilisation (about 4 × 10¹⁴ useful FLOP/s each), that is 2.1 × 10⁸ GPU-seconds, about 58,000 GPU-hours.
E
What did Chinchilla change?

It showed that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should be scaled in equal proportion, about 20 tokens per parameter, whereas earlier large models had been made very large and trained on only about 300B tokens. A 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens with Gopher's compute beat the 280B Gopher on almost every benchmark.
M
Given 10²⁴ FLOPs, what model size and token count are compute-optimal?
Use C = 6ND and D = 20N: C = 120N², so N = √(10²⁴/120) = √(8.3 × 10²¹) ≈ 9.1 × 10¹⁰, about 91B parameters, and D = 20N ≈ 1.8T tokens. Check: 6 × 9.1 × 10¹⁰ × 1.8 × 10¹² ≈ 10²⁴.

Follow-up: Would you actually train that model? — Only if inference volume is small. If it will serve heavy traffic, a 30-50B model trained on 3-5T tokens gives slightly higher loss for the same training compute but halves or better the cost of every token served.
M
Why did Kaplan and Chinchilla reach different conclusions?

Both found power laws, but Kaplan et al. concluded optimal model size grows as C^0.73, so most extra compute should go to parameters, while Hoffmann et al. found exponents near 0.5. The main explanation is the learning-rate schedule: Kaplan used one cosine schedule length for all runs, so models trained on fewer tokens than the schedule assumed were evaluated before their learning rate had decayed, which understates what short runs and therefore smaller models achieve. Chinchilla matched the schedule to each run's token count. Smaller models in Kaplan's study also excluded embedding parameters, which shifts fits at small scale.
M
What are Chinchilla's three methods, and do they agree?

Approach 1 takes the minimum loss over many training curves at each compute level; approach 2 trains models of several sizes at fixed compute (iso-FLOP profiles) and finds the minimum; approach 3 fits the parametric model L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β to all runs. Approaches 1 and 2 give exponents of 0.50/0.50 and 0.49/0.51; approach 3 gave 0.46/0.54. A 2024 replication by Epoch AI found the published approach-3 fit was biased by an optimiser that stopped early and by rounding, and their re-fit agrees with the other two methods.
M
What does each term of L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β mean?

E is the irreducible loss, the entropy of the text that no model can remove. A/N^α is the excess loss from a finite model: the error an infinitely trained model of size N would still make. B/D^β is the excess loss from finite data: the error from training on only D tokens. Compute-optimal training balances the two shrinking terms along C = 6ND.
M
Why are models like Llama 3 8B trained on far more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal?

Because compute-optimal minimises training cost for a given loss, not total cost. A model is trained once but may serve trillions of tokens, and inference cost scales with parameters. Training a smaller model much longer reaches a given loss with more training compute but far cheaper inference. Sardana et al. found that for expected demand of around a billion requests or more, it pays to train smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal, and that quality kept improving up to extreme ratios such as 10,000 tokens per parameter.

Follow-up: What limits how far you can push this? — Available unique data (repeating data gives diminishing returns), the training budget, and the fact that loss approaches the small model's capacity floor A/N^α.
M
How would you use scaling laws before a large training run?

Run a sweep of small models (for example 10¹⁸ to 10²² FLOPs) on the exact data mix, tokeniser and recipe planned for the big run, fit loss against compute and the optimal size against compute, and extrapolate to the target budget to choose N and D and predict the final loss. During the big run, compare its loss curve with the prediction: a run that falls short signals a bug or a data problem early.
H
Scaling laws are smooth in loss, yet some abilities seem to emerge suddenly. Reconcile these.

Loss is an average over all tokens; a particular task depends on a few tokens being right, often all of several steps at once, and benchmarks score with all-or-nothing metrics such as exact match. A smooth improvement in per-token probability can therefore produce an abrupt jump in exact-match accuracy. Studies show many 'emergent' jumps become smooth with continuous metrics such as the probability of the correct answer. Some capabilities do improve sharply, but predicting them requires a model from loss to task performance, as Llama 3's two-step prediction did.

Follow-up: How do you forecast a downstream metric then? — Fit loss versus compute, then fit task metric (or the model's log-likelihood of correct answers) versus loss on related smaller models, and chain the two.
H
How do data quality and repetition affect scaling laws?

Higher-quality data shifts the curve down (lower loss at the same compute) and can change the optimal ratio; one study found a lower tokens-per-parameter ratio is optimal on higher-quality data. Repeating data gives diminishing returns: a few epochs over the same tokens are nearly as good as fresh data, but many repetitions are worth much less, so when unique data runs out the effective D grows slower than tokens processed. This is why data filtering, deduplication and synthetic data matter as much as compute at the frontier.
H
A colleague fits a scaling law on five runs and predicts the 100× larger run's loss to three decimals. What do you check?

Whether the runs span enough orders of magnitude and are each trained to the end of their own learning-rate schedule; whether the fit includes an irreducible term (a pure power law without E over-predicts gains at large scale); whether the small runs used the same data mix, tokeniser and hyperparameter scaling rules as the big one; how sensitive the extrapolation is to dropping any one run; and whether confidence intervals are realistic. Epoch AI's replication found Chinchilla's own published intervals implausibly narrow, a cautionary example.

Follow-up: What else can go wrong in extrapolation? — Hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size must themselves be scaled correctly, or the large run underperforms the law for reasons unrelated to N and D.

sum: How a probability distribution becomes text: greedy and beam search and why they loop, pure sampling and its unreliable tail, temperature, top-k, top-p (with a five-token cut-off worked by hand) and min-p, repetition penalties, determinism, and which settings suit which task.
prereq: lm3
At every step the model's LM head produces one logit per vocabulary entry for the next token; a softmax turns them into probabilities that sum to 1.
ml5
Softmax converts scores into probabilities by exponentiating and normalising; cross-entropy trains the model to give the true next token high probability.
ml15
Temperature scaling divides logits by a constant T before the softmax; T > 1 flattens a distribution and T < 1 sharpens it, without changing which class is most likely.
lm5
Generation is a loop of decode steps, one token per step, each reading the KV cache of all previous tokens.
why:
Two teams build products on the same open model. The first team's chatbot gives lively, varied answers but occasionally wanders into nonsense halfway through a paragraph. The second team's summariser is reliable but painfully repetitive: on long documents it repeats the same sentence three times and then stops. A third engineer, asked to extract invoice fields as JSON, gets valid JSON nineteen times out of twenty and a creatively reworded key on the twentieth. None of them changed the model. All three problems live in the few lines of code that turn the model's output into words: the decoding strategy.

A language model does not produce text. At each step it produces a probability for every token in its vocabulary, often 100,000 or more numbers. Something has to choose one token, append it, and run the model again. The obvious choice, always take the most likely token, turns out to be one of the worst for open-ended writing, and the other obvious choice, pick randomly in proportion to the probabilities, has its own failure. Between them lies a small family of techniques with names you will see in every API: temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, repetition penalties, beam width, seeds.

These settings matter for an AI engineer for three reasons. They change product behaviour as much as switching models does. They decide whether evaluations are reproducible and comparable. And interviewers like them because they have exact answers: given a distribution, you can compute what top-p keeps.

This lesson starts with the generation loop and the distribution the model hands you. It covers greedy decoding and beam search and why they degenerate, pure sampling and its unreliable tail, then temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p, each worked by hand on the same five-token distribution. It continues with repetition penalties, determinism, and constrained decoding, and ends with how to choose settings per task. The public case is Holtzman et al.'s study of neural text degeneration, which introduced nucleus (top-p) sampling. The lab implements every sampler in NumPy and runs them on a small bigram model so you can watch greedy decoding loop.
primer:
The generation loop

Generation is a loop. Feed the prompt to the model; it returns, for the next position, one logit per vocabulary entry; a softmax turns these into probabilities that sum to 1 (lm3). A decoding strategy picks one token from that distribution. The token is appended, the model runs again (reusing the KV cache, lm5), and so on until an end-of-sequence token or a length limit. Everything in this lesson happens in the "pick one token" box. The model's weights never change; only the rule for using its probabilities does.

Two families

Maximisation strategies try to find a high-probability output: greedy decoding takes the top token every step; beam search keeps several candidate sequences and returns the most probable one it finds. Sampling strategies draw randomly according to the probabilities, usually after reshaping them with a temperature and cutting off the unlikely tail. Maximisation is predictable and suits tasks with one right answer. Sampling gives variety and, perhaps surprisingly, more human-like text.

An analogy: ordering at a restaurant

Imagine choosing dinner by a friend's recommendations, each with a confidence. Greedy decoding always orders the top recommendation; after a week you have eaten the same dish seven times. Pure sampling orders in proportion to confidence, including the 1% recommendations, so occasionally you get something absurd. Temperature turns up or down how much you trust the ranking. Top-k says "only consider the top five", top-p says "only consider dishes that together make up 90% of my friend's confidence", and min-p says "ignore anything much less recommended than the favourite". The analogy breaks in one important way: dinners are independent, but tokens are not. One absurd token changes the context for every token after it, which is why an occasional bad pick can derail an entire paragraph and why truncation matters so much.

Why the choice compounds

Decoding is not a one-off choice but hundreds or thousands of them in a row, and each one becomes part of the input to all the others. That is why small differences in strategy produce large differences in output. Suppose a sampler has a 2% chance per token of picking something the model itself would consider a mistake. Over a 500-token answer, the chance of at least one such pick is 1 − 0.98⁵⁰⁰, more than 99.99%. Whether the text recovers from that pick depends on how far off it was: a slightly odd word is harmless, a token from the far tail can send the rest of the paragraph off course. Conversely, a strategy that always takes the safest token never makes that kind of mistake but slides into its own failure, repetition, because safe choices reinforce themselves. Good decoding is about controlling both risks at once: cut off the far tail, but leave enough randomness to keep the text moving.

Where you meet these settings

Every LLM API (application programming interface, the web endpoint you call) exposes some of these knobs as request parameters: temperature, top_p, sometimes top_k, presence and frequency penalties, a seed, and a maximum number of tokens. Open-source inference libraries expose more, including min-p, repetition penalty and beam width. The defaults vary by provider and by library, and a surprising number of production incidents are caused by a default that changed or a parameter that was silently ignored. Knowing what each parameter does to the distribution lets you read an API reference and predict the effect before you run anything.

The example used throughout

After "The capital of France is", suppose the model gives five candidates (a real model has a whole vocabulary, but five keeps the arithmetic visible): "Paris" 0.50, "the" 0.25, "a" 0.12, "London" 0.08, "banana" 0.05. Every method below is worked on these numbers.
body:
1. What the model hands you

At each step the LM head outputs a vector of logits z, one per vocabulary entry, and the softmax p_i = exp(z_i)/Σ_j exp(z_j) turns them into probabilities. For a vocabulary of 128,000 tokens, that is 128,000 probabilities summing to 1. In a typical position the distribution has a handful of tokens with most of the mass and a very long tail of tokens with tiny probabilities each. The shape varies wildly between positions: after "The capital of France is" nearly all mass may sit on " Paris"; after "My favourite colour is" it is spread across dozens of colour words. A good decoding strategy must behave sensibly at both kinds of position.

A useful single number for the shape is the entropy, H = −Σ p log p: zero when one token has probability 1, larger when probability is spread out. Our five-token example has H = 1.30 nats. The lab prints the entropy after each transformation, which makes it easy to see which ones sharpen and which flatten.

2. Greedy decoding

Greedy decoding picks argmax p at each step: "Paris" in the example. It is deterministic, cheap and often correct for short factual answers, classification ("positive"/"negative") and extraction, where the most probable token usually is the right one. For longer open-ended text it has two well-known problems. First, it is short-sighted: the best first token does not necessarily start the best sequence. Second, and worse, it loops. Language models assign higher probability to continuing a pattern that is already present in the context, so once a phrase has repeated, repeating it again becomes the most probable continuation. Holtzman et al. showed the probability of a repeated phrase increases with each repetition, a positive feedback loop. Greedy decoding always follows the most probable path, so it walks straight into the loop and stays there. The lab's small bigram model shows it: greedy text from the word "the" has 49% repeated three-word sequences within 40 words, while sampled text has about 1%.

3. Beam search

Beam search tries to fix short-sightedness. It keeps the B best partial sequences (the beam), scored by total log-probability. At each step it extends every partial sequence by every possible next token, scores all the extensions, and keeps the top B overall. At the end it returns the best complete sequence. With B = 1 it is greedy; larger B explores more. Worked in miniature with B = 2: suppose step one gives "Paris" (log-prob −0.69) and "the" (−1.39). Extending "Paris" gives "Paris ." at −0.69 + (−0.22) = −0.91 and "Paris ," at −0.69 + (−1.90) = −2.59; extending "the" gives "the city" at −1.39 + (−0.36) = −1.75. The beam keeps "Paris ." (−0.91) and "the city" (−1.75). It found a sequence greedy might miss if, say, "the city of light" turned out more probable in total.

Two practical details. Because log-probabilities are negative and add up, longer sequences always score lower, so plain beam search favours short outputs; implementations divide by a length term (length normalisation). And beam search is the standard choice in machine translation and speech recognition, where the output is tightly constrained by the input and the most probable output is usually good. For open-ended text it amplifies greedy's problems: it finds even more probable, even more generic and repetitive text. Holtzman et al. measured 28.94% repetition with beam width 16 on GPT-2 Large, and noted that with large beams (64 and above) GPT-2 degenerated into repetition, even with substantial human context.

4. Why maximum probability is the wrong target for open-ended text

The intuition that "the most probable text is the best text" fails because human writing is not maximally probable. Holtzman et al. plotted the probability GPT-2 assigned to each token of real human text and found it fluctuates constantly, with frequent low-probability words: people make surprising, specific choices. Beam-search text, by contrast, sits at uniformly high probability and reads as bland and repetitive. Their Table 1 quantifies it with perplexity (the exponential of the average negative log-probability per token, lower meaning more predictable to the model): human text scored 12.38, greedy 1.50 and beam search 1.48. Maximisation produces text eight times "more predictable" than people write. Good open-ended decoding should therefore aim to produce text that is about as surprising as human text, not as unsurprising as possible. That reframing is the core of the paper.

5. Pure sampling and the unreliable tail

The opposite approach is to sample the next token at random with exactly the model's probabilities. On our example, "Paris" half the time, "banana" one time in twenty. Sampling produces varied text with no loops, and in principle it reproduces the model's distribution faithfully. The problem is the tail. In a real vocabulary there may be tens of thousands of tokens each with tiny probability, but together they can hold 10-30% of the mass, so sampling regularly picks one. The model's probabilities for those tail tokens are poorly calibrated: each individually is "unlikely but not impossible", yet most of them are nonsense in context. One nonsense token then becomes part of the context, the model tries to continue it, and the text derails. Holtzman et al.'s pure sampling gave perplexity 22.73, far less predictable than human text, and incoherent passages.

6. Temperature

Temperature reshapes the distribution before sampling: divide every logit by T, then apply the softmax.

p_i(T) = exp(z_i / T) / Σ_j exp(z_j / T)        equivalently   p_i(T) ∝ p_i^(1/T)

Worked on the example. At T = 0.5, each probability is raised to the power 2 and renormalised: 0.25, 0.0625, 0.0144, 0.0064, 0.0025, which sum to 0.3358; dividing gives [0.744, 0.186, 0.043, 0.019, 0.007]. "Paris" rose from 0.50 to 0.74 and "banana" fell from 0.05 to 0.007; entropy fell from 1.30 to 0.78 nats. At T = 2, each probability is square-rooted: 0.707, 0.500, 0.346, 0.283, 0.224, sum 2.060, giving [0.343, 0.243, 0.168, 0.137, 0.109]; the distribution flattened and "banana" doubled to 0.11. As T approaches 0 the top token's share approaches 1 (greedy); as T grows the distribution approaches uniform. Temperature never changes the ranking, only the gaps. It is the same operation as temperature scaling for calibration (ml15), used here not to fix calibration but to trade predictability for variety. Lowering temperature reduces tail sampling, but on its own it pushes towards the repetitive regime: Holtzman et al.'s top-k 40 with T = 0.7 had 8.86% repetition.

7. Top-k sampling

Top-k removes the tail by count: keep the k most probable tokens, set the rest to zero, renormalise, sample. With k = 2 on the example: keep 0.50 and 0.25, total 0.75, renormalised to [0.667, 0.333, 0, 0, 0]. Top-k was used in early GPT-2 demonstrations with k = 40. Its flaw is that k is fixed while the distribution's shape is not. When the model is confident (one token at 0.95), k = 40 still lets 39 unlikely tokens in; when it is uncertain (probability spread over 200 reasonable words), k = 40 throws away good options and makes text narrower than it should be. Holtzman et al. found top-k = 40 too predictable (perplexity 6.88) and top-k = 640 close to human perplexity but with poor quality scores.

8. Top-p (nucleus) sampling

Holtzman et al.'s proposal sizes the candidate set by probability mass instead of count. Sort tokens by probability, accumulate, and keep the smallest prefix whose cumulative probability reaches p (the nucleus), then renormalise and sample. On the example with p = 0.9: cumulative sums are 0.50 (Paris), 0.75 (+ the), 0.87 (+ a), 0.95 (+ London). The sum first reaches 0.9 at "London", so the nucleus is the first four tokens, total 0.95. Renormalising by 0.95 gives [0.526, 0.263, 0.126, 0.084, 0]: "banana" is gone, everything else keeps its relative odds. If instead the model put 0.93 on "Paris", the nucleus would contain "Paris" alone and top-p would act like greedy; if probability were spread over 200 plausible words, the nucleus would contain most of them. The candidate set adapts to the model's confidence, which is exactly what top-k lacks.

In their experiments with GPT-2 Large, nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 produced text with perplexity 13.13 (human 12.38), a vocabulary distribution and diversity close to human text, 0.36% repetition (human 0.28%), and the highest HUSE score of all methods, 0.97. Top-p became the default sampling method in most LLM APIs.

9. Min-p and other adaptive truncation

Top-p has a weakness at high temperature: flattening the distribution moves mass into the tail, so the nucleus can admit many poor tokens. Min-p (Nguyen et al., 2024) uses a threshold relative to the top token: keep every token whose probability is at least min_p × p_max. With min-p = 0.2 on the example, the threshold is 0.2 × 0.50 = 0.10, so "Paris", "the" and "a" survive and "London" (0.08) and "banana" (0.05) are cut; renormalised over 0.87 they become [0.575, 0.287, 0.138]. When the model is confident (p_max = 0.95) the threshold is 0.19 and almost everything else is cut; when it is uncertain (p_max = 0.05) the threshold is 0.01 and many options survive. Its authors argue this keeps text coherent at higher temperatures, enabling more creative output. Other adaptive methods exist (typical sampling, which keeps tokens whose surprise is close to the distribution's average; mirostat, which steers the sampled surprise towards a target), but top-p and min-p are the ones you will see in practice.

10. Order of operations and common defaults

Libraries apply these steps in a pipeline: penalties on the logits, then temperature, then truncation filters, then sampling. The order matters (truncating before or after temperature gives different sets), and it differs between libraries, so check it when you port settings from one stack to another. Typical API defaults are temperature 1 with top-p 1 (pure sampling from the model's distribution, relying on the model being well-tuned after post-training), and many applications lower temperature to 0.2-0.7 or set top-p to about 0.9. A setting of temperature 0 is usually implemented as greedy decoding. Because the settings interact, a sensible practice is to tune one knob (often temperature) and leave the others at neutral values unless there is a measured reason.

11. Repetition, frequency and presence penalties

Penalties modify the logits of tokens that have already appeared. The repetition penalty from the CTRL paper (Keskar et al., 2019, describing Salesforce's 1.6-billion-parameter conditional language model; the penalty was their remedy for greedy decoding's loops) divides a previously generated token's logit by θ (if positive), with θ = 1.2 found to balance truthful generation and lack of repetition with greedy decoding. API-style presence and frequency penalties subtract a constant once a token has appeared, or a constant times its count. Worked: with a frequency penalty of 0.5, a token that has appeared three times has 1.5 subtracted from its logit, dividing its probability by about e^1.5 ≈ 4.5 before renormalisation. Penalties are blunt. They cannot tell a pathological loop from legitimate repetition, so they damage code (a variable name must repeat), structured output (JSON keys repeat by design), names and technical terms. Use them lightly, mainly with greedy or low-temperature decoding where loops are likely.

12. Determinism, seeds and reproducibility

Sampling uses a random number generator, so setting a seed makes it repeatable on identical hardware with identical batching. Greedy decoding has no randomness at all. Yet even greedy outputs from hosted LLMs can differ between calls, because the logits themselves vary slightly: GPU kernels add numbers in an order that depends on batch size and contents, floating-point addition is not associative, and when two tokens are nearly tied a tiny difference flips the argmax, after which the whole continuation differs. For products that need consistency, use temperature 0, constrain the format, and cache answers; for evaluation, run multiple samples and report variance rather than trusting a single run.

13. Constrained decoding

When output must follow a strict format, such as valid JSON matching a schema, a function call, or one of a fixed set of labels, decoding can enforce it directly. At each step the decoder computes which tokens would keep the output valid under a grammar and sets all other tokens' logits to −∞ before picking. The model still chooses among valid tokens, so content comes from the model while validity is guaranteed. This beats both "please output JSON" prompting (which fails occasionally) and post-hoc repair. Many serving engines and APIs provide structured output modes built on this idea; lm16 uses it for tool calls. Constrained decoding composes with the methods above: you can sample with temperature and top-p among the valid tokens.

14. Stopping: end tokens, stop sequences and length limits

Decoding also decides when to stop. A chat model normally emits a special end-of-turn token (lm1) when its answer is complete; the decoder stops there. Applications can add stop sequences, strings that end generation when produced (for example a closing tag or "\nUser:"), and a maximum token limit as a safety net. Each generation reports a finish reason: the end token, a stop sequence, or the length limit. A rising share of length-limit finishes is one of the best signals that something is wrong, since it usually means repetition loops, a broken chat template that hides the end token, or a prompt that invites unbounded output. The limit also bounds cost and latency, because every generated token is a decode step (lm5).

15. Choosing settings by task

TaskSuggested decodingWhy
Classification, extraction, short factual answersgreedy / T ≈ 0, constrained formatone right answer; consistency matters
Code generation (single answer)T ≈ 0-0.2, no repetition penaltycorrectness; identifiers must repeat
Code with tests (pick the best of n)T ≈ 0.6-0.8, top-p 0.95, n samplesdiversity raises pass@k
