These are starting points, not rules. The right setting is the one that maximises your task metric on a held-out set, and it should be recorded with every evaluation, because a model's measured quality depends on it.
deep:
The positive feedback behind repetition

Why do models make repeated phrases more likely? Training text contains many legitimate repetitions (lists, refrains, code), and attention makes copying earlier context easy: induction heads (lm2) predict "whatever followed this token last time". Once a sentence appears twice, the model's in-context evidence that "this document repeats" is strong, and the probability of a third repetition rises. Holtzman et al.'s figure 4 shows the probability of a repeated phrase climbing with each repetition. Maximisation decoding converts that rising probability into certainty. Sampling breaks the loop because it occasionally takes a different path; training-side remedies (penalising repeated tokens during training) also exist but are less common than fixing decoding.

The beam search curse

In machine translation it was observed that increasing beam width beyond a small value often makes translations worse, sometimes catastrophically: very wide beams find outputs with higher model probability that are shorter or even empty. This shows the model's probability is not a perfect measure of quality: the search finds the model's errors when it searches hard enough. The same principle reappears in RLHF as reward hacking (lm6): optimising hard against an imperfect score finds its flaws. Small beams with length normalisation are the practical compromise for constrained tasks.

Temperature, calibration and the tail

If a model's probabilities were perfectly calibrated, pure sampling at T = 1 would reproduce the training distribution exactly, including its variety. In practice probabilities in the tail are over-estimated relative to how often those tokens are good: models trained with cross-entropy are pushed to assign some probability to every possibility (any zero probability on a real token is an infinite loss), so they spread small amounts of mass widely. Post-training (lm6) also changes calibration, typically making chat models more confident. Truncation can be seen as a correction for tail miscalibration, which is why it helps even for models that are well calibrated on their top choices.

Sampling many and choosing: self-consistency and best-of-n

Decoding need not produce a single sample. Self-consistency samples several reasoning chains at moderate temperature and takes the majority final answer, which improves accuracy on maths and reasoning because errors are diverse while correct answers agree. Best-of-n samples n responses and picks the one a scorer (a reward model, a test suite, a judge model) rates highest. Both trade inference compute for quality, the "inference-time scaling" mentioned in lm7, and both require diversity: with greedy decoding all n samples are identical. Their cost is n times the generation, partly offset because the prompt's KV cache can be shared across samples (lm13).

Diversity across samples versus quality within one

Two different things are often both called "diversity". Within one long output, you want variety: no loops, natural word choice. Across many outputs for the same prompt, you may or may not want variety: a brainstorming tool wants ten different ideas, while a customer-support bot should give the same correct answer every time. Temperature and truncation affect both at once, which is why the right setting depends on the product. When you need consistency across calls but natural text within one, use low temperature with top-p rather than pure greedy decoding, and cache answers for repeated questions.

Where the logits are modified matters for serving

Logit processors run on every decode step for every sequence in a batch, on vectors as long as the vocabulary. Sorting 128,000 probabilities for top-p at each step is non-trivial at high throughput, so serving engines implement sampling in fused GPU kernels, sometimes using approximate or partial sorts. Constrained decoding adds a grammar state per sequence and a mask computation per step; naive implementations can become the bottleneck, which is why efficient grammar engines precompute token masks. Speculative decoding (lm13) must also reproduce the target sampling distribution exactly, which constrains how draft tokens are accepted under sampling.

Contrastive and guided decoding

Several methods change the scores rather than just truncating them. Contrastive decoding scores each token by the difference between a large model's log-probability and a small "amateur" model's, favouring continuations the strong model likes but the weak one does not, which suppresses generic, repetitive text the weak model also predicts. Classifier-free guidance, borrowed from image diffusion models, contrasts the model's predictions with and without part of the prompt to strengthen the prompt's influence. These methods cost an extra forward pass per step and are less common in production than temperature and top-p, but they illustrate a general point: decoding is a place where you can inject extra information or preferences at inference time without retraining.

Decoding and evaluation metrics

Many benchmark numbers are sensitive to decoding: pass@k for code depends on sampling temperature; multiple-choice benchmarks may be scored by comparing log-probabilities of options rather than generating at all; open-ended judge-based evaluations can change with temperature. Two models compared at different settings are not comparable. Good practice is to evaluate each model at its recommended settings (or sweep a few), fix seeds where possible, run multiple samples per item, and report the settings alongside the scores. lm14 returns to this.
prod:
The public case: "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration" (Holtzman et al., 2019)

In 2019, GPT-2 was the most capable public language model, and its generations were famously uneven. Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes and Choi asked whether the problem was the model or the decoding. They generated 5,000 passages with GPT-2 Large (762M parameters) conditioned on WebText prefixes, under every common strategy, and compared them with the human continuations on several statistics: perplexity under the model, diversity between generations (Self-BLEU), how closely word frequencies matched human vocabulary use (Zipf coefficient), repetition, and HUSE, a combined human-and-statistical score.

Their Table 1 is the case in numbers. Human text: perplexity 12.38, Self-BLEU 0.31, repetition 0.28%. Greedy: perplexity 1.50 and 73.66% repetition. Beam search with width 16: 1.48 and 28.94%. Pure sampling: perplexity 22.73, too random. Sampling with temperature 0.9: 10.25. Top-k = 40: 6.88; top-k = 640: 13.82; top-k = 40 with temperature 0.7: 3.48 and 8.86% repetition. Nucleus sampling with p = 0.95: perplexity 13.13, Self-BLEU 0.32, repetition 0.36%, and the highest HUSE, 0.97. The conclusions: maximisation is an inappropriate objective for open-ended generation; pure sampling fails because of the unreliable tail; and truncating the tail adaptively, by cumulative probability, gives the most human-like text. Nucleus sampling was quickly adopted and top-p remains a standard parameter in essentially every LLM API.

Failure modes in production

Repetition loops in long outputs. Summaries or reports that repeat sentences, usually with greedy or very low temperature on long generations. Fix with sampling plus top-p, a mild penalty, or a maximum-length guard and loop detection.

Occasional derailment. A chat answer that turns into nonsense mid-paragraph, typically high temperature without truncation, or a provider default changed. Lower temperature or add top-p/min-p.

Broken structured output. Mostly-valid JSON with occasional invalid keys or truncation. Use constrained decoding or structured-output modes, temperature 0, and no repetition penalty.

Irreproducible evaluations. Scores that move between runs of the same model. Fix and log settings and seeds, run several samples per item, and report confidence intervals.

Settings lost in migration. Moving from one inference library to another changes the order of temperature and truncation or the meaning of a penalty, and output quality shifts. Re-validate settings after any stack change.

A decoding-related incident pattern

A common real-world sequence goes like this. A team tunes prompts with an API playground whose default temperature is 0.7, then ships code that calls the API without specifying temperature, so the provider's default of 1.0 applies. Outputs in production become noticeably more varied and occasionally off-topic; nobody changed the model or the prompt, so the investigation looks everywhere else first. The cure is cheap: set every decoding parameter explicitly in code, store the configuration with the prompt version, and include decoding settings in the evaluation harness so that a change in them shows up as a change in scores before it reaches users.

What to log

For every generation in production: model version, decoding parameters (temperature, top-p, top-k, min-p, penalties, max tokens, stop sequences), seed if used, finish reason (stop, length, content filter), and token counts. Monitor the rate of length-limit finishes (often loops), invalid structured outputs, and repetition statistics in a sample of outputs.
myths: The most probable output is the best output.

For open-ended text it usually is not. Greedy decoding and beam search, which chase the highest-probability continuation, produce bland, repetitive text: Holtzman et al. measured 73.66% repeated content for greedy and 28.94% for beam search with width 16 on GPT-2, against 0.28% in human text. Human writing is not maximally probable under a language model; it regularly picks lower-probability words.
Temperature 0 makes an LLM deterministic.

It makes the sampling step greedy, but the logits themselves can differ from run to run: batched GPU kernels sum numbers in different orders depending on batch composition, and floating-point addition is not associative, so near-ties can flip. Serving APIs also vary hardware and batch. Expect high but not perfect reproducibility, and design evaluations accordingly.
Top-p and top-k do the same thing.

Top-k always keeps exactly k tokens, which is too many when the model is confident (it admits junk) and too few when many continuations are reasonable (it cuts good options). Top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability reaches p, so the number of candidates adapts: one or two when the model is sure, hundreds when it is not.
A higher temperature makes the model more creative.

It flattens the distribution, so unlikely tokens are sampled more often. Some of that is welcome variety; much of it is the long tail of tokens the model considers nonsense. Past a point text becomes incoherent. Truncation (top-p, min-p) is what lets higher temperatures stay coherent, by removing the tail before sampling.
Decoding settings are cosmetic; the model's quality is what matters.

The same model can look excellent or broken depending on decoding. Pure sampling on GPT-2 gave text with perplexity 22.73 against 12.38 for human text (too random), greedy gave 1.50 (too predictable). Evaluations, A/B tests and benchmark scores all depend on the decoding configuration, which must be reported and held fixed.
Repetition penalties fix repetition.

They divide or subtract from the logits of tokens already generated, which reduces loops but also penalises tokens that should repeat, such as variable names in code, names of people, or required JSON keys. Strong penalties produce awkward synonyms and broken structured output. Prefer sampling with truncation and use penalties lightly.
lab:
Goal: implement temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p, check them against the hand calculations, then generate from a tiny bigram language model to watch greedy decoding loop and sampling escape, and run a small beam search. NumPy and the standard library only, about a second.

import numpy as np, importlib, re, collections
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

def softmax(z): z = z - z.max(); e = np.exp(z); return e / e.sum()
def process(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None, min_p=None):
    """Turn logits into the distribution actually sampled from (the usual order: temperature, then filters)."""
    p = softmax(logits / temperature)
    keep = np.ones_like(p, bool)
    if top_k is not None:
        keep &= p >= np.sort(p)[-top_k]
    if top_p is not None:
        order = np.argsort(-p); cum = np.cumsum(p[order])
        n = np.searchsorted(cum, top_p) + 1                  # smallest prefix whose mass reaches top_p
        mask = np.zeros_like(keep); mask[order[:n]] = True; keep &= mask
    if min_p is not None:
        keep &= p >= min_p * p.max()
    q = np.where(keep, p, 0.0); return q / q.sum()

# ---- 1. the lesson's 5-token example
tokens = ["Paris", "the", "a", "London", "banana"]
probs = np.array([0.50, 0.25, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05]); logits = np.log(probs)
print("tokens      ", tokens)
for label, kw in [("T=1", {}), ("T=0.5", {"temperature": 0.5}), ("T=2", {"temperature": 2.0}),
                  ("top-k=2", {"top_k": 2}), ("top-p=0.9", {"top_p": 0.9}), ("min-p=0.2", {"min_p": 0.2})]:
    q = process(logits, **kw); H = -(q[q > 0] * np.log(q[q > 0])).sum()
    print(f"{label:11s} {q}   entropy {H:.3f} nats")
print("cumulative mass in order:", np.cumsum(probs))

# ---- 2. a tiny word-level bigram 'language model' from standard-library docstrings
text = " ".join(importlib.import_module(m).__doc__ or "" for m in ["json", "csv", "argparse", "logging", "subprocess", "threading", "pathlib", "random", "heapq", "zipfile"])
words = re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())
vocab = sorted(set(words)); idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
counts = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]): counts[a][b] += 1
def next_logits(w):
    l = np.full(len(vocab), -1e9)
    for b, c in counts[w].items(): l[idx[b]] = np.log(c)
    return l
def generate(start, n, rng=None, **kw):
    out = [start]
    for _ in range(n):
        l = next_logits(out[-1])
        if rng is None: nxt = vocab[int(np.argmax(l))]                      # greedy
        else: nxt = vocab[rng.choice(len(vocab), p=process(l, **kw))]
        out.append(nxt)
    return out
def repetition(seq, n=3):                                                     # share of repeated 3-grams
    grams = list(zip(*[seq[i:] for i in range(n)])); return 1 - len(set(grams)) / len(grams)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(f"\nbigram model over {len(vocab)} words")
g = generate("the", 40); print("greedy      :", " ".join(g[:16]), "...", f"| repeated 3-grams {repetition(g):.0%}")
for label, kw in [("T=1.0", {}), ("T=0.7", {"temperature": 0.7}), ("top-p=0.9", {"top_p": 0.9})]:
    reps = [repetition(generate("the", 40, rng, **kw)) for _ in range(50)]
    s = generate("the", 15, np.random.default_rng(1), **kw)
    print(f"{label:12s}: {' '.join(s)} | mean repeated 3-grams {np.mean(reps):.0%}")

# ---- 3. beam search on the same model: highest-probability sequences, not the most interesting
def beam(start, n, width):
    beams = [([start], 0.0)]
    for _ in range(n):
        cand = []
        for seq, lp in beams:
            l = next_logits(seq[-1]); lps = l - np.log(np.exp(l - l.max()).sum()) - l.max()
            for j in np.argsort(-lps)[:width]: cand.append((seq + [vocab[j]], lp + lps[j]))
        beams = sorted(cand, key=lambda c: -c[1])[:width]
    return beams[0]
seq, lp = beam("the", 12, 4)
print(f"\nbeam (width 4): {' '.join(seq)}  | log-prob {lp:.2f}, per word {lp/12:.2f}")

What to look for.

  1. Section 1 reproduces the lesson's numbers: T = 0.5 gives [0.744, 0.186, 0.043, 0.019, 0.007] (entropy 0.78 nats, down from 1.30), T = 2 gives [0.343, 0.243, 0.168, 0.137, 0.109], top-k = 2 gives [0.667, 0.333, 0, 0, 0], top-p = 0.9 gives [0.526, 0.263, 0.126, 0.084, 0] after cumulative sums 0.50, 0.75, 0.87, 0.95, and min-p = 0.2 keeps three tokens.
  2. Section 2 builds a bigram model over 565 words. Greedy text falls into a loop (49% repeated 3-grams); sampled text at T = 1, T = 0.7 and top-p = 0.9 averages about 1%.
  3. Section 3 runs beam search with width 4: a single high-probability sequence (average log-probability about −1.0 per word), fluent-looking fragments stitched from the most common transitions.

Try next. Add a repetition penalty to greedy decoding and watch the loop break, then count how often it blocks a word that should repeat.
recap: At each step a language model outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary; decoding is the rule that turns that distribution into one chosen token, and the same model gives very different text under different rules.

Greedy decoding takes the most probable token every time and beam search keeps the best few partial sequences; both suit tasks with one right answer but loop and go bland on open-ended text (73.66% and 28.94% repetition in Holtzman et al.'s GPT-2 experiments).
Pure sampling draws from the full distribution, which is diverse but keeps landing in the unreliable tail of thousands of individually unlikely tokens, so errors compound.
Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens and renormalises; with k = 2 the example becomes [0.667, 0.333, 0, 0, 0].

Top-p (nucleus) sorts tokens and keeps the smallest prefix whose cumulative probability reaches p: with p = 0.9 the cumulative sums 0.50, 0.75, 0.87, 0.95 keep four tokens, renormalised to [0.526, 0.263, 0.126, 0.084].
Min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least a fraction of the top token's, so the threshold rises when the model is confident; with min-p 0.2 the cut-off is 0.1 and three tokens survive.

Holtzman et al. found nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 produced text closest to human statistics: perplexity 13.13 against 12.38 for human text, 0.36% repetition, and the best combined human-and-statistical (HUSE) score of 0.97.
Repetition, frequency and presence penalties lower the logits of tokens already used; they reduce loops but can damage code, names and structured output.

Choose settings by task: greedy or low temperature for extraction, classification and code; moderate temperature with top-p for conversation; higher temperature for brainstorming; constrained decoding for strict formats; and always report the settings with any evaluation.
glossary: Decoding that keeps the B highest-scoring partial sequences at each step, extending each by its best tokens, and returns the best complete sequence.
The number B of partial sequences beam search keeps.
Restricting each step to tokens allowed by a grammar or schema, for example only tokens that keep the output valid JSON.
The procedure that turns the model's next-token distributions into generated text.
Bland, repetitive or incoherent text produced by a poor decoding strategy rather than by a bad model.
A measure of how spread out a distribution is, −Σ p log p; zero for a certain outcome, larger when many outcomes are plausible.
Choosing the single most probable token at every step.
Human Unified with Statistical Evaluation: a score that combines human judgements of quality with a model's probabilities to measure both quality and diversity.
Dividing a sequence's log-probability by (a function of) its length so beam search does not favour short outputs.
A string that ends generation when the model produces it, set by the application.
The raw score the model gives a token before the softmax.
Truncation that keeps tokens whose probability is at least min_p times the top token's probability.
Sampling from the smallest set of most-likely tokens whose total probability is at least p, renormalised.
The exponential of the average negative log-probability per token; lower means the text is more predictable to the model.
API parameters that subtract a constant from the logits of tokens that have appeared (presence) or in proportion to how often they appeared (frequency).
Dividing positive logits (or multiplying negative ones) of already-generated tokens by a factor such as 1.2, from the CTRL paper.
Choosing the next token at random according to the (possibly modified) probabilities.
The starting value of the random number generator; fixing it makes sampling repeatable on identical hardware and batch layout.
A diversity measure: the average overlap of each generated text with the others; higher means less diverse.
A divisor T applied to logits before the softmax; T < 1 sharpens the distribution, T > 1 flattens it, T → 0 approaches greedy.
Sampling only from the k most probable tokens, renormalised.
The many low-probability tokens whose combined probability is substantial, from which pure sampling often picks a poor token.
drill:
Compute — what does the sampler keep?

A model's next-token probabilities are 0.40, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.08, 0.04, 0.03. Which tokens survive top-k = 3, top-p = 0.8 and min-p = 0.25, and what are the renormalised probabilities for top-p?

Answer

Top-k = 3: 0.40, 0.20, 0.15 (sum 0.75) → 0.533, 0.267, 0.200.

Top-p = 0.8: cumulative 0.40, 0.60, 0.75, 0.85. The sum first reaches 0.8 at the fourth token, so keep four tokens with total 0.85: 0.40/0.85 = 0.471, 0.20/0.85 = 0.235, 0.15/0.85 = 0.176, 0.10/0.85 = 0.118.

Min-p = 0.25: threshold 0.25 × 0.40 = 0.10, so keep 0.40, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10 (the same four tokens here) with the same renormalised values as top-p.

Note that top-p and min-p agree on this distribution but would diverge if it were flatter or more peaked; top-k ignores the shape entirely.

Diagnose — the summariser that repeats

A document summariser built on an open model with greedy decoding sometimes outputs the same sentence three or four times before hitting the length limit. What is happening and what do you change?

Answer

A greedy repetition loop: once a sentence has appeared, the model assigns higher probability to repeating it, and greedy decoding always follows the most probable path, so it never leaves the loop until the token limit. The rise in "finish reason = length" is the telltale metric.

Options, in order: switch to sampling with a moderate temperature (around 0.3-0.7) plus top-p 0.9, which breaks loops while staying focused; or keep near-greedy decoding and add a mild repetition penalty (about 1.1-1.2) or n-gram blocking, checking that names and key terms can still repeat; add loop detection that stops generation when a sentence repeats; and check the prompt and chat template, since a malformed template can also cause run-on output. Evaluate the change with a summary-quality metric and the repetition rate on a held-out set of documents.
qa: E
What is decoding, and name the main strategies.

The model gives a probability for every possible next token; decoding chooses one, appends it and repeats. Deterministic strategies pick by probability: greedy takes the top token each step, beam search keeps several partial sequences and returns the highest-probability one. Stochastic strategies sample: pure sampling from the whole distribution, or sampling after reshaping it with temperature and truncating it with top-k, top-p or min-p.
E
What does temperature do?

It divides every logit by T before the softmax. T below 1 exaggerates the differences, so likely tokens get even more probability and output becomes more predictable; T above 1 shrinks the differences, spreading probability towards unlikely tokens. T near 0 is effectively greedy. It never changes the ranking of tokens, only how peaked the distribution is.
E
Why does greedy decoding repeat itself?

Each repeated phrase makes the same phrase more likely next time: once a model has produced 'I don't know. I don't know.', the most probable continuation is another 'I don't know.' Holtzman et al. show the probability of a repeated phrase rises with each repetition, a positive feedback loop. Greedy always takes the top choice, so it cannot escape; sampling occasionally picks something else and breaks the loop.
M
Apply top-p = 0.9 to probabilities 0.50, 0.25, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05.

Sort descending (already sorted) and accumulate: 0.50, 0.75, 0.87, 0.95. The first point at or above 0.9 is after the fourth token, so the nucleus is the first four tokens with total mass 0.95. Renormalise by dividing by 0.95: 0.526, 0.263, 0.126, 0.084; the fifth token gets 0. Then sample from that.

Follow-up: What if the model were confident, say 0.93 on the top token? — The nucleus would contain only that token, so top-p behaves like greedy exactly when the model is sure, which is the adaptivity top-k lacks.
M
Compare top-k and top-p.

Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens regardless of the distribution's shape. When the distribution is peaked, k = 40 still admits 39 unlikely tokens; when it is flat, k = 40 may cut many good candidates. Top-p sizes the candidate set by cumulative probability, so it shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is uncertain. Many systems combine them (top-k as a safety cap, top-p for adaptivity).
M
Why is beam search good for translation but bad for open-ended generation?

In translation the output is tightly constrained by the input, and the highest-probability translation is usually a good one; beam search finds higher-probability sequences than greedy. In open-ended generation many continuations are acceptable and the highest-probability ones are generic and repetitive, because probability rewards safe, common phrasing; beam search makes that worse by optimising harder. It also favours short outputs unless lengths are normalised.
M
What is the 'unreliable tail' and how do truncation methods deal with it?

A vocabulary has tens of thousands of tokens; most are individually very unlikely, but together they can hold a meaningful share of the probability, say 10-30%. Pure sampling therefore regularly picks one of them, and one bad token derails everything after it. Truncation methods remove the tail before sampling: top-k by count, top-p by cumulative mass, min-p by a threshold relative to the top token.
M
How do temperature and top-p interact?

Implementations typically apply temperature first and then truncate on the resulting probabilities. A higher temperature flattens the distribution, so a fixed top-p admits more tokens; a lower temperature sharpens it, so top-p admits fewer. Tuning both at once is redundant for many tasks; a common practice is to set one and leave the other at a neutral value, and to check the order of operations in the library you use, because it differs.

Follow-up: What does min-p add here? — Its threshold scales with the top token's probability, so it keeps text coherent even at higher temperatures; its authors argue this lets you raise temperature for diversity without the incoherence top-p suffers.
M
A user complains that the same prompt gives different answers each time. What do you check?

Whether sampling is on (temperature above 0, or top-p below 1 with sampling); whether a seed is set and supported; whether the provider guarantees determinism (most do not, because batching and hardware vary); and whether the prompt actually differs (timestamps, retrieved documents). For tasks needing consistency, use temperature 0 or low, constrain the output format, and cache answers to identical requests.
H
Explain Holtzman et al.'s argument for nucleus sampling, with their numbers.

They generated 5,000 passages with GPT-2 Large and compared decoding methods with human text on perplexity, diversity (Self-BLEU), vocabulary distribution and repetition, plus HUSE. Maximisation methods produced text far more predictable than human writing (perplexity 1.50 greedy, 1.48 beam 16, against 12.38) and very repetitive (73.66% and 28.94%). Pure sampling was too unpredictable (22.73). Nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 came closest to human text (13.13, 0.36% repetition) and had the best HUSE score, 0.97.

Follow-up: Why not just lower the temperature? — Low temperature with top-k (k = 40, t = 0.7) gave perplexity 3.48 and 8.86% repetition: it moves towards the bland, repetitive regime rather than towards human-like text.
H
Why can temperature 0 still give different outputs across calls, and how do you handle it in evaluation?

The logits depend on floating-point arithmetic whose summation order depends on batch size, batch contents and the kernels chosen, so tiny numerical differences can flip near-tie argmaxes, and one flipped token changes everything after it. In evaluation, run each item several times or report variance, fix as much as possible (model version, hardware, batch size of one where feasible), and prefer metrics robust to small textual differences.
Follow-up: Can a server make it fully deterministic? — Yes, with batch-invariant kernels and fixed reduction orders, at some throughput cost; some inference stacks offer this as an option.
H
How would you choose decoding settings for (a) extracting fields into JSON, (b) a customer chat assistant, (c) generating test ideas?

(a) Greedy or temperature near 0, plus constrained decoding to a JSON schema so the output always parses; no repetition penalty, since keys and values legitimately repeat. (b) Moderate temperature (around 0.5-0.8) with top-p around 0.9, so responses vary naturally but stay on track; evaluate with real conversations. (c) Higher temperature (around 1.0) with top-p or min-p to keep it coherent, and sample several candidates, then deduplicate or rank. In all cases fix and log the settings and check them with task metrics, not intuition.
H
How do decoding choices affect benchmark results such as pass@k?

pass@k estimates the probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes the tests, so it depends directly on sampling diversity: greedy decoding gives one answer and pass@k cannot exceed pass@1, while higher temperature lowers pass@1 but can raise pass@10 or pass@100. Similarly, self-consistency (sample many reasoning chains and take the majority answer) needs diverse samples. Comparisons between models are only meaningful at the same, reported decoding settings, ideally each model's best.

sum: The whole RAG pipeline from ingestion to cited answer: chunking arithmetic, keyword and dense retrieval, hybrid fusion and reranking worked by hand, context assembly under a token budget, the places it breaks, and how to evaluate retrieval and answers separately.
